VIVO is something of the vegetable about an epitaph. It is a tomb motto. ME (just introduced)--" What a very homely man that gentleman near the piano is, Mrs. Hob- son." Mrs. Hobson—" Why, that is Mr. Hobson." He (equal to the occasion)--" Oh, indeed! How true it is, Mrs. llobson, that the homely men always get the prettiest wives." "YES, it may be angel cake," said Jones, who had been persuaded by his best girl to test her culi- nary abilities, "but for the last two nights since I tasted it, I've seen more little devils, hobgoblins, snakes, hyenas, and wild cats, than would crowd - a seven-storey pandemonium." "I SHALL be happy," said an expiring husband to hi a wife, who was weeping most dutifully by the bedside, "if you will only promise not .to marry that object of my unceasing jealousy, your cousin Charlcs.""Maiie yourself easy, 'love," said the expectant widow, "I am engaged to his brother." PROFESSOR HUXLEY holds that an acre of good fishing.ground will yield more food in a week than an acre of the best land w ill produce in a year. Huxley evidently never tried catching fish himself. If he had he would know that one fish to each square mile of water is about the average now-a- day s. LITTLE Dick—" I am so glad to have a new little brother now. He and sister and I make three, don't we r Mamma—" Yes, dear; but what of that 7" Dick—" Well, there's only two drum- sticks to a chicken, and one of us will get some other part now. I'll be the one sometimes. I'm tired of drura-sticks." Bixsics.—" Held on! What's your hurry I" Jinks—" Nearly driven to death. Half a bushel of letters to answer this morning and no one to help do it." "What has become of that pretty girl type- writer you Lad ?" " She's no use any more. She went and got married." "You don't say so. Whom did she marry AT a debating club the question was discussed, whether there is more pleasure in the possession or the pursuit of an object. "Mr. President," said an orator, "suppose I was courting a gal, and she was to run away, and I was to run after her, wouldn't I be happier when I catch'd her than when I was run- lag after her 7" A FARMER travelling in a foreign land for the first time, becoming somewhat anxious about the condition of his live stock, telegraphed home :—"ls things all right at the barn John Breen." His stable boy, whose conversation was proverbially laconic, immediately telegraphed back: —"John Breen,—Things is. Robert." REGINALD—" Papa, can I have a piece of mince- - pie '1" "You may if you will promise not to tell mamma that I gave it to you." (Pie is devoured in silence.) Reginald—" Please can I have some more?" Papa (sternly)—" No more, sir!" Reginald (after a pause)—" If you don't let me I shall tell mamma.', He got it. Reclres.—To make a lemon drop: let it fall off the table. To make a stomach cake: use plenty of unripe fruit. To make a (n)ice (s)cream : stick a pin in the baby. To make pastry neatly: have everything in apple-pie order. To make cats-sup: give them milk. To make a nice pickle; hunt in a drawer for something in the dark. AN honourable anecdote has been told of Queen Elizabe.h. When she came to the crown, a knight, who previously had insolently behaved to her, be- sought her pardon, suspecting to be sent to the Tower. She replied, "Do you not know that we are descended of the lion, whose nature is not to harm or prey upon the mouse, or any other such small vermin 2" A HEAD of a household, whom fashion alone forced to the opera and to the concert-room, was (nap asked why he subscribed to a certain series of concerts which were remarkable for their dryness. "You do not appear to be much amused," said the Inquirer. "I am not—far from it; in fact, these performances bore me dreadfully, and send me to sleep." "Then why do you come? Why do you subscribe 7" "Well, only for the sake of the ex- quisite pleasure I feel immediately each concert is over." A SCOTCH clergyman was one day catechising his flock in the church. The bedral, or church-officer, being somewhat ill-read in the Catechism, thought it best to keep a modest place near the door, in the hope of escaping the inquisition. But the clergy- man observed, and called him forward. "John," said he, "what is baptism I" "Ou, sir," answered John, scratching his head, "ye ken, it's just sax- pence to me, and fifteenpence to the precentor." Flips Dr. Johnson, in his tour to the Hebrides, visited St. Andrews, he was shown over the library. The then librarian had been exhibiting some of his rare literary treasures. "Have you got," asked Johnson, "such and such a book?" "No, sir, we have not. It is a very expensive book, and, I fear, beyond the means at our command." "Oh," said, he, "you'll get it by degrees "—alluding to the habit which then prevailed of selling degrees. H.--It is no use talking, Mary. The Bible is a history of men. Women are mentioned only inci- dentally as they had influence on the actions of men. The book says very little about women compared to what it does about men. W. (musingly) —You may be right after all, John, now when I come to think of it. There is one thing, at any rate, it says about men that it does not say about women. H. (smiling)—' thought you would come to your senses, Mary. What is it the book says about men that it doesn't say about women? W. (placidly) It says, "All men are liars." Then the husband arose and put on his hat and went out to see what kind of a night it was. A WELL-KNOWN Connecticut clergyman had a deacon who insisted upon leading the singing at the prayer meetings. He was a great blunderer, and he sang all the melancholy tunes he could think of. The hymn was given out— "I love to steal awhile away." The deacon began "I love to steal" to Mear, when he broke down. He started with Dundee, "I love to steal." The third time he commenced and broke down, when the pastor arose and gravely said, "I am sorry for our brother's propensity—will some brother pray 7" KOSCIUSKO MURPHY'S finances are not in a flourishing condition. He, however, managed to scrape together money enough to buy a ticket for the play. While he was looking at the performance a man right behind him said:—" Your shabby old hat annoys me very mach; I can't see the perform- ances," " Shake' " said Murphy, turning around and extending his hand. "I thought I was the only man that was annoyed by the shabbiness of that hat, but it seems that I've got a fellow-sufferer." "1 Ant an agnostic!" remarked a young man, in swelling accents. "And an agnostic is what?" inquired an elderly gentleman. "An agnostic," replied the fresh youth, in a manner expressive of his pity for his interlocutor's ignorance—" An agnostic is a fellow, you know, who isn't sure of anything." "I see," replied the old gentleman. • " But how does it happen that you are sure you are :an agnostic 7" Mr. Spurgeon, addressing his stu- dents, said this term was a new invention, but 'lrlng the ebvious derivation of the word they might- use for an agnostic the older and more familiar name of an Ignoramus! A GOOD story is told of Judge Kent, the well- known American jurist. A man was indicted for burglary, and the evidence on the trial showed that his burglary consisted in cutting a hole through a tent in which several persons were sleeping, and then inserting his head and arm through the hole and abstracting several articles of value. It was claimed by his counsel that, inasmuch as he never actually entered into the tent with his whole body he had not committed the offence charged, and must therefore be discharged. Judge Kent, in reply to this plea, told the jury that if they were -not satisfied that the whole man was involved in the crime they might bring in a verdict of guilty against as much of him as was thus involved. The jury, after a brief consultation, found the right arm, the right shoulder, and the head of the prisoner g-uilty of the offence of burglary. The judge sentenced the right arm, the right shoulder, and head to imprisonment with hard labour in the State prison for two years, remarking that, as to the rest of the man's body, he might do with it what he pleased. The Dean of Norwich, says the "Sunday School Chrdnicle;""has expressed his intention of becoming a district visitor in one of the poorest parishes of ..the city, where he is told that bricks will be hurled. at him, to which he replies, "All right; that's the place for me."

Lady Anne Blink with her husband and (laugh- ' ter, have, says" Irish Ltfe;' adopted the mannere and customs of the Arabs, having permanently pitched their tents on the border of the Egyptian desert, and in their food and dress conforming to the usages of the natives.

-- Mrs. Olive Washburn, of San Francisco, is about I to devote the bulk of her fortune to the founding of a Nationalist Colony in California. Bellamy's "Looking Backward" theories are to be followed here, and all people of good moral character will be admitted, irrespective of religious belief. Over `.20,000 will be spent in buildings, and improve- ments. •

Mr. Lidderdale, the governor, of the Bank of Eng- I land, who carried the City safely through the reeent crisis, is a Scotchman. He is a native of Castle Douglas, and has for some years been a merchant in London, largely engaged in foreign trade. The moment he heard of the embarrassment of the firm 1 of Parings he saw the situation, and took bold and far reaching measures for the purpose of averting a general panic.

Mrs. Annie Besant has just resigned her member- ship of the Fabian Society, and theosophy gains at the,the expense of social democracy. Most people don't know enough about the former to tell why it is out cf harmony with the latter. By way of com- pensation for the loss, the Fabians have, during the last fortnight, recruited three times as many mem- bers as ever in the same time before. The essays are still selling at the rate of about three hundred a week.

The Jewish custom of wearing the hat at the re-, ligious rites was a great boon to Mr. Gladstone at Lady Rosebery's funeral on Tuesday. The weather was extremely cold, and exposure to the air during the walk through the cemetery and at the grave would have been nothing less than dangerous to a man turned eighty. But as it was he got through the ceremony without physical inconvenience, though of course his feelings were profoundly stir- red by sympathy far the bereaved husband and the little motherlessboys.

Count Julius Karolyi died on Sunday at Buda- Pesti). at the age of 58, of cancer on the tongue. He managed to keep his complaint a secret from every- body, even his family, to the very last. Shortly be- fore his death he was reconciled to his brother. Gabor, with whom he had not exchanged a word for 23 years. Count Julius was the bead of the house of Karolyi, and was in his time the finest man in all Hungary. He was skilled in all manly sports, and was most popular. He leaves two sons and a daughter.

Tke passing of the Address in reply to the Speech frond the Throne on the first night of the opening of Parliament is an event unknown for fifteen years But it is a return to the ancient order of things, the desuetude of which Mr. Gladstone, on Tlesday night, lamented. Previous to the rise of the Home Rule party it was the usual custom, except where a motion challenging confidence in the Government was moved, for the debate on the Address to be con- fined to speeches from the two Front Benches, and the Address was usually agreed to in good time for members to get off for dinner.

The Rev. J: P. Bannin, who mist in the Italian Church on SunAroir oy denouncing Mr. Parnell frem the pipit, is a priest of 15 years' standing, having been ordained in 1875. There is a seeming anomaly in the fact of an Irish-born priest like Father Bannin being rector of the Italian Church, but it is a mistake to suppose that that ornate place of worship is attended exclusively by Italians. On the contrary, there is hardly an Italian to be seen amongst the large congregations that assemble there at eleven and seven on Sundays to hear the splendid music rendered by the choir.

Mr. W. Beckett, M.P., who met hi's death under sad conditions on Monday, was little heard of in the House of Commons. Mr. Beckett was the head of the Yorkshire banktng firm of W. Beckett and Co. He was Chairman of the Yorkshire Conservative Newspaper Company, a director of the Great North- ern and the London and south Western Railway Companies, Besides his railway and banking busi- ness Mr. Beckett took an interest in Church matters and agriculture. His elder brother is Lord Grim- thorpe—of which title he was the heir. His son, Mr. E. W. Beckett, is Tory member for Whitby. Mr. Beckett was sixty-two.

Dr. Koch, according to the Berlin correspondent of the Daily News," is not an early riser. His us- ual hour is nine o'clock. He takes a long time to dress, as he is very particular, and makes his toilet at once for the day. Instead of drinking coffee for breakfast Dr. Koch takes a thick soup made of Hour, into which he breaks an enormous quantity of toasted black bread. After this simple meal he re- pairs to his laboratory, which he does not leave till two o'clock. At this hour dinner is served. it con- sists of soup, roast meat, and a light pudding. He takes his soup after the pudding.

On the stroke -of three a white horse frour the livery stables stands before the door. On this animal the Professor trots terisklv of ta the Thier- garten. This ride, for which be wears a rather peculiar riding suit, and an enormous slouch hat, lasts about an hour. The rest of his time till eight in the evening is devoted solely to study. At the supper, as sumptuous as the dinner is simple, there must always be three or foal- sorts of meat.- Dir. Koch drinks during his meal large quWtities of soda water. After his supper,.and sometimes dur- ing his supper, he receives the visit of friends and acquainances with whom he remains in lvvely con- versation till midnight. Then lie goes replied, bn when there reads all sorts of political and scientifric• magazines and papers' as ho has not euffictentr leisure time during the day.

George Rice, the Taunton signalman, has been finally acquitted, as might have been expeeted. No thanks, however, to Justice Granthani, who seems, to have done his best to impress the jury with the view that the man's mistake necessarily involved consequences of a criminal nature.. Even Justice. Grantham, however, together with the jury, the grand jury, the coroner's jury, and everyone else who has expressed an opinioia on the case, agrees that the worst culprits are the Great Western Rail— way Company. The true moral of the Taunton accident is that either a stricter control by the Board of Trade over rail way administration is im- peratively required, or else that the criminal respon— sibility for" accidents". should rest on managers , and directors as well as signalmen and engine— drivers. -

The associations for supplying starving school children with free meals have oombined,and, as the tondo Schools Dinner Association, make an appeal for support—signed by such men as the Duke of Westminster, the Lord Mayer, Mr. Mundella, and Mr. Diggle. They only ask for .£1,500,t0 meet the requirements of the coming season. This is a small , sum, but it is capable when wisely expended et fill- ing many empty stomachs. At a penny a bead it would mean three hundred and sixty thousand meals. Last year meals were supplied at the costs of '9ld. pet meal. The dinners are distributed under the immediate supervision of the local managers and teachers, and care is taken that only the most deserving children are helped. ContributiOAS should be sent to Lord Kinnaird,treasurer of th,o fund, 1; Pall-mall.

Mr. Wemyss Reid's "life,- Letters, and Friend- ships of Richard Monekton Mines, first Baron Houghton," will be in the hands of the public in a few days. The following is one of the best stories that has yet been told of Sydney Smith :—Rogers, corpulent, leering, ungainly, with the complexion of a lemon—once asked Sydney Smith's advice, under the following circumstances. He thought it was his duty to go down to.posterity on canvass ; more- over, by doing so a poor artist could be helped, and in away which would not hurt his pride. But Rogers knew that he was an ugly fell4w, so he asked Sydney Smith to suggest the mostbecoming i posture n which to sit for his portrait. 3 The viv- acious canon solemnly looked the author of" Plsig- Isures of Memory "up and down, and then he saWl, in most serious and critical tones, "Well, Rogers, there is a very expressive attitude we clergy. use in first getting up into the pulpit which might suit you very well. We no this"—covering his face with his hands.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29. 1890.

While we support the uresent appeal, we can- not regard the system of tree dinners, as at present organised, as permanent. As we stated the other day, the Paris Town Council supplies the children of the poor with a free meal a day, in order , that they may be able to benefit from free education. „rodliCation cannot feed on an empty stomach. In some German towns free breakfasts are also supplied to necessitous children. When we have free educa- tion our municipalities will have,to face this ques- tion of free meals.

In the Queen's Bench Division on Monday, the case of De Souzo v. Cobden, an action to recover penalties from the defendant cameon, for having acted as County Councillor, although disqualified from so acting. The Prosecuting counsel explained that plaintiff did not wish to put the penalties in his pocket, and he had no personal feeling against Miss Cobden, but he thought it [ intolerable that a lady, being ineligable, should act.

THE HAMPSTEAD TRAGEDY. On Monday, at the Old Bailey, London, the Recorder, in charging the Grand Jury, said there were numerous cases in the calandar in which life had been lost or en- dangered by violence sufficient to justify a criminal charge, but the most serious was the one with the circumstances of which the Grand Jury would be per- fectly familiar from the report ,s in the public prints. The name of the accused was Mary Eleanor Pearcy, and she was charged with the murder of a young woman named Phabe Hogg and her baby. There were overwhelming reasons why the prisoner should be placed on her trial for the commission of this offence.
The Grand jury at the Central Criminal Court on Tuesday returned a true bill against Mary Eleanor Wheeler, alias Pearcey, for the murder of Mrs. Hogg and her child.

div.head: LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS.
div.p: LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS.
By L. GORDON RYLA-NDS, BA. (Continued.)

The epistolary warfare in the columns of the "Warrington Guardian "produced much polemical writing of considerable ability, but the letters which attracted the greatest amount of attention were those which appeared over the signature of' Oliver West," and soon became generally known as 'the 01

ever West' letters. These letters appeared at fret- , , quent intervals throughout the year 1856, comment- ing freely upon municipal Matters, and vigorously satirizing any Rarrington public man who seemed to be impelled by jealousy, personal feeling, ambi- tion,love of notoriety, or party spite, rather than by a desireto promote the best interests of the town. Personalities were carefully avoided, but many ' prominent inen who had been guilty of mean or spiteful conduct in public matters had their actions held up to public scorn in a way that made them writhe. Nearly every one in Warrington was asking who could be the author of these letters. Some of those attacked pretended not to mind; others went about vowing vengeance, and inquiring for the author. The excitement became very great; several names were mentioned, and one or two leading men were charged with the authorship; but the secret was known to -very few, and was perfectly well kept. The Editor of the "Guardian," even though an action for libel was instituted against him by one man who had been most unmercifully ridiculed, yet refused to disclose the name of the author ; and, however near the truth men's guesses and suspicions may havelbeen, the secret is as much a secret at this day as it was 40 years ago. As the writers are now dead, there is no indiscretion in saying that these letters were the work of more than one man, and that Mr. Peter Rylands, Mr. J. G. MeMinnies, and the Rev. Ralph Allen Mould were the joint authors. Mr. Rylands was suspected at the time of having a hand in the production of the letters, but it was impossible for such suspicions to be confirmed. On the 15th of October, 1856, the new market was opened. Before this time the Warrington Market-place had been simply an open Square; now this gquare wao covered ever with a shed, and a new shed and convenieut Market Hall built adjoining it. For some years the question of a market had been discussed in Warrington. In 1852 a scheme had been proposed which met with I much opposition, and had to be abandoned. In the fol- lowing year, however, Mr. Rylands again took the questiun up and succeeded in getting a Warrington Improvement and Market Act passed by Parliament. A committee of the Town Council was then formed, of which Mr. Rylands was elected chairman; but then arose questions of cost, site, size, form, &c. Some men kept Iraising discussions OR side issues to disguise their hos- tility to the whole scheme; some obstinately, insisted I upon their own pet plan, and would hear of no other; and some, by, advocating a niggardly and cheese-paring policy, would have spoilt the new market altogether. However, by the employment of much tact, and with the assistance of other public-spirited men, Mr. Rylands I brought the matter to a triumphant conclusion. The I foundation-stone was laid in October, 1855, and the market was opened amid universal acclamation a year later. In this year a Police Bill'was passed by Parlia appointing In2.,spectors ' -0,,,,0ri0-prwvrantglhai

, town whose force wag up to a certain fixed strength should receive a Govern- ment grant in aid. Colonel Woodford, the Inspector under whose supervision the Warrington Police Force came, sent a letter to the Watch Committee representing to them that the town was much under-policed, and recommending that the number of the force should be increased from 11, at which it then stood, to 24. Mr.

Rylands raised a discussion in the Town Council on this letter, but the Watch Committee refused to take any action. In May, 1864 Mr. Rylands again returned to the charge with a motion that Colonel Woodford' s sug- gestion be acted upon,. and supported his proposal in a long and closely-argued speech ; but after a discussion, which lasted two days, the motion was lost by 21 votes to 5. Mr. Rylands kept raising this question at intervals, and his argument, backed up•by constant complaints of rfnchecked depredations, began to produce some effect, so that when in January, 1883, Colonel Woodford again drew attention to the inadequacy of the Police Force, it was clear that a good many of the old opponents of an increase were beginning to waver. In Pecember of that year the Watch Committee themselveacameforward with a recommendation for the appointment of one more inspector and two constablea„.which was endorsed by the Council. The force now amounted to 15, which was, however, still far too few for agarge and rapidly increas- ing town like Warrington • but public opinion was grow- ing, new members were :being elected to the Council, and in March, 1864, Mr. Rylanclihad tte satisfaction of carrying a motion of no-confidence in the Watch Com- mittee "by 18 votes to 2. AI new Committee was appointed which at once recommended am increase of the police force to 29 men in all ; this-proposal was adopted by the Council, and thus Mr. Rylands won the battle which he had been fighting for nearly years, and to his exertions Warrington at length owed the advantage of an efficient body of police. Meanwhile the town had been iturnanywaysimproved; a Cemetery had been opened,. a Public- MR hod been built, the Museum and Free Library had been completed, and other public works of greaterror less utility had been I carried out, in all whieb improvements Mit. Rylands took an active part. In 1859 he had been nnanimouslyinvited by the Liberal I party in Warrington to stand as the Liberal candidate in opposition to Mr. Greenall, who - had represented the borough since 1847 ; but was obliged to decline owing to the pressure of business engagements. Prom, that time, I however, he continued to take an active part intim dis- cussion of public questions,. addressing meetings on various political subjects both in, Waraington and else- where, and in 1583, when he was againasked to, stand, he forts-id himself in a position to consent to do- so. Mr.. Greenail had then held unehallenged possession of the seat for 2/ years and the eandidaturoof Rylands excited much bitterness of feeling among the Tory party' in theborough. As the conteatiaroceeded and die-Tories ' began to perceive that Mr. Rylands would :be a very dangerous opponent, their bitterness -greatly increased, ' and an speeches at their meetings very strong expressions began to be made use of whieh'provelted retaliation on , the part of their opponents, and thus as the election day drew near party strife in Warrington grew more intense and more envenomed than ever-before-or share:. As the ' conyietien was- more and more born. in ammo the minds of the leaders of the Tory party thattbere wash very, strong probability of their losing the election ,they became like man striking out at random, and so long as they could only succeed in hitting their adversaries they were not particular as to the fairness of their blows.. Perhaps he most discreditable of their tatics was ties publication in the "Warrington Guardian ""of a series of lettOrs as advertisements, Med with-coarse abuse of Mr. Ryland§ and his leading supporters. The two great questions on which the election was fought where the Disestablisliment of the Irish Church,. and the Ballot. These miserable letters, which were signed "'Benjamin Darby,"made no attempt whatever. to argue out these great questions or others- with regard to which the Liberal and Tory parties were at variarma. There was no-discussion of principal'in therm. They attacked not measures but men. The feet that Mr. Rylands had aresed to be a Dissenter, and become a Churchmaa, was turned to hisdiscredit ; the amount of money he-had subscribed to local chari- ties. etc_ was ferreted out and compared with that sub- scribed by the wealthiest men in the-town an order to make him appear mean. In every possible way, pre- vious actions of his were misrepresented and placed in, an odious light. It is, however, pleasant to think that: such contemptible tactics fa.tied' to effect their pure-

pose. Of t the nominatlotiday and the clay of the election the excitement in the streets ofiVi'arrington was intense, aad order was with difficulty maintained. Matters came to a crisis about a quarter of an hour before the close of the poll, when a 1111M0117 was rapidly circuhted among the Liberals that a number of working men belonging to their party had been made (bunk and shut up in a yard by the opposite party. A body of Liberals went to the place indicated, but were stepped at the gate by a band of rough men armed with bludgeons, who succeeded in preventing an entrance being made, and seriously injured three of those who, attempted to enter." The poll closed at four o'clock, when according to the Conservative figures, Mr. Greenall hada majority of 78, and according to the Liberal figures, a majority of seven. It was scarcely possible for anyone to doubt that Mr. Gieenall was really elected, and the night was spent by- the Tories in frantic demonstrations of joy. The morn- ing, however, brought them an unpleasant shock; forthe Mayor announced that according to his ofScial polling book, Mr. -Rylands had received 1,984 votes and Mr. Greenall 1,957, giving Mr. Rylands a majority a 27. div.head: AN M.P. KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.
div.p: AN M.P. KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.

Mr. Wm. Beckett, M.P., for the Bassetlaw division of Nottinghamshire, met with his death on Sunday by be- ing knocked down and cut to pieces by a train. Mr. Beckett arrived at IN imborne, on the London and South, Western Railway, by the two p.m. train from London, and went out of the station. He was seen shortly after- wards in the drive which leads to Canford Minor, the residence of Lord Wimborne. The drive passes under the railway, and between this and the station is an iron girder bridge spanning the river Stour. Later on Mr. Beckett appears to have got on to the line to walk back to the station. He was seen on. the bridge referred to just as the 350 train from Bournemouth came up. The engine passed him, but his hat was blown off, and in trying to recover it he was dragged under the train, it is supposed by the force of the wind. He must have met with his death instantaneously. His body was taken to the Railway Hotel, where it now lies. The identity of the deceased was first established by the name," W. Beckett. Esq., M.P.," on the collar of his coat. There-was also in one of the pockets a pass for the London and South-Western Railway bearing his name, he being a director of the Company, and among other money ther3 was a £lOO note and a £5 note, the latter bearing the stamp of the Bachelor's Club.

WARRINGTON v. BLACKLEY IST.

This match was played at Blackley on Saturday last In miserable weather on a wet and swampy ground which was more like a combination of a mud heap and ploughed field than a Lacrosse ground, thus anything like reliabls play was impossible and the game was of a ragged nature scrimmaging being the principle feature. In pouring rain Bennett and Milner faced at about 3.40 p.m. and thelatter got the ball at the face the home team quickly looked dangerous but owing to the small ground the attack was very crowded and any attempt at combination was useless. The play was very even in the first ten minutes.the balltravelling from end to end, and the play was fast and furious. The visitors point and goalkeeper kept their charge intact for a long time, but at last W. A. Gordon scored for Blackley. This made the Warringtoniara liven up a bit. Bennett came down the field with a spurt and passed to Smith whose shot went wide of the post. J. Gordon threw up the field Bardsley secured and ran cibwn the wing and scored. The game had barely been recommenced when Garnett getting possession transferred to Williamson, who had hard lines in not scoring the ball going just outside the. ,post, the score at half time being, two to nil, in favour of ,Blackley. The second' half was, in favour a the home 'team, the visitors defence being kept hard at work. It was, a dismal exhibition and there was no regret when time was called.-Blackleirr,—

div.p: JACK SLADEN'S FIGHT.

A NAVVY STORY. Jack looked at the fire awhile, then turned to me and said: "There's a thing I never told a soul, that I've a mind to tell you now, and have had a mind to tell you before." "Tell me, Jack," I answered. "Its a nasty thing," said Jack, "and maybe it'll shock you. You must know that about forty years ago I was working down in Devonshire, and there was a man there named Fennel. He was a big, fine man, but a bully and a blackguard. Well, one day he was ill-usinga poor woman that lived with him as his wife, when I came tip and saw him, so I went for him, and we rolled into a ditch, and the police came up and he was took up. But that wasn't the end of it. I thought he was a cur to batter a woman about, and I went evidence against him and got him six months. He was main wild about it, and says he Sure as God's me judge,' says he, 'l'l/ do for you, Jack Sladen, when I get out.' And I says, All right,' I says, 'l'i yer man.' "But before he came out I'd a good offer for Canada, and I took it. I took it, and went to work for a man that had a big farm and corn mills out in Canada West, and I was doing very well there, and likely for doing better, when an awful thing hap- pened me. "There had been heavy rains, and some of the country was flooded, and one night I was taking a mug of ale at the store, when the boss came up on his pony, and called me out. He said,one of the dam walls was going, and be, was off 'to collect a gang of men to stop it, and Go;says he, ' down to the old mill and see how many picks and shavels we have in store.' And with that he rode off, and away I went for the old mill. "It was a horrible dirty night, and the road ankle deep in muck. I blundered along till I got to the old mill and I left the gate open and went in. As I was going up the steps I heard the gate swing.l I stopped to listen, but there was no other sound; so, thinks I, It was the wind,' and I went up and lit the pine torch and counted the to'ols and came' down to the second storey, which was an empty room ; and there I set the torch in a. stanchion of the wall wail(' I filled my pipe. "I had fill'ed the pips and was about to light it , when, looking across the' room to the ladder-hole, 'there I see elace. a_white face, level with the floor, .61414:116..-eyverrctsed on me—and that face was th( of Dick Fennel, and no other. "I was a bit taken, you may guess, for I thought Dick' was in England, and I half feared I'd seen a ghost. But I spoke up, and says, If ;that's Dick Fennel, why, Dick come forrard ;' and •with that he comes up the ladder and stands looking at me with the flicker of thertorch, and making his Natures change, and the rain,beating ()tithe winders Outside sounding like the pattering feet of 's million little devils. Speak, ye fool' says I. 'What are you doing here?' Then Fennel steps a pans-or two nearer and says ha-,' Jack Sladen, he says, I've found you, and I wen't lase yen-1 swear be that.' 'Otir says I. Andbwhat do you want of my?' And he grins a horrid grin and says,,' E want yourlife of yea Sladen, and be 2tod I'll have•it.." "'Well, I saw it was no uswto argue. It threw away my pipe, and I rubbed my:shoes on the floor. Fennel laughed. No flghting'll, save yo', says be; I'm going to kill yer„ like the dog:you are,' and he drew oat, a pistol, and be stepped forward, as he coe' cl it. It was well for me became so clbse to make sum_of hiSaiM. As he coelMd the pistol I put my weight on my left foot, aad; as he raised the pisteki kicked up my night foot us-quick as Leould. "Dams just in time. The bullet( struck the wall abont seven feet up, and straight behind me:. The pistel,fiew out of his hand and felbunder the win- dow.. I looked after it. It was a, single barrel. Youpshould have brought a revolver,' I saysl. and slipeafr ray coat. 'lt don't signify,' says he, Ti shall have-the pleasure of straggling youf instead.' Then he ot'Ywith his coat, and we fell to work. "we was a good match. Both over six feet high, both of an age, both in training, and ,both scienced men- He was about an inch the taller,- I was a bit the stiffer, but he was big-boned, so. it makee no odds.- " I feinted with the left and he Ibt out with the right ;but I ducked and got round him Then he feinted and we both countered. Efln got it on the nose,ligot it under the chin; . and •both, of us went downs , " Vire; was up again in a creak z. and :flew at each I other like wolves. It;was- the hardest, quiekest, savagest fight ever I Was in at. We. fought up and downbattering each others faces tcepelp, banging each other against the walla, zoning over and over and fibbing like fiends all the time; until after about five minutes we both had to 'pause for breath a and stood looking at each other in, the • torchlight—the rain pattering at the winders all the. while and the watt', gurgling and hissing down belbw the' floor we stood on. " I shall never forget that' moment.. Our clothes was torn to shreads, our faces cut to, ribbons, the blood was streaming all overam. Nunes face was all red blood, only his teeth showed white: Ais eyes I couldn't see; indeed, I was needy blind. We nevarsaid a.word. We understood each otherr quite. I knew that Fennel would kill me if he couldt. and I hadrgot my blood up, and I felt that Eshould kill him if Leould. He made the first move. He tried to get at the pistol under the winder, but h sprang at him ankhe had no time. We clenched, and for about a minute we both strained every nerve and sinew in the wrestle. It was awful." Seek, as he told me his story,.hal got very much exited. His huge fist lay clenched on the table, his eyes stared wildly tit me. II felt very glad that I had not been either 'one of the combatants in that fight in time old mill. The end• of it," said Jack,. 'came like this. niinel had driven me back-near to-the winider, and I,was trying all I could to, bend him over, when I felt him grip my knife,. I. had a knife in a hip pocket, bur had been too- fair a man to, draw it on him. The handle had worked up in the scuffie,and ;he took it and stabbed me in the-back. The point' Istruck my brace buckle and scored my ribs. He .I.,ifted his arm again,-andd)mado a big effort. I set imy teeth in his left wrist, and I put myfootagainsk 'his stomach, and kicked like a mule. He went fly- ing backwards, and fedi with a great crash on the floor, I nearly falling on him; and as he fell'"-- Jack's voice here is &mere hoarse whisper—" as he fell the floor opened under him, and he vanished. There was a crash, anda splash, and the torch went out, and I was standing alone in the dark, on. the edge of a great pit with the water rushing amongst , the piles below, and carrying Fennel's corpse along ' with it." Jack leans back in his seat, and wipes his forehead with' his hand. "He was dead and gone," says Jack; "nobody never saw him, again, and nobody in Oat place ever saw me again, for I cleared out that night, and as soon as I was fit to travel. I set off back to England." Jack pours out some more whisky. "Twas the worst fight lever saw," he says, "and the worst night's work / ever did; but it was him or me for it, and his death was accidental. I never knew there was a trap in the mill floor until he went through it, and it might just as well have been me as him." Seeing Jack so concerned, I hastened to assure him that he was in no way to blame, and, what with my own.eloquence and his own whisky and tobacco, .I left him a fairly good humour; and now I will leave you—and I hope in the same state.— From the Sunday Chronsa

THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
. OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANI7B COBB, ht.
CHAPTER VI.
DBOkB TEE EMPEROR. "Is he dead ?" asked Ririe, starting quickly for- ward.

"Hold, my son," uttered the monk, laying his hand upon the young man's arm. "Surely you have nothing to fear. It was none of your work—no more than if you had run your sword to the heart of a wild beast that had attacked you." "But I did not touch his heart," quickly returned the youth. "I was careful of that. I would have struck him upon the head with the flat of my sword, but I feared I might break his skull." "He is not dead yet," answered the surgeon, as Ruric pressed forward and asked the question a second time. "He has only fainted from the shock of the blow, coupled with his own fears and pas- sions."
"But will he die 2" Runic asked, kneeling down by .the fallen man's side.
-" I cannot yet tell," the doctor said, at the same ime wiping the blood away, which was flowing

"But why not probe the wound now?" suggested the monk. "Now is the best time, for the place is not yet inflamed; and while he is thus insensible he will be free from pain." The surgeon at once saw the truth and propriety of this,and he proceeded to act upon the suggestion. Having selected a probe which appeared applicable, he examined the wound. Runic watched him eagerly, and with a painful expression. 1I do not think this wound is mortal," the sur- gegn reported, as he carefully felt his eway along the course the steel had taken. "It has passed below the right lung, and only severed some of the smaller blood-vessels. I think, with proper care, he may recover." "Thank God !" fervently ejaculated Runic, with his bands clasped. "But why so anxious?" asked Urzen. "You were ready enough to accept his challenge." Aye---else you would have called me coward," returned the gun-maker, with a flashing eye. "had I refused to meet him that fatal word would have

met ine at every turn. I knew that such a man as he was no, cope for me at any game where strength of arm and sleight of hand were required- So I meant to disarm, him, and then give him up, his life, be- lieving that such a move would end the combat. You know how I labored to spare, him. But I could not. Yet I would not have the life of a fellow-being—a countryman—upon my hands in such a quarrel- My father died fighting for his country—and so would I die if my death must come frotothe hand of man; but to die thus would be a curse upon my name, and to inflict such death upon another would be a curse in my memory.' _ _ _

" I believe you, my son," the monk sal& "Only if the Count dies you shall not allow such feelings as you mention to overcome you. In no,way are you to blame for thiAs," "True, father—you speak truly," added the sur- geon. "The-young man has acted most nobly, and no blame can,be attached to him."

Runic seemed somewhat relieved by these assur- ances, and having seen the Count's wound dmssed, and assisted in bearing the insensible form to the sledge, he tooltAlaric'eproffered arm and proseeded to his own testa. "Who is that monk?.'" asked the lieutenant, as ;they entered their sledge; only know that he is called Valdimir," re- 'turned Ifutlc..—rhave-mmiky-Goan. him once before.

Have you everseen him ere -this ? " • - I " Yes—several times about our barracks. He has been there when some of our poor fellows have been sick and dying. He seems to be a good-hearted man, and I should judge, quite intelligent." "I agree with you there," our hero said. "-I think he js a good man; but there is nevertheless a' mystery about him. which, I cannot solve. Hie countenance is familiar to me, and yet I cilium tell where, nor when I have seen him.' , , "Aye,?' added'Alario quickly and eagerly; "that isiorecisely the case with me. lam very surethat /have seen that man under different circumstances. And others of our company have thought the same."

The two men watched the-movements of the monk while they thus spoke,. and they noticed that he entered his sledge and drove off towards Borodino. "'Rune," said the -lieutenant, after they had rid- den some little distance,. and at the same time gazing wonderingly into,his-empanion's face, "you handle the sword like a magician. By my soul,Pd give all I own at this present moment—my com- mission and ail—if P could handle the sword a& yon can." 'I do understand the weapon passing well,l re- turned the youth modestly;: ". but I have worked hard to gain the science: "Ah—tis not all science," he officer added. "That wondrous strength of yours is a host in itself."' "-And yet," said Rnric; "I have seen weaker men than myself who would overcome me easily—or, at least, who might overcome tne." "-But they were not in this city," suggested Orsa, with a peculiar shake of thehead. . "'True Alaric. lam not iwthe habit of mention- ing.my ewn powers ;;but yet I may say that there is no man in Moscow who is-my superior in the use of any sort of offensive arrns.7 The lieutenant readily admitted the truth of this, and then the conversation turned upon the subject of the Count, and the, course he had pursued with respect to the event which had just transpired. This conversation lasted until they reached the door of Rune's residence, and having thanked his-friend for- his kindness, and expressed a hope that at some time he might have, opportunity to ireturn some adequate favour,, the gunmaker entered the house.

he widow sat in her great chair by the fire. She was pale and anxious. Tier brow was supported by her hands, and at every sound from without she would start up with a frightened expression and listen. At length the sound of bells struck upon her ear—they came nearer and nearer—and they stopped at her doer. She- would have arisen, but she could not. With her hands clasped:she bent eagerly forward, and listened with frantic-interest Soon the door opened. Surely no one but, lba would enter without knocking. She started to her feet— the inner door opened—a male form stood before , her.

" Mother !" "Ruric ! My boy! Safe !" She tottered forward and sank upon tho bosom of her noble son,and whileshe wound her arras tightly. about him, she murmured her thanks to God. By and by the widow became more calm, but still there was an earnest, eager look of fear upon her face. P-uric saw it, and knew well what it meant. "Mother,' be said, "the Count is not dead." "Nor wounded?" she uttered, quickly and eagerly. • Yes—badly. But listen: I could not help it." And thereupon he related all the circumstances con- nected with the conflict. When he had concluded, his mother pondered a few moments,, and then she said: "Surely, ray son, I will try and suffer nothing from this, even should the wicked man die. In all; you acted upon the defensive. from the first ha has only been intent on attacking you; and on the battleground he would have killed you if he could,. "Most surely he would, mother. Aye—he would' not have hesitated to stab me in the back could he have gained the opportunity. He was mad beyond all self-control, and his eagerness to kill me was only equaled by his chagrin at being overcome by one whom he had hoped easily to conquer." After this Runic went to his shop, but Paul mani- fested no great emotion upon beholding him. " You seem to take it as a matter of course that I should return alive and well," said the gun-maker with a smile. "Why—of course," returned the boy, composedly. " What would a score of such men as he be to you? Conrad Damonoff hold a sword before Runic Nevel ? No, I only smiled when I heard his challenge. I should have as soon thought of being anxious about your return from a marten hunt." Rune smiled at his boy's peculiar eagerness of ex- pression, but he felt a degree of pride in his words, nevertheless. It was towards the latter part of the afternoon that Runic was somewhat startled by seeing some of the imperial guard approaching his house; and ere long afterwards his mother came to him pale and trembling, and informed him that he was • wanted by the Emperor's officers. "Oh!" she groaned, with clasped hands, and tear- ful eyes, " they will take you from me now!' "Fear not, my mother, the youth confidently returned. "The Emperor will not blame me when he knows all the Particulars, But come—let us go
• Ruric found the officers —three of them—in tk• kitchen, and he asked them if they sought him. "We seek Runic Revel, the gun-ruaker,"zeplied the leader.
"I am the man, sir. May I know_ what is wanted?"

" Cannot you guess ? " "Why—yes. I suppose it must be on account of the duel which was fought this morning." "Exactly." "And who wants me ?" " Who should want you but the Emperor?" "Oh, they will not take my noble boy from mei cried Claudia, catching the officer by the arts. "Tell our good Emperor that Russia has taken my huir band from me—that be fell in his country's caused Tell him my boy was not to blame—" " Hush, mother," interposed Runic. "rear net yet."

"Come," said the leader. and Peter will not brook delay." "But they will not harm him !" the mother fran-P tically cried, clinging now to her son. "No,- no, my mother. Rest you easy here until I return." And then turning to the guard he addedp "Lead on, and I will follow." "Now rest you easy, my dear mother ;" and with these words Rurie gently set her back into the chair,. and then hastened out aftir the officers. •In the entry he put on his bonnet and pelisse, and then followed his conductors out to the street, where stood a double sledge, with two horses attached. " You seem to look upon the killing of a Russian nobleman as a very small affair," said one of the officers, after they had started on their way. "Is he dead then Ruric quickly asked. "The doctors think his case a critical one. But that is not the thing; you would have killed him if you could." "No, no. By heavens, 'tis not so! All who were present wilt swear that I tried to spare bun." "-Very well," returned the bfficer. "We shall see about that when we come to the palace. Perhaps you may go clear; but upon my soul. I would not willingly occupy your place." Runic cared not to argue the point with those who knew nothing about the circumstances, so be remained silent during the rest of the ride: It was near sundown when they reached the imperial palace, and. Runic was conducted at once into the Emperor's presence.
"It is growing late

- The Emperor Peter was in one of theimaller au- dience chambers, sitting. at a large table covered with purple velvet heavily wrought with gold, and upon either hand stood some of his private attend- ants. He was a yotvng man, not yet so old as Ruric by some three years, but his face already wore a mature look. His frame was soli!, but not large-- being rather slight than otherwise in physical bulk. His dress betrayed negligence and carelessness,. and 'wit:a in marked contrast with the rich garbs of his ' attendants. Such was Peter of Russia—yet .a youth —small inframe, and careless of these graces which go to.malte up the sum, of court life; but still able to bear the affairs of a great nation upon his shoulders.. Within that head worked a mighty brain, and in that bosom beat a heart thirsting more for the good of Russia than for self or kindred. Ruric saw Stephen Hrstrn and the surgeon there ; and he also saw the Duke of Tula there. He met the Duke's eye, and a peculiar sensation of fear rims through his mind as he saw the stern, threatening expression that rested upon Olga's face. " Sire," spoke the leader of those who had eon. - ducted the prisoner thither, "Ruric Nevel stands before you." " Ah,' uttered Peter, casting his eagle eye over the forms before him. " Nevel—advance." With a bold, yet modest step, Runic advanced to. the table, andwith a low bow he awaited the Em- peror's pleasure. There was a shudder perceptible. in the frames of those who wished the prisoner well? for well they knew their mighty ruler's iron will and sternness of legal purpose. (To be contimeed)

FUNERAL SERVICES.

The funeral service Lin memory of the men who lost their lives in the Serpent was held on Sunday in the- Church of Santa Maria in Jabina. The crews of the Lap- wing and the Spanish gunboat Macmahon came ashore at Camarinas, and proceeded together to the cemetery, where they rendered the last honours to the dead:: upon whose graves many wreaths have been placed. Seven more bodies have been washed ashore at Camarinas, and were buried on Saturday. The British Consul at Corunna attended the funeral, service at Camarinas. The Lapwing, after the cere- I many, saluted the Spanish flag with twenty-one guns.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR CARLLSLR.

Between four and five o'clock on Tuesday morning a. special train consieting of two carriages and an enginm. and van, conveying Mr. W. E.. Malcolm, of the Scots Greyz, and his servant, to Langhorn, on the North British line, ran off the line near Carlisle station. mrt Malcolm and his servant had arrived at Carlisle by the. Midland express,, and were being conveyed in a special train to Sir Frderick Johnstone' s residence, Wester I Hall, Dumfriesabirec The engine' a few minutes after leaving Carlisle,.left the rails and fell down an embank.- ment, the driver, _Mark Inglis % being crush to death,. and the soker's leg caushed. The carriage containing Mr. Malcolm and his servant kept the rails, encipher and the guard were uninjured. The stoker's leg was. afterwards amputated.

THE POLITICAL- CRISIS.
MR. PARNELL'S POSITION,
IfIntgATENED RETIRSMENT OF )LEL GLADST9Nt.

The Press Association is authorised to state that the eontents of the fonowing letter from Mr. Gladstone to Yr. Aim Morley were communicated to Mr. Parnell in the course of Tuesday afternoon Charlton-gardens. Nov. 24th, 1890. Mr. dear Mr. Morley,—Having arrived at a certain tconclusioa with regard to the continuance at the pre- sent moment of Mr. Parnell's leadership of the Irish party, I have seen Mr. M'Carthy on my arrival in town, and have inquired from him whether I was likely to receive from Mr. Parnell himself any commsnication on the subject. Mr. M'Carthy replied that he was unable to give me any information on the subject. I men- tioned to him that in 1882, after the terrible murder in the Phosnist Park, Mr. Parnell although totally removed from any idea of responsibility, had spontaneously written to me and offered to take the Chiltera Hun- . dreds—an offer much to his honour,but Which I thought ' it my deity to decline. While-clinging to the (hope of a communication front Mr. ParnelLto whomsoever addressed, [thought it neces- sary, viewing the arrangements for the commencement of the scssion to-morrow, to acquaint )ar. Dl‘Carthy with the conclusion at which, after using all' the means of ob- servation and reflection in my power,ll had myself ar- rived. It was that, notwithstanding the splendid ser- vicerrendered by Mr. Parnell to his country, his con- tinuance at the present moment in the leadership would • be productive of consequences disastrous in the highest degreeto the cause of Ireland. think I may be warranted in &eking you so far to espand the conclusion I have given above as to add that the continuance I speak of would not only place many hearty and effective friends of the Irish cause in a posi- tion of great embarrassment, buttwould render my re- tention of the leadership of the Liberal party, based as it has been mainly upon the prosecution of the Irish cause, • almost a nullity. This expansion of my views I begged Mr. M'Carthy to regsrd as confidential, and not 'intended for his col- leagues, if he felt that Mr. Parnell contemplated spon- taneous action; but I also begged that he would make , known to the Irish party at their meeting to-morrow afternoon that such was my conclusion, if he should find that Mr. Parnell had not in .contemplation any step of the nature indicated. I now write to you, in case Mr. M'Carthy should be unable to communicate with Mr. Parnell, as I under- stand you may possibly have an opening to-morrow through another channel. Should you have math an opening, I beg you to make known to Mr. Parnell the conclusion itself which Ihave stated in the earlier part of this letter. I have thought it tbest to put it in terms simple and direct, much as I should have desired,had it been within my power, to alleviate the personalmature of the situation. As respects the manner of conveying what my public duty has made it an obligation Is say, I rely entirely on your good feeling, tact, and judgment. Believe me sin- cerely yours, W. E. GrAnstrorm.

To the Right Hon. John Motley, M.P. The" Daily News" says :—We understand that Mr. Gladstone's letter te Mr. Motley, which was shown to Mr. Parnell on Tuesday night, contained an important postscript. In this Mr. Gladstone intimated, not ob- scurely, that if the decision ef the Irish party to retain Mr. Parnell as their leader remained unaltered, he should himself feel it necessary to reOnsider his own position, as all probability of carrying Home Rule in his 'lifetime would have disappeared. Mr. Morley and Sir William Harcourt are in , entire accord with Mr. Gladstone as to the necessity for Mr. Parnell's retirement, and the former had a piallonged Interview with the Nationalist leader at the House of Commons on Tuesday afternoon, for the purpose of urg- ing him to give way. Mr. Gladstone did notesee Mr. Yarnell on the subject, but as the evening wore on, and Mr. Parnell's determination continued apparently unshaken, the leader of the Opposition resolved to com- municate to the Press his decision in the mattes. The tenour of Mr. Gladstone's letter soon became 'known amongst the Nationalist members, and great excitement followed. Hon. gentlemen gathered in groups in the corridors and lobbies, and isensternation marked every face. After some informal -consultation of this kind, another meeting of the Irish party was called. The second meeting of the Nationalist party was held in the conference-room of the House of Commons, at nine 'clock. It was not so largely atttended as the first. A copy of Mr. Gladstone's letter to Mr. Morley was read to the gathering, and considerable discussion took place in reference to its contents. All present admitted that after such a pronouncement the gravity of the situation had increased tenfold. Mr. Parnell did not remain st St. Stephens long after the commencement of the debate on the Address, and he was consequently absent from the meeting. For this reason, it was decided to postpone any decisive action for the present. The copy of Mr. ;Glad- stone's letter was sent to Mr. Parnell, and the meeting adjourned until next day, the member for Cork 'being apprised of the fact. Mr. Gladstone allowed it to be known on Tuesday morning that if Mr. Parnell was re-elected chairman of the Irish party, he would give no countenance to any amendment to the Address, and-the sudden termination of the debate on Tuesday night is-traceable to this cause. Details as to what took place at the meetings have not been allowed to leak out, bat it is reported that Mr. Parnell, in addressing his followers, put himself entirely in their hands, and only consented-te act again as fixer leader when he found that they unanimously decided upon it. The result ef the meeting, Which bicame known in the lobby a few minutes before four o'clock on Tues- day, was received (says the Press Association) with un- concealed disappointment by the general body of the Liberals, who had hoped that the opinions so openly expressed during the last few days woald lead to the ' adoption of a different course. The Conservatives and Libels" Unionists are jubilant at an event which they Sr. confident will rend the Home Rule alliance to the core, and. the Liberals made no attempt to conceal their apprehension as to the ultimate result of the present posi- tion of affairs. After the meeting on Tuesday afternoon Mr. Parnell had a long conference with Mr. John Morley in Mr. Gladstone's private room. He then informed Mr. Morley of what had transpired at the meeting of his party and pointed out that he had beeen unanimously re-elected chairman. During the evening there ensued consider- able speculation as to the course which would now be followed. It was felt, eyen by those not in the secrets of the front bench leaders, that the matter could not remain where it was, and that a more decisive develop- ment must shortly be announced. SCENE AT TUESDAY NIGHT'S CONFERENCE. The Press Association states that a stormy scene took place at the second meeting of .the Nationalist party, which was held in the conference room at the House of Commons, on Tuesday night, after the contents of Mr. Mr. Gladstone's letter to Mr. Morley had become known. Mr. Justin M`Carthy's conduct in making no mention at the earlier meeting of the views which Mr. Gladstone ex- pressed to him on Monday was the subject of very ad- verse criticism. We have reason to believe that the bulk of the Nationalist members who attended the afternoon's meeting were satisfied that after being re-elected to the chairmanship, Mr. Parnell would intimate to his fol- lowers his determination to take no part in active politi- c:43lWe for the next few months. There is no doubt that had the meeting been placed in possession of Mr. Gladstone's views, there would not have been the same unanimity which characterised the proceedings. More than one Irish member declared late on Tuesday night, that had they been aware of the strong objection which Mr. Gladstone entertained towards Mr. Parnell's reten- tion of the leadership.they would have openly advocated his immediate retirement. Later several prominent Nationalist members waited on Mr. Parnell with the ob- ject of asking him to reconsider his position. Thirty- eight members signed a requisition calling upon Mr. Par- nell to summon another meeting of the party for Wed- nesday afternoon. The Irish members having read the explicit declaration in Mr. Gladstone's letter, which they consider as an ultimatum, that if Mr. Parnell does not re- tire Mr. Gladstone will do so, are rapidly becoming con- vinced that there is only one way out of the complica- tion. FURTHER MEETINGS OF THE IRISH PARTY. MR. PARNELL ADVISED TO RETIRE. A meeting of the Irish party was held in the House of Commons Committee room No. 15, at two on Wednes- day afternoon. Amongst those present were Messrs. Justin M'Carthy ,(vice-chairman of the party) j. IJuntle 'CarthY. Knox, Tuite, Donal Sullivan, Com- M mene,/layden. Arthur O'Connor, Leamy. .T. J. O'Kelly, Barry. Colonel Nolan, rierce Mahone,. Swift Mac Neill, Joseph Nolan, D. Crille,W. A.M'Donald, Peter M'Donald, Blane, Condon, Sheehy, John O'Connor, P. J. O'Brien, Sir Thomas Es:nor:de, E. E. Harrington, Webb, Lane, Morrogh, Malley. I. A. Dickson. Murphy, Dalton Dr Kenny, Dr. Fitzgerald, Fox, Deasy, Pickerton, Flynn, and H. Campbell. Mr. Parnell who arrived at five minutes post two, entered the room without any de- monstration being made. Amongst the late arrivals were Mester. Quinn. Sheehyn, Foley, and Richard Power. Mr. Stack, Mr. Harrison, Dr. Tanner, and Mr. ceneyput in a late appearance. Mr. Parnell presided, and ir opening said the meeting had been called in con- sequfnce of a requisition which had been addressed to him the previous evening. The most careful precau- ties were taken to ensure the secrecy of tie proceedings, a member of Parliament 3eing stationed on the inside of the door to guard against the intrusionpf any Pressmen or strangers. "Mr. Barry, member for South Wexford, was the first to broach the subject of the day. He appealed to Mr. Parnell, as a coadjutor of eleven or twelve years stand ing, not to take a step which might prejudice for years the cause in the promotion of which they had been so long engaged. He referred in touching language to the services which Mr. Parnell had rendered to the party, but urged that the present crisis was one which demanded a personal sacrifice for the good of the country, and he put it to the Nationalist leader whether in the light of Mr. Gladstone's letter it would not be the wisest course br him to retire for a period from the leadership of the " Mr. Comp:dies, another old coadjutor of Mr. Fantail,

_ f ono:wed. He said he bad been associated with their leader for Timmy years, and he thought he wagtherefore 'entitled to speak. He would regret as deeply as any one Mr. Parnell's retimment • but he felt that expedi- ency demanaled that be should adopt this course—at any rate for a time. " Mr. Testin McCarthy, in an eloquent and impas- sioned speech, dwelt at lengtkowthe sacrifices which Mr. Parnell bad made in the cause of his country. Having referredto Mr. aladstone'sletter, howev3r, he had come to the conclusion that the situation had undergone a material change since the previous day, and he endorsed the new which had been expressed by the last two speakers as to the advisability of the position being re-

considered. Mr. Sexton took the same view, and in a speech which lasted neaay three-quatters of an hour made certain suggestions with a view to an amicable settlement. He regretted the abienze cif Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien at ' each a juncture, but thought that the beet course to adopt wodld be to askevery member of the party for an .expression of opinion on the subject of the leadership. The proposal was reostved with applause. Ilr:Dene referred to the case of the tenants on the Ponsonhy estate, and pressed upon Mr. Parnell the un- desirability of taking any action which would be likely to prejudice them. He reminded the member for Cork that the farmers on this estate had been waiting for p. 'prolonged period it the anticipation that their prospects vrould be improved by a general eleotion, and he ex- pressed an earnest hope that their expectations might not be disappoiated just as they were on the verge of reilisation. He 'appreciated to the full the sacrce's %Alt,' Mr. Parnell had made in the cause of Ireland, but he thought the temporary retirement of their chief would be the best thin that could happen at the present junc-

ture. "After some further conversation, in the course of which Colonel Nolan and others hoped Mr. Parnell weuld stick to his pest, and not permit himself to be dictated. to by Mr. Gladstone, when his own party had spoken unanimously in favour of his retention of the leadership, the meeting was adjourned in order to allow members who had charge of bills to proceed to the House and take, part in the ballot, which was fixed for 3.30 pax. At five o'clock the conference was resumed, and further speeches viere delivered. Mr. Sheehy spoke at some length with regard to the Smith-Barry tenants, on whose behalf he had been labouring for a long time, and taking: the same fine as Mr. Lane. asking what would happenl to these unfortunate people if the next general, election went against the Home Rule party. The 4 people in Tipperary were living on in the hope that an appeal to the constituencies would bring not merely comfort and prosperity to the country, but their own restoration to their homes. For the sake of the Smith-Barry tenants he appealed to Mr. Parnell to consider carefully whether it would not be best for him to retire /or a time from the leadership.• After some further discussion, in the course of which Mr. John O'Connor spoke strongly in favour of Mr. Parnell% con- tinuance at the head of the party, a suggestion was made that the meeting shonld be postponed until Monday, so that time might be given for obtaining the views of the absentee members. Some members objected to this, and further discustion took place, bet eventually the propos- al was adopted amid cheers.—Mr. Parnell, who through- out the proceedings had maintained the attitude of a listener, closed the proceedings by simply leaving the chair. When the Irish members returned to the lobby they found a large number of English and Scotch 'Liber- als awaiting the result of the meeting. A. strict pledge of secrecy had,however,been exacted, and all that could be elicited from the Nationalists was that the meeting ' had been adjourned until Monday. This indefinite re- sult was received with obvious disappointment, many hon. gentlemen on the Opposition side being led to ex- pect that the day would not close without a solution of the difficulty. In the course of the evening it was con- fidently predicted in some Liberal quarters that Ms. Par- nell's retirement would be announced after next Monday's conference, but many indications go the other way. tip to Wednerday night no official reply had been received to the communications addressed to Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien in America on the subject." The Central News says much bitterness was manifested towards Mr. Parnell at Wednesday's meeting, and it is evident that if he should retain his positition as leader of the Irish party half of the members would be replaced by other nominations at the next election. At the second meeting there was a distinct reaction, several of those who desired his resignation without ceremony now talked of having reconsidered their position and the position of the party. They asked if after all it was consistent with the dignity of the representatives of Ireland that they should be driven to east out their chosen and greatly be- loved leader: Three members protested that when .they elected Mr. Parnell on Tuesday they had no expectation that he would in a few hours come and ask to be relieved of his position, and be permitted to retire. Such an idea wasloreign to their intentions and their desires. The wish to save Mr. Parnell was now as strong as the earlier conviction that he must be sacrificed, and the meeting closed with an expressed hope that by means of porrpalers witlrthe Liberal leaders a way out of the difficulty could be found. 'LIBERAL FEELING IN THE COUNTRY. Mr.'Gladstone's letter has made a very profound im- pression upon his followers. The Liberals who had manifested a disposition to resist the expulsion of Mr. Parnell have with scarcely an exception abandoned that attitude. They feel that upon loyalty to Mr. Gladstone now depend their seats in Parliament. Mr. Labouchere strongly approves of the course taken by Mr. Gladstone. On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Liberal leaders took place in Mr. Gladstone's private room at the House of Commons. The right hon. gentleman was present. It is understood that in the interval before the next meet- ing of the Irish merebers proposale will be made to Mr. Morley and Sir William Harcourt with a view of relaxing the strain and rendering the resignation of Mr. Parnell unnecessary, but the Central News" learns that a second letter, even stronger than Mr. Gladstone's, calling ' for his resignation has reached Mr. Parnell from a leader of the Liberal party. Telegrams received from all parts of Great Britain on Wednesday show that among Liberals there is practically a unanimous opinion that Mr. Parnell should retire from public life. Indications of this univer- sal opinion have reached the Liberal Central Offices by post and by telegram in such numbers as to leave no doubt that as far at any rate as the constituencies are concerned the Liberal Home Rule Alliance will be con- sidered at an end should Mr. Parnell continue to lead the Irish party. Mr. Gladstone's letter, although it came as a complete surprise, has received the enthusiastic appro- val of the provincial Liberal Associations, and numerous' telegrams to that effect were received in London in the 'course of the day. SIR C. RUSSELL AND MR. PARNELL. Sir Charles Russell, Q.C., M.P., addressed his consti- tuents at Hackney, on Tuesday evening. The Morley Hall was crowded. He alluded to the trial which had occupied the public attention so recently. Although he was not called upon to advise anyone connected with that trial, yet the fact that he was so closely associated with Mr. Parnell in the Commission trial made it addi- tionally difficult for him to speak without a lively sense of pain (the name of Mr. Parnell was received with hisses and counter-cheers). Sir Charles (resuming) said it was unjust to charge the Irish people with indifference to ' morality because they had refused to dissociate them- selves from their leader, who had borne so much for them. There were many Irish hearts heavy that day, and there were many who recognised as clearly as he (the speaker) did that the needs the situation required that Mr. Parnell should bow his head to the storm (cheers), that Mr. Parnell should recognise that he had inflicted a serious wound upon the consciences of the people of both countries, and that he had done much to damage the cause in respect towhich his efforts had been so splendid. WIDNEB NATIONALISTS AND MR. PARNELL. At a meeting of the T. P. O'Connor (Widnes) branch of the Irish National League, held under the presidency of .Mr. J. HoWI3I, at St. Paul's Chambers, Mr. P. Whelan moved the following resolution :—" That the members of this branch, representing about 14,000 of the people of Widnes, in union with the rest of our fellow-countrymen throughout the civilised world, feel it our duty to raise our voices in solemn protest against the outrageous at- tacks of the anti-Irish and Tory press of England upon the wader of the Irish people, Charles Stewart Parnell. We do sincerely regret the incidents which have befallen Mr. Parnell, but we fail to see what the question of morals has to do with the question of politics, and so long as Mr. Parnell shows that he has the Irish cause at heart, so lour, do we pledge anew our entire confidence in him as the leader of the Irish people. His loyal devotion to the national cause of Ireland has won for him a fame that is destined never to die, and we sincerely trust that the cause for which he has so courageously struggled will soon terminate in a glorious victory for the suffering people of Ireland." Mr. Williamson seconded the re- solution, which was carried unanimously. A WARRINGTON REFERENCE TO THE PARNELL CASE. Preaching in the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, on Sun- day morning, from the words—" Judge not, that ye be not judged," the Rev. John Gunnell said that they, as Christian men, were bound to condemn immorality. They could not say that with one part of a man they had nothing to do. They must take the man as he was. He contended that no aublic man of immoral character was fit to be a leader in any political action. They wanted a healthy political morality to pervade the country, and they, as individuals, should do what they could to in- crease a sense of Christian morality on the public life. of England, for in that lay their safety and salvation. They should not witness wrong, and not lift up their hands to expel it.
