div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 180.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 180.
HEAVY RAINS AND FLOODS.
THE SHIP CANAL AGAIN ISUNDATED.
HOUSES AND 'TOADS FLOODED AT WARRINGTON.

The extraordinarily heavy fall of rain on Sitar - day and Sunday, resulted net only in a second ,and still-more serious and extensive inundation of the Ship Canal works, but to such a flooding of telds and roads and houses in the neighbourhood of War- rington as has not been equalled during the last quarter of a century. THE FLOODING OF THE CANAL.—A, NARROW ESCAPE. The Ship Canal works were on this occasion practically flooded between Warrington and Manchester. On Sun- day the slyer Irwell rose to an unprecedented height,and at night the water broke into the Ship Canal cutting and locks at Barton and rapidly pursued its way in the direction of Varrington. In addition, the "water from the swollen Mersey again found its way in'to the canal at Rixton Leys, a few miles from Warrington, in the direc- tion of Manchester, and on Sunday the -cutting, from that point to the looks at Latchford, was for a second time completely sebmerged. No further damage was done at Latchford, but in the locks therethe water again reached a height of about 40 feet. Fortunately, the water did pot penetrate beyond Latch- ford, and the 'low level line et the London: and North - Western Railway, which was ser- iously damaged by the previous flood, did! not suffer a second time. The -cutting extending from Latchford towards VVilderspool also escaped the invasion. In some places here the water was at the beginning of the week still from ten to twelve feet deep, butin others it had been reduced to two or three feet. The additional damage done by Seinday's flood, especially in the neighbourhood of Warrington, was not so serious as might have been supposed. A bridge at Statham TM +washed away, and loose timber was floating about in all directions. In one or two places, also, the banks threatened to fall in. This was particularly the case near 'what is known as the "Skew Bridge" and at Morris Brook. As an incident " of the flood it may be mentioned that a large dredger that was stationed at Cadishead was carried from its moorings and boated down the river. It dashed against an en‘iank- ' anent at Rizton, which gave way, and let a large volume of water into the cutting. The dredger itself was ulti- matelydashed to p.; ooes. A boab et Partingbusn lnarhb wooden" shoot" that carried away the water which then, of course, began to pour into the canal. The same , place gave way a fortnight ago, and it had just been re- paired when the second breakage occurred. Luckily, the flood was not attended 'by loss of life, but several 1 narrow escapes are reported. At Cadishead, a foreman ,joiner was standing on a portion of the bank of the cut- ting when it gave way, and it was only with great dim- culty that he was extricated from his perilous position on the floating mass which was being carried away on the surface of the water. In the flood a fortnight previous the sections of the canal nearer to Manchester escaped any seriousitiflow of water, but not so on tttis oceesion. The swollen river gradually rose, on Sunday, until the Salteye cutting above Barton Bridge, which has been finished and runs into the river at the western end, became a small turbid lake. Millions of tons of flood water poured in here, but with no cessation in the rainfall the river still rose. It gradually topped the embankment in the next lower section, and at ten o'clock—at first in a small stream— poured from the new 'waterway into the old bed, from which it had been diverted just above the Barton aque- duct. So great was the rush of water that in fifteen minutes the section on either side of the bridge was filled. As Sunday were on there was hope that no further flooding would take place. Ganes Of men were set to work, and weak or threatened parts of the em- bankments which cross and re,cross the sections were strengthened. But as heavy rain continued to fall the force of the water became irresistible. Further west, in the section that runs by Sticking Island, the low fields that lie to the south of the Canal are indented in the middle for about half a mile, so that with a heavy flood they form a gathering ground for the accumulated waters. Here wide wooden water "shoots "—small square aqueducts—have been built. These, in case of heavy rains, carry the water from the southern side of the Canal into the Irwell„ which runs at a slightly lower level than thafields on the northern side of the Canal. But with the height to which its waters were brought by the flood the river itself topped the outlet of these aque- ducts, and thus the water, which should have been car- ried over into the Irwell, was penned back on the southern land around Bent's fields. It gradually rose, and late on Sunday evening poured over the nanks— they here break abruptly on the Canal—in hundreds of miniature waterfalls. Gangs of men worked for a time in the darkness and rain, but with the crumbling earth and the dull rush of the ever-increasing flood there was imminent danger, and their task was perforce stayed. All day on Monday the pent-up water from this land ponied into the Canal bed, hewn out of the red sand- stone. On Sunday night the water had here reached 21ft. above the lower sill of the Canal, at noon on Mon- day it stood at 261 t., and at niglip it had reached 30ft. The latest influx was in the Trafford Park section. Considerable labour had been employed to save this from flooding, as in from three to four weeks' time it would practically have been completed. The Manchester end of the section at tho Park corner meets the Irwell almost on the direct force of a bend, and a strong embankment ran across to keep the Canal bed try. This stood until about seven o'clock on Monday morning, when the con- ' stant force of the water made a small breach through the

embankment. In an almost inconceivably short time theriverAore a huge piece out of the embankment, and the section, like the others, was filled. From the Trafford Docks to Irlam the whole of the 'cuttings were to a greater or less extent under water. There must have been a vast amount et plant submerged. Some steam navvies had no more than their heads above water, and in some places they were lost to sight entirely. The tops of the funnels of pumping engines were all that remain of them to be seen. In round figures some 3,000 men were thrown out of work on the sections between Irlam and Manchester, and although employment was to be found for a great number of these in pumping and upon work in the cuttings and other parts of the Canal nearer Eastham, yet many must remain idle for weeks to come. HUTS INUNDATED NEAR LYMM. The newly erected bridge across the canal cutting, near the brickfield, Lymm, was on Sunday morning again washed away. The water in the canal cutting from Lymm to Latchford on Sunday morning was three or four feet higher than it was at any time when the Mersey broke in a fortnight ago. In several places the sides of the canal fell in, and one place. near to the Latchford locks, it was deemed nececeary to move the overland route from the side of the cutting, and to lay down a new line of rails. The occupiers of the huts at the brickfield, Lymm, had a bad time of it early or Sat-1 urday morning. The water began to find its way into 1 them about six o'clock, and by ten in some of the huts it had risen up to the windows. The women and children were taken across the canal on rafts, but before they could get to a place of satety they had to wade across the flood in the Lymm meadows, which was about two feet deep in the roadway. In the neighbourhood of War- burton and Partington the floods were very extensive, and many of the men who live on the Cheshire side of the river were unable to set to their work. ROADS AND HOUSES FLOODED IN WARRINGTON. The water in the Mersey at Warringeon continued to rise gradhally throughout Monday, and later on in the afternoon it found its way into Knutsford-road, and all the adjoining streets. At eight o'cleck Knntsford-road was under water for a quarter of a mile, namely from Pin Mill to the houses immediately opposite the Weir. The water became deeper and deeper, and at ten o'clock in some places it was from two to three feet deep. The kitchens of most of the houses, especially those in Tun- stall's-row, were soon flooded, furniture was hastily re- moved and placed in the bedrooms. Spreading over Knutsford-road the water rushed onwards in streams threughthe side street, into the Old-road, which soon et...tame impassable, and the occupied et the heusee were almost as sorely inconvemenceo as those living on the banks of the river. Most of the tenants of the houses, from the Primitive Methodist Chapel to the end of Tun- stall's-row deserted their lower rooms and took refuge lathe 1 bedrooms (in which fireswere lighted), from the open win- dows of which they Watched the vehicular traffic below. Vehicles of all descriptions were-brought into requisition to convey the inhabitants to Latchford to their respective homes, but some who could not find vehicles to hand , resolutely plodded through the water. One rev: gentle- man was seen wading almost knee deep through the i street on his way home, and several men, who had divested themselves of their shoes and stockings, passed from house to house making themselves useful to their neighbours in a variety of ways. To the juvenile portion of the community the floods were a source of unfailing amusement, and they were seen paddling about in evi- dent enjoyment. The vicarage, the residence of the Rev. F. Slater, was surrounded by water, and Alderman Davies of the Old Warps, was a prisoner, the carriage drive leading to the house being several feet under water. The lodge at the entrance to the ground was entirely surrounded with water which also covered all the fields round about. The "Island" near the Weir was con- cealed from view, and all that was visible on that spot was the cottage and trees. THE FOOTBALL FIELD AND WILDERSPOOL MEADOWS. _

Wilderspool Meadows, including that portion of them which is used as the ground of the Warrington Football Club, were completely covered with water on Monday, so that the fields resembled 'a great lake. The field in which St. James's Church is situated was covered with a depth of two or three feet of water, and on the ground of the Football Club the forms which have been Placed in the field for the convenience of sp3ctators and any other loose pieces of timber were to be seen floating abqut. In another field near here a number of willow sticks be- longing to Mr. Hutchinson, were surrounded 7iith two or three feet of water. WILDERSPOOL CAUSEWAY..

...... Monday night was an anxious time for the tocupiers of houses along Wilderspool Causeway. The liver had risen rapidly during the day and gradually ad:merged the roadway at the back of the houses. The waters then invaded the back yards and continued to rise lin it forced Its way beneath the doors into the sculleries. fortunately, however' in most cases it went no further, tut the resi- dents of the locality were kept in suspens, till nearly 'midnight, when the water reached its higheit level ,and then began to recede very slowly but perceitibly. wARBINGTON BRIDGE. One of the most iiteresting aspects o the flood vets to be seen at Warington Bridge whe considerable crowds of people gathered both on Sand and Moneay. The rising river rued through the arc es of the budge with great impettosity and in the opition of some the , structure was in emsiderable danger oi being damaged, though, fortunatly, these fears turned out to be eatirely [ groundless. Tb, waters, however, ibse till they were within a vpry Aort distance of the leprnost stones of the arches, and, am necessary consequette. all tra,,"' on the river was stored for the time betty. A short distance lower down lie water was at sucha height that the foot- paths acros, the river at the siees of the iron railway bridge were submerged, and, of course, the footpath to
Arpley Meadows undefe railway bridge was coin pletelY blocked.

FLOOD 9r OF HOWLEY. Itlowley was anal, part of the town which was teriously flooded. 'Ttltiwater found its way into several of the streets near M I) the discomfort an A. Nayloes timber works, much Tie streets which v 3 the most badly inconvenience of the inhabitants. submerged was Farrel-st., which nit along iwele in a very the Rectory garden, and that gaden was also foded. Wright-st. and Egerton-st. serifs conditios, and at the end of New- st. t small tereOary bridge was erected to enable passengers to got flm street to fteet• , sTPPAGE OF WORKS. In tie afternoon If Monday the waters rose to such a height is to tempe?rily stop some cf the works adjacent to the rirer. Mr. tutchings, of the firm of Messrs. J. C. and W. V. Hutclugs, sent his men away during the Afternoor, as he fared they would be untble to gat home owinp to he Mersf having overflown its banks. Sub- sequently he wate' got Into the flues at tle tannernand it was °wag to c.-1 similar cause that oplrations were suspended t the glowing places of bushing e—Measrs. John Tattesall Claliffe, Limited, Messrs Fairclotgh, Mersey Minh Mr R. A. Naylor, Howley Timber Mils, the Ship Canal Company's carrying department tnd Howley Mills. pobably the greatest sufferer was 11r. Naylor, whose mills and yards were flooded, aid from 100 to 150 n thrown out of employment foi a few days. The r even found its way into the office. At Howley Mill damage done was not serious, ail the water in th at the bottom of Ellesmere-St. wa in several place, Ir four to five feet deep on Tuesdal mornin,g. ALDIRM DAVIES A PRISONER. One of the pride of the flood was the prevention of Alderman Davies tro fulfilling an engagement to preside at an entertainment the Co-operative Hall, on Mon- day evening. Alder n Davies' residence, Old Warps, was, as we have befol mentioned, surrounded with the waters of the overfloyeg Mersey, and hence the Alder- man and his househokWere, so to speak, isolated from the rest of the world is the time being. The water on Mondabight found its way into several of the streets of WarriNon. One or two houses in the Packet Stage, off MersaJet., were flooded, and the occu- piers were compelled t remove their furniture. The tenants of one of the hesss were unable to leave in the ordinary way, and the vel sight was presented of a small boat moored near fe door for their convenience. div.head: OFFICIL REPORT.
div.p: THE OFFICIL REPORT.

Oa Monday:—/iir:l:e-a.:l7Wlliiarn;—(-chief engineer) visited • the various sections)f the works, and in the afternoon, the following offical report was issued The engineer's report wi, reference to the recent floods is that, so far as it ea be ascertained, no injury whatever has resulted te ts permanent works. The greater part of the work with the area affected by the flood, is either completedor nearly so, and the water will be allowed to retrin where it is, and the remaining excavation will btonapleted by dredging. The Manchester and Salford Qui have been filled with water, and the former will live to be pumped out, as they are not quite finished. Ise walls of the Salford docks are however, completedabove the highest water level, and the excavation also eing finished it will not be necessary to pump the wate out. The Mode Wheel locks, which are iv a very forvard state, will be at once pushed on to corapletion, whEr the large sluices there will admit of the river up to thEManchester docks being run off nearly dry in order to curiplete thE works. Be- low Mode Wheel hats the water rill have b be pumped out, but the worls will no be stcpped, as the walls are considerably abort water level. Lower dcwn the river the Warburton aging was filled with waer, but it is fortunately compbted, and the water will rat, therefore, require to be punned out. . Subsequently, a 7.30 p.m., the following addition to the report was isEued. All the dams stood inn between Stickings and Irian, but the river Irwell oveflowing the meadows above Stickings, and finding a low course below Davyhulm(, flowed into the cutting btween the new locks at lrlan and Barton, wa.shing awar a portion of a field at the pint of which it entered be cutting. There are now atwork in this length sevenz.entrifugal pnmps, and fouradditional ones will be putto work at once, and it is eipected that the water will b pumped out from the cutting and from Irlam and futon locks before the end o' the year. Part of the wallsif the locks are above water level, and will allow of tie work pro- greasing; and as the water is lowered by the jumps more ruen will be put on each week. No damage be occurred to the work between Latchford and Eastram, either from the gale or flood, and the men and dant which have been thrown out of employment on Ulf upper sec- tions will be set to work on the lower parts if the canal for the present. div.head: GREAT FLOOD OF 1866.
div.p: THE GREAT FLOOD OF 1866.

The greatest flood from which Warrington and its neighbourhood has suffered within ,he last fifty years was on aacuraay, riovember 17, 1866. With regard to the flood, an account written at the tim says :—" It was at six or seven o'clock when th flood assumed a threatening aspect: the current i/

the river was unusually strong, and the water rose with great rapidity, overflowing the banks and en- tering such houses as were within reach. In a very short time linutsford-road was under water, the fields on either side were flooded,haystacks were un- dermined and swept away, and sheep, if not horned cattle and horses,were drowned. In Arpley,especially 'on the Lancashire side were the effects of the disaster apparent. At ten o'clock the highest point of the flood was reached, and the state of things then in the low- lying parts of the town, particularly in Mersey-st., and Latchford, was most serious. The river at Warrington Bridge was within two feet of the crown of the highest arch, and only a few inches below the stone footway on the edge of the river leading towards Arpley, rushing on at a terrific rate. Arpley, seen from the railway station, was a vast sheet of water,extending as far as the eye could reach ; the Recreation ground was covered,and boats *ere out upon it, and we are informed that in several fields parties were out in,koats searching for sheep,a consider- able number of whieff, it was feared had perished. As to the height of the flood some idea may be formed when we mention that it extended as far into the town as Fennel-st., and Dial-st., up to the Bridewell steps, the water in the kitchen of the Old Crow being a foot or more in depth. Along Wilderspool-road it was impossible for foot passengers to proceed; be- tween the bridge and the level crossing people were carried in carts or other conveyances, and the houses on the river side were of course, all flooded. The water reached almost to the window sills of the houses in Arpley View, and the inhabitants were imprisoned, finding it necessary to betake themselves to their bedrooms for safety. Knutsford-road was, however, in the worst plight. It was impossible for conveyances of any kind to get along, even her Majesty's mails were detained. As far as Black Bear Bridge and extending on either side, it was one vast waste of water. In Bake- ouse-yard the water was three or four feet deep, and veral people who lived in cellar dwellings were corn- iletely drowned out. In James-st., the water rose as tigh as ths door steps of some of the houses. Five young igs belonging to Mr. Lawrenson, market gardener, Drished ; and a small stack of hay, the property of the Erne party was swept away. The water rushed down linces.s-st. and Fountain-st. with great rapidity. Nwrs. Roberts, Dale and Co. will have suffered great I Its, but until the water has completely subsided it will ,be impossible to form any estimate. T 1.3 whole works were flooded, and the workpeople had tceeturn home.

4ther establishments in Latchford, in addition to that wehave ntmed, felt the effects of the flood. Messrs. Edtsten aid Son's pin mill was stopped, the workmen beitg unatle to get up to it; and at Messrs. Hadfield's cothn mill tome privies were undermined and fell. Some of tie stockbelonging to cow keepers and others was with difficuty s%ved. Uri cellar at St. Elphins, the crypt of the Parish Chunh, andmany other places in that locality were flooded. Inlowley-lane and Dutton-st.. the cottages were flooded° such an extent that the furniture in the kitchens wasloating about, and the cottagers were ob- liged to take tfuge in the upper storeys of their dwell- ings until the were rescued." LOODS IN 1828 AND 1837.

_ Previous to 666 two other great floods are reported in this centur3—one on St. Swithin's Day, 1828, and another on St.'homas's Day, 1837. The height of these floods is marks by small brass plates at a cottage door near Arplev-viv, and the flood of 1888 Zlid not come within six inds of either of these,plates. From an ins3ction of these brass plates we find that the flood of 18`g was the highest, that of 1837 being next but about ten aches lower. The highest point of the flood of 1866 wi about eight inches below that of 1837, and the high w:er mark of the flood of this week is about another ght inches lower than that of 1866.
GENEAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.
SERMOr BY THE REV. 3. YONGE.

The Rev. J.Yonge, preaching in the Wycliffe Church, on Suday evening, after briefly discours- ing upon the Ni,rds of Psalm 72, the 12 to 14 verses, dwelt upon Geeral Booth's scheme. He said he wanted to mak everybody present that night fami- liar with at lest the outline of this scheme for the help of the helless, and the physical and moral sal- vation of the scially lost. General Booth, he said, had been faceo face with the social problem for five and twent years as a preacher of the Gospel to the outcast downcast, downtrodden, hopeless, poor, and lost. His sphere in every town in the Kingdom, lIICO notably in London, had been where it was all vi u poverty, and crime. He had been sickened and dheartened, as many another had been, with the appaAt impossibility of doing more than merely peck athe outside of this endless tangle of mo- notonous underrowth—the great slough of despond of our tune. Wt was it, then, that the General proposed to do? He imposed to cut a way to the light for the wretched beins in our own land who were living in social darknet and misery. He proposed that a serious practical endavour should be made to improve the con- ditbn of our,ocial outcasts. He believed he had the ' inarumentalty for this stupendous enterprise—the ants for arrying it out,—ready to his hand in the nembers of us army. Further, the General believed tlat he coud make a reasonable trial of the scheme, lith fair prospects of success, if he was provided with ;1100,000 to start with, and an annual income of 1,000 t.• f01i0.... The General wt v.. to Speak et ...._ sacrifit.,e of girls in this Christian country. and asked whether the lot of a negress in Central Africa, was much worse than that of a girl driven into vice by the menace of her employer, compelled to sin in order to live, and then cast out into the streets? The blood boiled, the General said, to think of these enormities, callously inflicted, and silently borne by these miserable victims. And, the General went on, nor was it only women who were victims, although their fate was the most tragic. General Booth said the denizens of darkest England for whom he appealed were, Ist, those who in a month would all be dead from sheer starvation, were they exclusively dependent upon the money earned by their own work ; and, 2nd, those who by their utmost exertions were unable to obtain the minimum allowance of food which the law prescribed as indispensable even for the worst criminals in our gaols. Of this class of people General Booth estimated that there were three million in Great Britian,which was about one-tenth of the whole population. The rev, gentlemen said it was most inspiring to note that it was the "hideous wreckage" that General Booth dared to face. It was not a select portion ;it was tilt "the aristocracy of the miserable" that he went forward to help. The preacher then went fully into the proposed scheme, and, at the close cf his sermon said the scheme seemed to him to be one which had attracted support and e,ontributition from the congregation at Westminster Abbey ; from bishops and canons of the Church of England ; from Royalty itself; from a leading actor of the day who kad promised .£l,OOO if 99 others would do likewise ; a scheme which drew £650 from one of their own churches the previous Sunday in Bristol, and £420 from another of their churches at Liscard, and it was stirring their people at St. Helens to stimulate a town movement to raise £1,000; and a scheme which was doing things like that by all Ithe churches, should not be cold-shouldered by them. He (the preacher) confessed he hardly knew how or what to suggest that night as to methods of help. The next Sunday was their Foreign Missionary Day; and they must first do their duty by that claim. But he then put the matter before them in its freshness and force, for them to think over and talk over. Perhaps xt month, or at the latest next year, they could con- trive some scheme of help. Perhaps a united movement could be made in the town; for it was a national affair, it being a claim to meet a national necessity. lie believed it could be compassed by united Christian con- verstion. Let Churchmen and Nonconformists join in the movement. Their doing so would be an up-flashing, an out-gleaming of the dawn of the millennial glory. ..tte

div.head: SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A
div.p: SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A
HIISBA ND.
STRANGE LETTER HIGH A WARRINGTON
MAN.

At the Altrineham Petty Sessions on Monday before Messrs. R. H. Joynson, R. P. Gill, J. W. Side- botham, M.P.. and T. W. MiHick, a young man named Walter James Roberts, son of the pro- prietor of the Boar's Head public-house, Mold, was charged with deserting his wife and child, and with neglecting to provide for their maintenance., The defendant was represented by Mr. Bradley, solicitor,of Mold. Mr. Hockin appeared on behalf of the complainant. The evidence showed that the parties were married at St. Margaret's Church, Altrincham, on the 7th of June, 1882. They removed to Warrington, where for 18 months, defendant carried on business as a watch- maker and jeweller. While at Warrington,the defendant paid his attention to a young woman named Miss Edwards, who was said to five at Egremont, and a letter written by her to the defendant was intercepted by his wife, who took a copy of it and charged her husband with carrying on an unlawful intercourse with another woman. The defendant admitted it, and said if his wife would overlook the charge he would =duct himself better in the future. In November, 1884, they went to live at Mold, where Mrs. Roberts re- ceived a copy of a very curious letter which Mr. Fred Highly, Sankey Bridges, Warrington, had written to her husband. The writer stated that the defendant had told him some months before that he had tried to poison his wife, and that he would get rid of her. He also stated that the defendant told him that he had put some cyanide of potassium on a piece of meat and had given it to his wife. It appeared that at the time of the receipt of this letter Mrs. Roberts was very ill, wh'ich was attri- buted to the effects of poisoning, but on charging her husband with having given her poison he denied it, and the result was that a deed of separation was drawn up, under which defendant agreed to pay his wife I2s. 6d. a -veek. Under this deed he had paid her certain sums of money, but he fell into arrears, and, as he refused to provide a home for his wife, the present proceedings were brought to obtain an order against him.—The Bench made an order for the defendant to contribute 12.5. 6d. a week for the maintenance of his wife and children. The charge that the defendant had tried to . poison his wife was strongly denied by him.

div.head: RUNCORN AND THE StLIP CANAL
div.p: RUNCORN AND THE StLIP CANAL

The action of the Guardians of the Poor of Run- corn v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company came before the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, yesterday week, as a motion for an interim injunction restraining the Ship Canal Company, till the trial of the action or further order, from inter- fering with the sewage works of the plaintiffs.—Mr. Cozens Hardy. Q.C., in support of the motion, stated that under their Act of Parliament the defendant com- pany were prohibited from interferring with the sewage works of the plaintiffs without their express sanction, but they were now, while negotiations were going on, working close up to one of the sewers.—Mr. J. Napier Higgins, Q.C., on the part of the defendants, asked that the motion might stand over for a week to afford an op- portunity for answering the plaintiffs' affidavits.—Mr. Cozens Hardy had no objection to the motion standing overfor a week if the defendants would undertake not in the meantime to work up to sewer No. I.—Mr. Higgins was not prepared to give any undertaking, but understood that the sewer referred to would not be interferred with in the interval. He was instructed that these works had been going on since July, 1/389.—Mr. Justice North: But you have not touched these sewers, and the plaintiffs fear that you are now about to do so.—Mr. Cozens Hardy was informed that their steam navvies were about to work close by.—Mr. Higgins sug- gested that if the motion stood over till next day (Saturday) morning he might be in a position to give an undertaking which would save the time of the court, and the motion was ordered to stand over accordingly. On Saturday the matter again came forword. Mr. Cozens Hardy, Q.C., said he was happy to say that a temporary arrangement had been come to between the parties, which was to the effect that the defendants, by their counsel, undertook not to interfere with sewer No. 1 until next week, the motion to stand over until that time.—Mr. Higgins said he was quite prepared, on behalf of the defendants, to give the undertaking which had been referral to by his learned friend.—Mr. Justice North, on this undertaking, ordered the motion so stand over for a week.

Bad as the flood has been in the Mersey valley, it has not been so disastrous as the wide-spread floods in Germany, which have not only done great damage but resulted in considerable loss of life. It Is the one redeeming feature of the latest flooding of the Ship Canal that it has not been accompanied, ,so far as is known, with loss of life or limb.

• At Lady Rosebery's funeral, on Tuesday, Mr. Gladstone, replying to a friend's remark, is reported to have said, "Yes it is a chill morning, and many an old man takes his death through attending a funeral." Precisely; and why, above all others, ' should the Grand Old Man run such unnecessary risk? His doctor ought to put a veto upon his =attending another funeral.

Lord Salisbury is not such a master f phrases as the late Lord Beaconsfield; but his speeches are always good reading from a literary point of view. He made " a palpable hit" in the House of Lords,on Tuesday evening, when he said :—" There is always some difficulty with Irish leaders. Their strong point lust now is escapes. , Some prefer escapes by water, some prefer fire-escapes. (Laughter.)"

Macdonald's confession removes all doubt as to his being the murderer of the Belmont school- mistress. His past career and latest atrocity place him in the Catagory of what General Booth calls -" moral lunatics " ; and if the Salvationist had his way with such men they would be placed under • control, like many other lunatics. As regards Macdonald, the chances are that he will be effec- tually controlled by being put out of existence.

--- It is not Lord Derby but Lord Airlie who has subscribed £l,OOO towards General Booth's scheme. he money thus far comes from all sorts and con- ditions of men. The Marquis of Queensbury, for instance in sending a cheque for £lOO, says point blank that he is not a Christian; but what does the label matter if, by assisting to feed the hungry, be helps in a work which is Christ-like in its ,character?

The members of the Haydock Local Board are like other authorities in feeling their way as to what they can do in the matter of technical educa- tion. There seems to be some doubt as to whether the Haydoek Mining School could be grafted on to a Technical School. The point is worth inquir- ing into. It ought to be possible, and we think it will be found possible ; the instruction given at a mining school is essentially technical.

There is another stir amongst the dry bones at Warrington but it is premature to assume as our neutral contemporary does, that the town is well on the way :to a Technical School. We appre- hend that there will be no small amount of private inquiry and public discussion before the Town Council votes anything from the rates. It will not do to take a leap in the dark.

From what we can hear of the preliminary talk of the Warrington Sub-Committee, it seems, to be thought that a Technical School might be worked by the ,Library and Museum Committee, and em- brace the School of Art as a branch instutition. But would it work well ? The Library,Museum, and Art Gallery constitute a special institution under special Acts of Parliament; and we are inclined to think there is already plenty for the Committee to do if they would do it well. A Technical School is too big a thing to be treated successfully in this particular way.

"The Whirlwind" which now appears as "the organ of Mr. Herbert Vivian "—the other pro- prietor-editor having been dropped on the way— continues its eccentric career. It deserves to live, for it is wide-awake, outspoken, and occasionally "just too ridiculous for anything." Mr. Whistler has contributed two characteristic sketches, and the first has gone up in price to five shillings—not a bad investment for those who in the first in- stance secured the paper and the sketch for a penny. •

The "Daily News" says :—" The statement which appeared, on Thursday; on the authority of one of the news agencies, that Mr. Justin McCarthy and Mr. Sexton were at the time of the meeting of Irish members which re-elected Mr. Parnell privy to the contents of Mr. Gladstone's letter to Mr. Morley, is absolutely without foun- dation. Neither Mr. Pariell, Mr. McCarthy, nor any other Irish member knew of the existence of the letter till the meeting was over."

This determines an important point, for it clears -Mr. Parnell of the charge of keeping his colleagues in the dark as to the contents of the letter. He .knew, of course, what Mr. Gladstone's views were as communicated through Mr. John Morley to Mr. McCarthy ; but the ultimatum could not be said to have been presented until the letter was made public. All this means that, as Mr. Parnell would not have" the way out" made easy, it is, inevitably, being made hard for him.

There is no particular lesson to be drawn from the fact that, while the bulk of the Liberal party voted against the first reading of Mr. Balfour's Irish Lead B 11, the Irish members voted for it. It is not at all unusual to vote for the introduction of a measure which will afterwards be opposed,the great figit being upon the second reading. Mr. Gladstone did not vote for the first reading, nor aid he v)te against it. He and several other ex- Cabinet ginisters walked out of the House before the divison was taken.

The jalgment of the Archbishop of Canterbury in the Bihop of Lincoln's case is a poor sort of compromse which satisfies neither one side nor the othet and will probably result in some of the issues be:lg brought before the Privy Council. The anti-Ritialists are certainly not satisfied; they want anoher Beaconsfield and another "bill to put down Rittalism." And they would still be "as you were. A Disestablishmbnt Act would be the beat way, f settling the differencesbetween tweedle- dam and weedledee.

Count lon Molke, who, being over ninety years of age, is te oldest great man of the day, has been questionecas to the way to grow old, lie says I think xoderation in all habits of life is good, and that no should never spend a whole day in- doors, notven rainy ones." This latter observa- tion harmaises with the Persian proverb to the effect that Allah does not count the days that are spent lithe chase." In other words, time spent in the opeuir is time gained; A dozen )od reasons might be given for out- door exercit, and, as the talk just now is of bacilli and disem germs, it is something to "make a menu of" tat oxygen and sunshine act either in deadening r dispersing bacteria, while at the same time iey operate in strengthening the body's natural poers of resistance. It is doubly wise therefore t, Go fch under the open sky, and list To Nure's teachings— for, to quoianother poet, "Nature never did be- tray the het that loved her."

. It takes rom the apprehension as to danger from risingq the river to know that the further we go bacthe graater the overflow. The river on Monday ght was about eight inches below the high-water irk of 1866, which was eight incheBl below the 113 of 1837, which again was ten inches below the git flood of 1828. It is a matter of course to shat the flood this week would have been somewt. higher if the o'er-charged river had not found Eie relief by filling the Ship Canal. Still, the obvation holds good that the floods of to-day allot as great as the floods of fifty years ago.

Last week we had to record the death of two personothrough being" gassed" at GOlbome, area,. on Saturday, there was aninquest on a man named Jrames, Daly who, was, "-gassed" at Widnes,. ft would seem, that workmen are ever ready to risk life in the performance of duty ; but the question ariseawhether the risk is always absolutely neces- sary. Special precautions ought to be- taken to guard against accideqts of tine kind, and we can- nnt but think employers will readily comply-with such suggestions its, practical workmen, may make for their- own proteetion, Granted that workmen do not like to be thought soft, it is well fot them to remember-that sometimes there are wivew and children to consider- as well' asthernseives..

Ir is a curious commentary on the E'kit Mr. Parnell. incertitude of human affairs that a breath of the seventh command- ment on the part of Mr.. CHARLES STEWART PAR- NELL shbuld be,the means of throwing the Liberal Party into a stateof excitement, and convulsion,and endangering, ma high degree, the cause of Home Rule. Mark Antony lest Actium" through, Cleo- patra'seyes,': anclPAnagET.n becomes the discrowned king through intriguing with Mrs. O'SHEA. /t is a terrible priceto pay for folly ; but it is a, price that must be paid, and that is a fact which the Irish Chief does not as yet realise. From, his point of. view, it, seems ridiculous that, because he has been made co-respondent in a divorce case, he should'not continue to render what aid he can to the people of Ireland. He-wishes to go on at as if nothing had happened; but it cannot be. Christ might content himself with saying to the woman taken in adultery—"Go and sin no more," but the world 'is not to that extent christianised. it-per- sists in throwing stones, if not in stoning to death; and,, always assuming that the stone- throrring is not. over-done, we are inclined to think the world is in the right. Mr. PAENFEL has sinned) and he has been found out, and society insists that he shall suffer: If a man will deliber- ately risk his reputation, he has no right to cry out when his reputation is irreparably damaged. But apart from any question of morality, it appears to us as clear as the sun at. noonday that, even if the Irisleader were innocent of the charge of which he has been found'.,guilty, it is his duty to retire when he finds—from whatever cause—that his retire- ment will help,the cause which he and his coun- trymen have so much at heart. That is what patriotism demands of him. His per- I sonal claims,---based as they are upon services of the highest' kind—are as dust in the. balance compared with the claims of his country; and we cannot understand why he shonid have hssitated after being told that his retention of the , leadership of the Nationalists might mean the retirement eNNIr. GLADSTONE and the wreck of the Home Rule cause. He took a wise and an honour. able coursowhen, upon hearing of the Phoenix Park. assassinations, he left it to the leader of the Liberal, party to say whether he should retire from public life; and it. was natural for Mr. Gr..Aosroxn to expect that the Nationalist leader would take a. similar course after the revelations of the Divorce Court. That he has not done so, and that he still hesitates,to do so 5 would seem to suggest that. Mr.. PARNELL, is lesssensitive than he was eight.years ago. He is hard, but he is finding that public opinion,is harder.. Sir CHARLES DILKE, after his sin had found him out, had to hide his diminished head; and Mr. PARNELL-stout as he is-wilt either be bent or broken by the present. storm. His col- leagues have talked to him pretty plainly, since they learned what they ought to have been told at their first meeting, namely, that in, the opinion of Mr. GLADSTONE his retirement was, in the interests of Home Rule, a necessity of the. situation. The theory that it is merely a question of leaving it to the Nationalists to determine who shall lead them, is seen tube suicidal when it is known that the re- tention of a particular leader means certain defeat instead of probable victory. It has been argued. that it would have been absurd to remove Wur ',moron- on the eve of Waterloo if a divorce case had gone against him; and we may grant that it would. But what—to extend and improve the analogy—if, on the eve of battle, it was found that a particular commander had, by his conduct, so shaken confidence in him that some not only of his own troops but those of the main army were not to be relied up- on Would it be absurd then to change the objec- tionable General It seems to us it would be absurd not to make the change; and that is how

the case stands with regard to Mr. PARNELL. He must go; to retain him, after all that has happened, would be a humiliation to the ablest and noblest commander-in-chief that the Liberal army has ever known; and, more than that it would be a crime against Home Rule.
It is a very far cry to India, or we "Sweating" The Natives. should hear much more than we do _

of the abominable practice of over- working the natives in the cotton factories of our great Dependency. If it were a matter in which Government had no title to interfere, we might console ourselves with the reflection that Alike many iniquities that are being perpetrated in this coun-
try, it cannot be helped. But Government is re-
sponsible for the regulati-m of the hours et work of women and children in Inuia as in England, and
in this way the people of this country become par- ties to a system of " sweating " which is a disgrace to us as a nation. It took years of agitation, and
the sacrifice of the health of thousands of cotton
workers, before the Factory Acts of this country were adopted; and it would seem as if the same process has to be gone through witi regard to
India. We are acting there asif we had learned. nothing at home, or as if we had no more to do with the government of the conntry thaA,the man
in the moon. The recent propowas of the. Govern-.
ment of India were to amend the India Factorl

Act, and yet leave it possible to work children, nine years of age nine tours v, day, while lads of twelve years of age and upwards Illare to be left without any protection. This meant that: they would be "compelled to work nearly four -times the, number of hours which lads of, that ago

are allowed to work in ;Eng,la.nd." The shameless injustice of such an " smenthiaent: is apparent when it is remembered thr.t. Sir • Xonsr GORST, the Under-Secretary for India, was an ad- vocate in the Berlin Conference for -fusing to employ children in southern countriefi4--even half-timers—if they were under twelve,years of. age. Preaching on these matters is one thing and. practice is another, and if Sir JOHN Goas7ldoe,s note want continental critics to fall foul of the British Government, he must get rid of the anomaly of protecting women and children in EnglaAd, and allowing them in India to be "sweated" out of 'everything that makes life dear. Lord Cnc4vi is, of course, in a large degree responsible as ChieNSecre- • tAtry.for.lnclia ; but Lord Caoss is of little use in legislation. He has no initiative, and no fence of character. He is not likely to move unless under pressure, and that pressure should be applied by the people of this country. We are glad to see that the,facts of the case have been admirably placed before the public in an address given by Mr; LIEKE-Y, HA...naisori, President of the Blackburn and District Chamber of Commerce. It seems that another grievance the natives have to com- plain ,of is that they aro paid monthly, and that the manufacturers. are sometimes several weeks tin arrears; that is to say that an opera- - two does not get paid for his work in these cases. until six or seven weeks after his pieces have been finished and booked.. Mr. HARRISON asks.— , "What would the people in our manufacturing districts think if they were paid by the month, and then a month in arrears. ?. Such a mode of pay- ment forces the operatives into the clutches of the " money-lenders.. The only, benefit that such aprac- tice canobring to the manufacturers is that it enables - them to draw the interest of the money that is owing to the operatives. The proceeding is sim- ply infamous." It is indeed infamous, and a stigma attaches to the Government that tolerates a practice which is as mischievous as the old truck system.. The remedy for these grievances is simple; me must treat the operatives of India as fairly as we treat the operatives- of Lancashire and Cheshire.. As the case stands. at present, we are handicapping manufacturers at homein order that mameacturers.abroad may grow rich by oppressing down-trodden natives, who are under British rule and should. be under British protection.

, ANNUAL TEA PARTY AND DANCE.

On Thursday evening the annual parochial te a party and dance in connection with St. Mary's Church was held in the Great Sankey Sunday School. Tea was on the tables at 6 30 p.m. and about 160 persons sat down to the tables, which were pre- sided over by the ladies of the congregation. After tea, the room was cleared, and dancing commenced at 8 p.m. Mr. Joseph Pownall was master of cere- monie.,and Mr., H. Stirrups' excellent band supplied the music under the leadership of Mr. Stirrup. There were. about 250 present at the dance which was kept tip until a late hour. he proceeds are in aid of the churchwardens' expenses.

. . COUNT' ToLsTor. On Wednesday evening, at the Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Societies' meeting, Mr. R. Garnett in the chair, Mr. John Gandy, of Warrington, read a paper entitled." Count Tolstoi." He gave a brief account ot, Count lolstoi's early years. lie was born on August 28th, 1828, and when he was two years old his mother died. His father died when he was ten, and he was atterwards brought up by his aunt. Mr. Gandy gave a description oc the books Tolstoi has written, and showed the ideas the author had in writing them. After his university career, he returned home to his estate, ancithere in- terested himself in trying to better the condition of his people, but they could not understand his ways, and he became disheartened and left the district. After this he employed his time in attempting to alleviate the condition of the beggars of Moscow. He was frequently deceived, however, some of them he found work for and others he provided tools for, but he often found they had slid back into their old ways and had sold their tools. In Moscow there are 50,000 poor paupers. In concluSion,the essayist recommended Tolstoi's works to the members. They were original and were written with the object of remedying the condition of the people and alleviat- ing the poverty and misery which is so prevalent amongst the poor class of people.in Russia. A dis- cussion followed, in which the following took part, the Chairman, Mr. Peers, Mr. White, Mr. SnoddY, land Mr. Watson. div.head: SANKEY.
div.p: SANKEY.

---- -- As stated a few weeks ago, there is a Movement on foot in Penketh and Sankey for seeing to their- being supplied with gas and water. Application has been made to the the Corporation of Warrington, who, as successor to the water company, will have the right to supply all water for this district, and the matter has this week been under the consider- ation of the Parliamentary Committee of the Town Council. It is estimated that the requisite supply would involve an outlay of several thousand pounds, and the question to be considered is as to the pros- pect of a demand equal to covering he interest upon this outlay. A deputation Was appointed to wait upon Mr. W. D. Jeans, solicitor, Warrington, who has the matter in hand,as representing certain rate- payers in the district to be supplied.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

REFUSING TO QUIT.—On Monday, at Oakmere Petty Sessions, George Fletcher, of the Five Crosses, Prod- sham, was summoned for being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Weaver Tavern, kept by Mrs. Sarah Edge, at Frodsham Bridge. on October 27th. P.C. Weatherley found the defendant in the tap- room fast asleep. He was drunk. He drew the atten- tion of the landlady to the man and his condition, when she said she had ordered him out, and that he had dis- obeyed her. He left when requested by witness.—Fined 2s. Bcl. and costs. TEFtEFT OE A COAT.—At Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday, William Ainsworth, platelayer,Frodsham, was charged with stealing a coat fro:n the shop of Messrs. J. Kay and Sons, clothiers, Main-st., Frodsham, on the 18th inst.—Ann Bullock, wife of H. Bullock, manager of the shop, spoke to seeing a man taking a coat from off a hook and run off with it.—Mrs. Eccleshaw, Newtown, Frodsham, said that at noon on the 18th inst. she saw the prisoner running along Main-st., with a coat under his arm. There waa a ticket attached to the garment. She shouted "You have been stealing," and thereupon he ran into the Queen's Head yard, threw the coat upon the wall, climbed over, and ran awaV.—P.C. Weatherly apprehended the prisoner, and charged him with stealing the coat from Messrs. Kay and Son's, in reply to which he said he did not know anything about it.—P. S. Doyle said the prisoner admitted the offence. Drink was the cause of it all. A fine of £1 and costs was imposed.

The Rev. J. Fell; one of the chaplains oi the Mersey Mission to Seamen, on Sunday evening preached a funeral sermon in the Mission room at Runcorn, on the death of Captain Charles Curtis. of the Schooner Blanche of Ply- mouth, who was with all hands, drowned through the wreck of that vessel on the East Hoyle Bank during the gale of the 7th inst. A collection on behalf of the viciovr and family realised £2 4s. Od., and a fund has been started at Plymouth with the same object, and the Duke of Edinburgh had contributed £5. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. Durrox's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. GASSED TO DEATN AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on Saturday, at Widnes Police Court, on the body of James Daley, aged 28 years, whose home was at 100, Cholmondeley-Si. Daley was employed as a fitter, at the Chemical Works of Messrs. Mathieson and Sons, and on the previous Tuesday, when fitting a steam pipe into a lead tunnel connected with an acid tower, the nitrous gas escaped. He complained of not being well. Hot tea and brandy were given to him at the house of the foreman and he so far recovered as to return to his work and finish the job in hand. On reaching home, however,he complained of being "gassed," and next day he died.—Dr. MacLennan said the deceased died from acute bronchitis probably caused by an irritant

gas. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-7. & W DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.-Advt. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Major Hazlehurst, and Mr. J. Handley, John Gleaves, carter, to Mr. Pilkington, contractor, Warringion, was summoned for cruelly illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. On the 13th inst, he was atAstmoor where he saw the defendant in charge of 4,Dree horses and a luny. The defendant was flogging tlie shaft horse, and the constable on examining the animal found a very large raw wound on the near shoulder. The horse was not in a fit state to work. Inspector Wilson R.S.P.C.A., deposed that the wound was 3 inches long and 1 inches wide, and it was stated that the defendant had used the wrong collar for the horse. A fine of ss. and costs 12s. 6d. was imposed. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.-Advt. HALTON COURT LEST, The Court Leet with view of Frankpledee and the Court Baron of her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen as Duke of Lancaster, Baron of Halton, Lord of the said manor and fee, was held on Saturday afternoon, in the Court-room at the Castle Hotel, Halton, the High Steward, Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, presiding. There was a good attendance, the following being pre- sent:-The Rev. G. D. Wray (Vicar of Halton), Messrs. H. Rowe (foreman of the jury), 'l'. Wright, John Lea, W. Stokes, H. Whitlow, C. W. Phillips, T. S. Burgess, C. Percival, T. Beswick, T. Lowe, A. H. Brook, Weir, &c. Messrs. J. Lea and W. Stokes were appointed burley- men, and Mr. A. H. Brook high bailiff. The oldest member present was Mr. T. Wright, who had been con- nected with the Court for 28 years, and has only missed one attendance. Afterwards the annual dinner was held, and the customary toasts proposed. ACME DOoR CHECKS AND SPRINGS.-Garland, Ironmonger, Earlestown and Warrington.-Advt. A HAPPY FAMILY AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Walter White was summoned for assaulting John Lewis, and the latter was charged with committing a similar Offence on Amelia White, his married sister.-Mr. .J. Burton appeared for Lewis, and Mr. E.W. Humphries for White. On Sunday the 16th, Lewis visited his father's house and It was alleged that he had no sooner got through the door way than White struck him two blows on the face and the father and a le`rother prevented further violence'. On the other hand, it was alleged that on the previous night Lewis had ejected Mrs. White from the house and used such violence that she was black and bruised in various parts of the body. On the Sunday; White wished for an explanation, and, words turning to blows, they had a set to for five minutes. The evidence was very contradic- tory. The summons against Lewis was dismissed and White was fined 25. 6d. and costs. , ROT WATER Ilzsme.-Garland sends estimates free. Warrington.-Advt. CONCERT AT ASTON. Under the auspices of the Aston, Dutton, and Preston Brook District brass band, a concert was held in the As- ton Board School, on Friday evening last week. A cap- ital programme had been arranged and the large audi- ence which crowded the room spent a most enjoyable time. The band, under the leadership of Mr. J. Woods, Runcorn, performed the overture "Minerva" and the waltz " Mia Belle," in a manner thar called forth unquali- fied praise. Mr. Kenyon sang" The holy Friar," with the necessary power and expression. Mr. J. Ravenscroft sang" He's in the Asylum now," in capital style, and in response to an encore gave 11 The powder monkey." The feature of the entertainment was the performances of Professor Miller, who udder three appearances sent the audience into convulsions of laughter by his humourous and amusing sallies, his repertoire including feats of conjuring, ventriloquism, juggling, and clowning, to- gether with songs, jokes, and conundrums. UMB.,,LLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-J. &W. BUTTONS Sankey-st.. Warrington.-ArA,t. BRUTAL TREATMENT OF A WIFE AT RUNCORN. Robert Nall, of Halton-road, was summoned at the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife, Eliza. The defendant pleaded guilty. The complainant said about half-past eight on the 20th of November, the defendant arrived home in drink, and abused her because she told him the chil- dren had eaten his tea. Be opened his pocket knife and told her to prepare to have her throat cut. She attempted to run away, but he struck her half a dozen blows on the side of the head and locked the doors. He then put the knife towards her throat, and she seized it and wrestled with him, and although he managed to draw the knife across her throat, it was the back side, the weapon having been turned in the struggle. Her hands were badly cut. She had been screaming loudly all the time, and the neighbours were at the door but could not burst it open, so she opened the window and tumbled out. -The defendant said he would not divulge" the secrets of his prison house." The magistrates could do with him just what they had a mind.-The complainant said she had never had a comfortable night during the sixteen years they had been married. He was continually threatening to murder her and she had left him a dozen times. He had never supported the children since they were born. He had never given her any money for three weeks, and there was never a Sunday when they had any meat in the house.-The Bench bound the defen- dant over to keepthe peace for six months, himself in £5 and two sureties of a similar amount, and to pay the costs. The defendant, who appeared to be without friends, was sent to gaol for two months in default. FLORiLnrE ! At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Jeaseph speak. man, of Witt-road, was sammoned by hie, wife Mary, for assaulting her. Mrs. Speakman also asked for a judical separation.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted, and stated that on Saturday night defendant returned home about half-past nine in a state of intoxication, and at once began to abuse his wife. He struck her a violent blow on the faee,"causing her a black eye. 7.e.then turned her out of the house, and afterwards appeared at a win- dow with a gun in his hand and threatened ta shoot her. The couple had been married 18 yearsylinct it WAS alleged that during that time he had subjected his wife to con- tinual ill-treatment.—The Bench sentenced the *defen- dant to a month's hard labour, and mated the wife a separation, at the same time ordering the defendant to pay ss. per week towards her support., FELONIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes fete; Sessions on Thursday, Joseph Killalea, of no residence, and Patrick McCreese, of Lugsdale-read, were charged on remand with stealing four ladies waterprooteloaka, value 245., from the shop of Thomas Jas. Dodd, draper, Waterloo- road. The cloaks were missed at Slime. on Saturday, and two boys named Michael Cawley and Jas. Duffy, deposed that they saw the prisoners run along Gerrard's Fold,and Killalea dropped the mackintosh produced. The other cloaks bad not been recovered.--The prisoners were corn- mitted to the Quarter Sessions for trial.—Ellen Coffey, of Runcorn, was also committed for trial on a charge of stealing 25i. from the person of Win, Rambling, of Sandy- lane, Weston Point. The prosecutor met the prisoner in Runcorn on Monday afternoon and "stood " her S'everal drinks. He afterwards accampanied her to a house in Pear-st, where he found he had been robbed. See our Almanack (Como along Jock) given with pb. of tea, Imperial Tea Co., Buttermarket-str., Warrington.—Ackt. ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT AT WIDNES. A young man named Albert Hornby, of Vine-st., was brought before the Widnes Magistrates on Thursday, charged with embezzling 0,15 e. id. from the Liverpool Sulphur and Copper Company,by whom he was employed. —Mr. W. T. Husband prosecuted, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. Mr. Knowles: admitted that several weeks ago the prisoner went to Liverpool, having in his posses- sion about 0 belonging to his employers. While in that city he got drunk,, and was, unfortunately,robbed of his employer's money. Since then he had been repaying this sum at the rate of 10s. per week. On the 15th inst., the prisoner was again sent to Liverpool and again got drunk,spending £31.5. id. of the money in his possession. Mr. Knowles contended that there was no felonious intention and added that the prisoner's friends were willing to refund the money. Haler these circumstances he asked the Bench to allow the case to be withdrawn. Mr. Husband agreed to this course and the magistrates , also assented. Prisoner was then discharged.

ANNOYED INTO A FIT AT RUNCORN. Thomas Outhwaite, of Parker-st., was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting a joiner's apprentice named Henry Gatley.— Mr. Burton appeared for the complainant, an Mr. E. W. Humphreys for the defendant.—Gatley said on the even- ing of the 19th November he walked past the defendant, who was standing between Bold-st. and Parker-st. He did not speak to him but when he got two or three yards away the defendant ran up to him, caught hold of him by the throat, and struck with a stick across the head and shoulders.—ln cross-examination witness denied that he had annoyed Mrs. Outhwaite. Corroborative evidence was given.—The defence was that the com- plainant and his companions were in the habit of annoy- ing Mrs. Outhwaite by shouting nasty expressions to her in the street, and it was alleged that on the previous evening to the one in question they had caused her to go into a fit which continued for several hours. The next night Mr. Outhwaite went to St. John's School to bring home his wife, and Gatley shouted obnoxious remarks to her, and Mr. Outhwaite administered a castigation, which he should ask their worships to say was well de- served .—Major Hazlehurst said while the Bench acknow- ledged that Mr. Outhwaite had received a certain amount of provocation, they did not think it was shown that Gatley committed the annoyance to his wife. —A fine of 10s. and costs 13s. 6d. was imposed. VOIMNTICEIW BALL. On Monday thenon-commissioned officers of the Ist Volunteer Battalion Prince of Wales (South Lancashire) Regiment held their annual ball in the the Drill Hall. Dancing was commenced at eight o'clock and kept up until three o'clock on the following morning, to music supplied by the band of the Regiment. which was under the direc- tion of Mr. S. Armstrong. There was about 150 couples present. The room had been neatly decor- ated for the occasion by the non-commissioned officers. Bugler-Major Plinston officiated as M.C. The refreshments were supplied by Pioneer-Sergt. W. Warburton. The following were amongst. those present ,—Lieut.-Colonel Bolton, Niajor Lister. the Rector ol Warrington (acting chaplain), Captains Ridgway, Gooch, Buckton, Baynes, Lieutenants Smith, Fdleston, Appleton, Chorley, and Fairclough, and Quartermaster T. Hutchinson. During an in- terval in the danoing,the health of Colonel Greenall was proposed by Sergeant-Major Fennelly and I drunk by all the volunteers and soldiers present in I uniform.

BITTEN BY A DOG : CLAIM FOR DAMAGES. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Deputy-Judge Goldthorpe, George Eccleston, a coal dealc: and carter of Peasley Cross, claimed £5O from William A. Duxbury, landlord of the Stanley Inn. Peasley Cross-lane, as damages for in- juries sustained by him through being bitten by a dog belonging to the defendant. ' Mr. B. H. Lomax appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. It was stated that on the 25th August last the plaintiff was delivering some coals at defendant's house, when the dog, a fox terrier, bit him on the thigh. Be was attended for a month by Dr. Casey, and he had to pay for assistance in his business during that period. Several neighbours were called to prove that the animal was vicious and snappish. For the defence Mr. Swift said that the dog was left by the previous occupants of the house, and the defendant was never warned that it was vicious or unsafe. He never knew it to be so. His Honour ultimately stated that he should reserve his decision. WOMAN, why:wOrk BO hard,? SMCLISST tOAP " does that, Try it —Advt.

METROPOLITAN RIFLE rtANGA COMPANV. It will be seen from our advertising columns that a limited Company, with the above title, has been formed for the purpose of purchasing over 1,000 acres of freehold land in Middlesex and Bucks, with a view to providing a small arms range and afford- ing the much-needed accommodation for rifle practice and drill instruction, for the various Metropolitan and neighbouring Volunteers. The capital is .EBO,OOO 1i 80,000 shares of .£1 each. There is every prospect of the venture serving a great public purpose, and proving an excellent invest- ment. The Secretary of State for War has given his approval of the site, and wished the Company every success. The rifle rangesiat present in existence in the neighbourhood of London are gradually being closed, and already the directors of the new Com- pany have promises to erect targets from Volun- teer regiments, rifle clubs, &c., representing about 10,000 men, whilst they are in communication with regiments representing another 10,000. It will be seen, therefore, that the Company has prospects of success which are of more than an ordinary kind. EXBMPTION P*o3l SERVICE ON CORONERS' Jtrnms. At the close of an inquest held' before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, at the St. he lens Town ! Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. T. Waterworth, , one of the jurors, asked at what age a man became exempt from serving on coroner's juries.—The Deputy Coroner said that when their names were taken off the lists of jurors for assizes and sessions, ' then they were fairly entitled not to be called upon by the police. But he did not see what could be done so long as their names remained on the lists. Mr. Waterworth said as far as he understood it that jury and other juries were not selected with such lists.—The Deputy Coroner replied that perhaps they were not always, but when a name or names had been taken from the list of possible jurors at the assizes, they knew the person or persons to be over 60 years of age, because, if he remembered rightly that was the age at which a man was en- titled to claim exemption. But until that was done a police officer had no means of knowing a man's age. Strictly speaking, people who were intelligent householders in the county of Lancaster were liable to serve as jurors, and the question for a policeman who had to summo 1 a jury was as to the intelli- gence of the man.—Mr. Waterworth said his name had been taken from the lists for this year. The Deputy Coroner said he had really nothing to do with the summoning of the jury. It was the duty of the police to do that, and if he had any com- plaint he must complain to the authorities.—Mr. Waterworth said he had no complaint to make.— The Deputy Coroner was quite sure if he repre- sented the circumstances to Chief Constable Wood, and stated that he had served his country long enongh in respect to juries he would not be again asked.—Mr. Waterworth said he had served on juries for 40 years.—The Deputy Coroner remarked that he thought Mr. Waterworth was quite entitled to ask Mr. Wood to excuse hira from future attend- ance. When a man had had 40 years experience, he thought he had done his duty in that respect, but. he (the deputy coroner) always regretted the loss of old faces.—The incident then terminated.

THINGS HEARD AND SEIM AT RUNCORN, &a. By 'AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDIINT."

That the bright frosty weather of the present week was warmly welcomed by the Runcorn people, who are in hopes that it will drive away the epidemic of typhoid fever from which the town is suffering. ' That the Runcorn Musical Society , has just past through the throes of a "great crisis- That in consequence of the better acoustic Prioperties of the Volunteer Hall, it has been arranged that the several concerts-of the season should be given in that building, but, unfortunately, ,the wife of Instructor Sorgeant Players has been for many weeks past,seriously ill, and this arrangement '.could not be carried out in consequence. ; That the conductor of the society, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys. declared that he would not conduct the Messiah, which is the subject of the next con- cert in the Public Hall, on the ground that the grand oratorio could not be ghen with credit in that building, and added emphasis- to his declaration by sending in his resignation to tlre Committee. That such an unlooked for blow-,coming within a very brief period of the concert, almost paralysed the Committee, and Mr. Humphreys was asked to reconsider his decision, but this-be declined to do, and the Committee eventually accepted his resigna- tion conditionally, that a general meeting of mem- bers approved. That such a meeting was hell on Tuesday even- ing, the occasion being honoured by the presence of the President, Mr. John Brundrit, and lively indeed were the proceedings. That Mr. Humphreys was. present and gave a speech explaining his position, and then retired until the subject was threshed) out with no lack of animation. That the ladies voted almost en Woe in favour of Mr. Humphreys being asked.once more to reconsider his decision, with the result that a motion to that effect was carried by a narrow majority. That a deputation was appointed to interview the Conductor, and Mr. Humphreys has consented to resume his position, take his wand in hand,and con- duct the practices and the concert.

div.head: RAILWAY SERVANTS CONCERT AT WIDNBS.
div.p: RAILWAY SERVANTS CONCERT AT WIDNBS.

With the object of increasing the funds of the Railway Servants Society Orphan Fund, a concert was held in the Baths Assembly Room, on Monday evening, when a large audience assembled. Mr. Eustace Carey pre- sided, and during an interval in the programme, he de- livered a speech in which he advocated the objects of the Society both to railway men and to public _support. He quoted figures to show the benefits to be derived from the society, and the necessity for its existence. In conclu- sion, he related an incident of graceful consideration on the part of a railway guard, which came under his obser- vation at Rugby, and said men possessing the valuable traits of most railway servants should not appeal in vain for public support. (Applause.) The quartette party from Runcorn, consisting of Nlessrs. Jones, and Birkett, and Messrs. Morris and Birkett, opened the programme with the carnovale (Rossini) which they rendered in a most finished and tuneful manner. In the course of the evening they also finely rendered "0 who will o'er the downs," "On the Banks of Allan Water," and "Softly falls the shades of evening," and their efforts were highly appreciated. Miss Poulson, who is the possessor of a cultured soprano voice,. contributed "Children's Home," and "The Bend of the River," and in response to an unanimous encore she sang "Coming through the rye." Miss Sunkin, Run- corn, was in capital voice and sang with admirable effect "Two merry hearts," " The Gift," and "Alone on the raft," and she obtained a recall for her rendition cf the last named song. Mr. Morrison, ever welcome to a Widnes audience, sang" When other lips" and "She was my boyhood's dream" with the requisiteexpression, and in response to an encore gave. "Queen of my heart," from "Dorothy." Mr. R. Morns (Runcorn) sang "Lon- don, Cheltham, and Dover" and " The blind sailors of Bristol," and the audience fittingly acknowledged his able vocalisation by a hearty encore. Mr. Hollinshead was also honoured with an encore for a splendid rendering of "Little Hero," he also contributed" Off to Philadelphia in the morning." Mr. W. E. Lancaster (Runcorn) ac- companied throughout in an able manner. At the con- clusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the proposition of Mr. Mear, seconded by Mr. J. Clarke, who announced that the concert had been a financial success. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-1. & W DITTTOIVB Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: SiffNDERING THEY LIBERAL CANDIDATE.
div.p: SiffNDERING THEY LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

By way of getting at the basis or lack of basis for the Tory slanders against the Liberal candidate, which have been circulated, the following correspondence has taken , place between Alderman•Platt and Mr. Loughlin : Lythgoe's-lane, Warrington, November 24th, MD. Dear have been asked to nominate you as a can- didatefor St. John's Ward. As an earnest Liberal,' give a warm support to, Mr. Gladstone's views as to Rome Rule, but I thing that any scheme for the separa- tion of England and Ireland would be disastrous to both countries, and I have no sympathy whatever witla dis- loyalty in any form. If.these are your views, I shalthave great pleasure in givingyou my cordial support. Yours truly, JNo. Pram—Mr: Felix Loughlin.

17, Buttermarket-st.,.November 24th, 1890. Dear Sir, —I have received your letter referring to the request that you should nominate me as a candidate for St. John's Ward. In reply to your enquiry, I have to say that I entirely, agree with the views you have expressed. It •is well known that I am an ardent supporter of Mr. Gladstone's i 1011143 Rule propasals,and, as to separa- tion, I have again and again publicly declared that such a policy would he disastrous to England, and still more disastrous to Irelanch. I give an emphatic contradiction to the slanders that, are being circulated to the effect that I have been a Fenian. I neither am, nor have I ever been a member -of that or any other secret society. There is no foundation, either, tor the absurd story that., on Jubilee day, I displayed a black flag with the repre- sentation of a skull and cross-bones. It is a ridiculous lie. What I did put out was a green flag, which had on one side the harp and "God save Ireland," and on the other " A Jubilse Gift to Erin : Coercion." This was a reminder to the Tories that their party had,. within a few weeks of .hibilee day, passed the worst coercion act that Ireland has ever known. I detest that measure to- day as I did then, ; and I am sure I am right in conclud- ing that other Liberals, after seeing the mischief it has done, abhor it as much as I do myself.. Trusting to have your support as a nominator, I remaim yours truly, F. Loccamus.—J. Platt, Esq., J.P.

Lythgoe'S•lane, Warrington, November 24th, 1890. Dear Sir,--r am pleased to get your straightforward reply to myletter, and your contradiction of the false reports which are being circulated in this Ward ; and shall nominate and support you with pleasure. Yours truly .imut Parr.—Mr. Felix Loughlin.

It wilt be seen that Mr. Platt is one a the nominator of Mr. Loughlin, and, it may be added, copies of th above correspondence were placarded on the wall' and distributed amongst the electors in the form o baudbitts.
