div.head: MEETING OF R. LOUGHLIN'S SUPPORTERS.
div.p: MEETING OF R. LOUGHLIN'S SUPPORTERS.

On Thursday evening a largely-attended meeting of the supporters of Mr. Loughlin, the Liberal candidate, was held in Brick-st. schoolroom. Alderman Platt was announced to preside, but it was explained that he•had written, expressing regret that, owing to a cold he had got through the severe weather, he would be unable to attend. Councillor J. H. Fleming was, therefore, elected to preside. There were also on the platform, besides the candidate, Pouncillors W. Pierpoint, J. Garner,. and H. Roberts, Mr. John Walker, Mr. Whitehead, and Mr. Clayton. The CHAIRMAN said he was sorry Alderman Platt could not be with them that night. As they were aware, Alderman Platt was an ardent Liberal, and, independent of that,he had a large stake in the town, and took a deep interest in its welfare. In Mr. Loughlin they I ad a can- 1 didate who was well known in the town, who was a res- pectable and an honest man, and who had shown that he was above any suspicion of doing anything that was in any way shaky. Some aspersions had been thrown at Mr. Loughlin, but he (the Chairman) knew that Mr. Loughlin would be able to meet them to the entire satis- faction of everyone. (Applause.) A resolution pledging those present to use all legiti- mate means to secure the return of Mr. Loughlin was then moved by Mr. Rain and seconded by Mr. W. DiceessoN. Councillor H. ROBERTS, in supporting the resolution, said that although Mr. Loughlin and himself were so dia- metrically opposed upon certain matters, they were in unity upon other matters, and it was a pleasure to him to be at that meeting that night. It was the first time in hi history that he had been able to come forward as aProtestant and as an Englishman to support the candidature of a matt who was a Roman Catholic and an Irishman. (Applause.) He did not, however; support Mr. Loughlin either because he was a Roman Catholicor an Irishman, but because he was of the same political faith as himself. (Hear, hear.) He did not Want to refer to the past history of local politics, but he would like to 'say that there was a time in the history of the Conservative party in War- rington when Mr. Loughlin and his compatriots were looked upon as gentlemen of the very first water. Things had changed since then, and the Tory party did not consider the Irishmen of Warrington with quite the same favour and in the same flattering light as they did a few years ago. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The Irishmen of Warrington now knew who their friends were, and they • were prepared to stand by their friends. (Hear, hear.) It was now the bounden duty of every Liberal not only in St. John's Ward,but in Warrington, to do what he could at the present moment to secure for the Liberal party in the Town Council a seat which rightfully belonged to it, and there was no doubt that if the Liberals of the Ward were loyal to their party Mr. Loughlin would be returned at the head of the poll. (Applause.) Having referred to the manner in which the Tories had made use of their majority in the Town Council, Mr. Roberts went on to say that they wanted help to purify the Watch Committee (Hear, hear.) The case of ex-Police Sergeant Shaw was one thing which showed that the Watch Com- mittee was either afraid to do the right thing or else it was incapable of doing it. He pointed out that although there were beine hauled up to the police court hundreds of men and women for being drunk,there was hardly ever one of the people who made these men and women drunk brought before the magistrates. What was the explanation of it? Let them look at the consti- tution of the Watch Committee, and they would find the explanation at once. Did they not think it was a dis- grace to have on the Watch Committee, a man who was a! brewer, a licensed victualler and the owner of several , beerhouses in the town ; while, at the same time, the 1 Conservative majority of the Council refused him (Councillor Roberts) a seat on the Committee because he was a teetotaller? Was that what they would call fair play ? (Cries of "No.") Mr. Roberts then I alluded to the allegations of disloyally made by the Tories ikainst Mr. Loughlin, and said he was surprised that a party which had so much to say about loyalty should support a member of the Orange party 1 which had been so conspicuously disloyal to the present 1 Queen. (Hear, hear, and applause.) 1 Mr. JOHN WALKER also supported the resolution. He expressed his pleasure at seeing the meeting so largely attended. It was cue of the best ward meetings he had seen in Warrington, and lie took it as an augury that they meant to do their duty on Monday next. (Hear, hear.) They must, however, keep in mind that that being a bye-election, and the Tories being disengaged in! other parts of the town, they would bring up their full numbers to secure the return of their candidate, and, that being the case. they Liberals should be ready to make sacrifices, and be determined that noLiberal voter should be missing on Monday. (Applause.) With regard to the attempts that had been made to disparage Mr. Loughlin, they found, when they had time to deal with those things, that they always reacted in favour of the man who had been abused. It was the Tory way to deal with matters of that kind. As a rule they had no principles to defend, and the only thing they could do was to abuse their opponents. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) If they were in earnest in that election, they would let the Conservatives of Warrington see that they could carry a Home Rule candidate for St. John's Ward, just as they intended to carry a Home Rule candi- date at the general election. (Applause.) They had in Mr. Loughlin a candidate who, he ventured to say, would be more than an average member of the Town Council. He would be a member of the Town Coun- cil who could bring more than an average intelli- gence to bear upon a great many important questions. ,Some of those questions he had referred to in his address.

He had referred in particular to matters of sanitation and the better housing of the poor, and he ventured to say that a great work needed .doing in Warrington in that respect, a work which would not be done except by men like Mr. Loughlin who inixed.with the poor. (Ap- plause.) He also pointed out that Mr. Loughlin was in favour of a free library and better baths. (Applause.) The resolution was then put pi the meeting and car- ried by acclamation. Mr. Looorttaii, on rising, was. received with loud cheers. He said there were two or throe of tha questions he had mentioned in his address whieh Very materially affected the well-being of many of the inhabitants of that ward. It had certainly not been a pleasure daring the past fortnight to go through scone of the streets of the 'ward, and he certainly thought the condition of those ,streets was nothing for Warrington to be proud of. He was of opinion that if many of the town cmincillors had been in the habit of going through those streets, they would have been altered. (Hear, hisar.), At the same time he could not help thinking that some blame rested upon many of the people who lived in those streets for , not " prodding" their representatives more than they had done. (Hear, hear, and laughter.), The Intercept- ing Depots, too, must affect a great many of the inhabi- tants, and he said, candidly. that he would not like to have one in the neighbourhood where he had to live. The golden rule applied there,, and what he would not like himself he would not wish others to have. (Applause.) The people living ,in the neighbourhood of the Depots were the people to know whether they were a nuisance or not,. and he believed they were pretty unanimous in the opinion that .the DepCits were at times, very offensive. He, therefore, thought the Town Council should be moved to either improve the Depots or do away with them altogether. (Hear, hear). Mr. Loughlin next spoke in favour of fraeing the library and improving the baths.. Their op- , ponents had, however, he said, chosen to fight that 1 battle on grounds entirely foreign to the issue. He was charged with being an Irishman—(laughter)---a charge which he could not and did not intend to deny. (Ap- plause.) He was next charged with being a Fenian, but he was not a Fenian, never• had been a. Fenian, and never should be a Fenian„ as he honestly believed there would be no more need for his countrymen adopting the means they for merly had to adopt. (Hear, hear.) Not only had they assaulted him in his naticnality, but they had also assaulted him in his creed. He had ascertained in going round canvassing that they had appealed to religious ' bigotry and if there was one thing more shameful than , another it was that. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had also charged him with great disloyalty for hang- ing out a black flag on Jubilee Day. The flag that , he:put out was not a black flag, nor had it upon it the 1 cross-bones and skull that it was said to have. (Laughter.) Mr. Loughlin then produced the flag which was of a faded green colour with the words "God save Ireland" on one side i • and a harp in the centre, and on the other side where the words, "Jubilee gift to Erin—Coercion," He had nothing to apologise for. At the time that flag was put out the Coercion Bill which had just beea passed and be- come the law of the land. The Mayor had invited the 1 townspeople to put etut the flags on Jubilee Day, and he did not think there would be any harm in patting that flag out just to remind the Tory party of the Jubilee gift they had given to Avland. (Hear, hear, and applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Loughlin referred in complimentary terms to the splendid services that were being given him by the English Liberal workers in the ward, and he sat down amidst loud applause. Mr. W. PIERPOLNT said he did not think fair play was being given Mr. Loughlin, and he thought it was his duty to come there that night to assure Mr. Loughlin that he had his utmost sympathy in the contest. With regard to those charges of disloyalty they all knew they were humbug from top to bottom„ and the men who gave utterance to them knew there was not a particle of truth in any of the statements. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that they had gone back years and years in eleclioneering,when they had all these kind of statements made use of in elections, and he thought their opponents had descended to something that was unfair and degrad- ing. (Applause.) He conciuded by moving a vote of thanks. to the chairman.
'I he vote of thanks was seconded byUouncillor Flood, supported by Councillor Shaw-Green, and heartily accorded. The meeting then ended. MEETING OF MR. HILL'S SUPPORTERS.

On Thursday evening a meeting in support of the can- didature of Mr. James Hill was held in St. Peter's Sfhoolroom, John-st. Councillor Robert Heaton occu- pied the chair, and there were also present Alderman J. Harrison, Councillors Dr. Cannell, Muir, and Hutchin- son, Messrs. A. W. Brundritt, W. Diggle, E. Mills, G. Jolley (hon. sec.), J. Hampson, and the candidate. The I Chairman read letters of apology for non-attendance I from Messrs. W. D. Jeans, John Roberts, and James Smethurst. He then said lie had great pleasure in ask- ing them to again support Mr. Hill, and he had no doubt that if they did their best they would return him at the head of the poll. They would see that Mr. Lough- lin said he put out a green and not a black flag, but he thought that that was merely a distinction without a difference. (Hear, hear.) Councillor moved a resolution in support of Mr. Hill. He remarked that he supported Mr. Hill principally because he was a Conservative, for before a man could be a Conservative he must be a thinking and intelligent man. Councillor Dr. CANNELL seconded the resolution, and said he supported Mr. Hill because, first of all, he was a workingman, and secondly, because he was a man of common sense, and was a man worthy to be a member of the Town Council. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON supported the resolution. Mr. Hill was not ignominiously defeated on the last occasion, and he (Alderman Harrison) would be disappointed if Mr. Hill was not returned by a majority double his pre- vious minority on the following Monday. If they voted for Mr. Hill they voted for a man who would endeavour to deserve the trust reposed in him. If they, on the other hand, voted for Mr. Loughlin they voted for an alien in nationality, an alien in blood, an alien in prin- ciple, and an alien, in short, of almost everything that was necessary to constitute a true patriot. (Applause.) Mr. HAMPSON supported the resolution, and said Mr. Loughlin was an Irishman at the head of the organisa- tion of men in the town, whose object was to get Horne I Rule for Ireland, whatever that might mean: (Laughter.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and car- ried with heartiness and unanimity. The CHAIRMAN, in calling upon Councillor Hill to speak, said with regard to Mr. Loughlin he (the chair- man), was once in a public-house some years ago with Mr. Loughlin and nine other Liberals, and the remarks Mr. Longhlin made conveyed to his mind that Mr.Lough— lin did not consider it a crime for anybody to murder a I Saxon. (Shame.) Mr. HILL, who vvaacordially received, then addressed the meeting, and remarked that he attributed his defeat r at the last election to the fact that he commenced can- vassing rather late and also that he had not sufficient workers. He was prepared to do what he could to im- prove the condition of the town, and he thought that he had already done a little in that direction. .He believed the common sense of the ward would prevail, and that he would be elected in preference to a Nationalist and Home Ruler. (Applause.) On the motion of Councillor Hutchinson, seconded by Mr. A. W. Brundritt, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman for presiding.

div.head: LYAI3I.
div.p: LYAI3I.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—A meeting of the members of the Wesleyan Band of Hope took place in the school- room on Monday evening. Mr. Alf. Robinson pre- sided, and a number of readings, recitations, &c., were

given. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—Sermons in aid of the above missions were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Lymm, on Sunday, by Mr. Birtwistle, of Didsbury. The congregations were not very large, consequent upon the unfavourable weather. ACCIDENT.—A young man named George Fairclough, son of Mr. J. Fairclough, of Lymm, met with an accident on Friday evening. Whilst climbing a ladder at the rear of the premises it gave way, and Fairclough fell te the ground. His arm was badly injured by the fall. Dr. Brabazon has since attended. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—COIIeC- tions were taken at the Parish Church on Sunday in aid of the above society. On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in the Parochial Schools, the Rector occupying 1 the chair. There was a good attendance. Mr. G.Ward, Manchester Diocesan secretary, was announced to be present. A miscellaneous entertainment was given. ALLEGED THEFT FROM A BEDROOM.—At the Lymm Police Court on Monday, before Dr. Brabazon, an old woman, named Mary Martin, was charged with stealing Bs. 6d. from the bedroom of Stephen Gibbons, at Sandy- lane, Lymm, en Saturday, the 22nd inst. Sergeant Christian said that the prisoner, who was a widow, visited Mrs. Gibbons, who was ill, on Saturday night. She stayed in the bedroom some time, and, after her departure,the money was missed. Information was given to the police, and he arrested her. The prisoner, who said she knew nothing about the money, was admitted . .
to bail until the next -Sessions.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

SYSTEMATIC ROBBBRY. At the Warrington ,Police Court on Thursday, John Bill was charged with having stolen a quantity of sack- ing value Is., the property of the Warrington Slate Com- pany, between Tuesday and Wednesday. Mr. Hunt said Mr. Roberts had informed him that a systematic robbery had been going on ter some time at the brick- field off Bewsey-road : and, in consequence of that in- formation he (the Chief Constable) directed Detective Monaghan to go to the field. From what was said to the detective, he, in company with another officer, went to the canal at Bewsey, and Monaghan then noticed defend- ant coming towards him carrying some sacking. The moment the prisoner detected Monaghan he dropped the sacking, and commenced to look around him as if noth- ing had occurred. The prisoner was accordingly taken into custody. Mr. Roberts said they had suffered from petty thefts a great deal during the last twelve months and they were now obliged to prosecute. Prisoner was committed to prison for one month with hard labour. CARRYING A LOADED REVOLTER. At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. P. Stubs, a young lad named Cornelius William Rooke, a turner, from Bradford, Manchester, was charged with having a loaded revolver in his pos- session, without giving a satisfactory account for the same. Police-constableWhitingham said he found Rooke at Martinscroft that morning at twenty minutes past one. He had then the revolver, powder, and bullets in his possession. The lad, on being asked by the magis- trates for an explanation, said he was paid off from the locks at Manchester because the works were stopped. He came to Liverpool, and as he could find nothing to do there he was returning to Manchester. He had been two nights without sleep, and was beginning to get dazed when the policeman took shim. He had lost his way owing to the roads being flooded. The revolver had been loaded since the sth inst. Sergeant Barnes said if the magistrate was satisfied with the explanation, he would not press the case. Rooke was discharged, the revolver being detained by the police pending inquiries. THEFT FROM A MARKET STALL. On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Mary Ann Hankinson of Cambrian's Place, was charged with stealing a pair Of child's boots value as. 9d. from the stall of Jos. Ridgby, in the Market Place, on Saturday even- evening.—Mr. Hunt said the defendant's husband left her about seven months ago, and went to America. About half-past eight on Saturday night defendant was seen at the stall in question by Isaac Bowers and his wife, who were assistants to complainant. They thought de- fendant's movements were rather suspicious, and watched her. At length Mr. Bowers thought he saw her put some- thing under her shawl and then walk away. Bowers fol- lowed her and said to her "Woman, I think you have some- thing under your shawl that does not belong to you ;" but defendant replied" No, I have not." Bowers then pulled her shawl at one side and found the boots, which he took possession of. Ultimately the boots were handed over to Detective Monaghan, and he arrested prisoner at her residence; and in answer to the charge she said "I did take thern."—Prisoner was dischaged with a convic- tion recorded against her. A SHOCKING ASSAOLT. A case of brutal and unprovoked assault was heard at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, the defendant being a Ship Canal labourer, named William White, who resides at Latchford, who was charged with assaulting a fellow-workman named George Sheldon, also resident at Latchford. Mr. Hunt stated that on Friday week, com- plainant had instructions to stop defendant and some other men from working. Defendant was annoyed at this; and, about a qua rter-past eleven on Thursday night complainant was proceeding along Knutsford- road, passing along Pin Mill, when the defendant went up to him.—Prosecutor said to him'' Well, now, come, I want no bother with you ; I'm going home."—Defendant then used threats, and struck complainant ; knocked him to the ground, and brutally kicked him. Defendant, along with a companion who was with him, helped com- plainant to his feet, and then defendant knocked him down again and kicked him; this being dose in the presence of a woman named Eliza Harris. Complainant was then lifted from the ground, and ultimately taken home. Evidence in support of this statement was given, by the prosecutor and Mrs. Harris; and Williams Barnes -defendant's companion, said the parties got to words about their work, which led to a quarrel.—Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or in default one month's imprison- ment with hard labour. As UNHAPPY ENGLISHMAN. Much amusement was caused at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, by the volubleness of a prisoner named John Well, a native of Birmingham, who was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, ire Bridge-st., on Saturday afternoon. After explaining to the magistrates the reason of his being in Warrington, defendant said that he was trying to get out of this rot- ten, poverty-stricken country. He was going to Liver- pool to endeavour to get on a ship to sail to another country, and, if he failed to get on a ship, he would drown himself. His right hand was mutilated, and he must get out of this country because he could get nothing to do. He had never beenin gaol, and he hoped the magistrates would not send him; in fact, it was not worth their while. In answer to further questions, defendant said he had been a military bandmaster for 27 years; but, owing to circumstances over which he had no control, he did not receive a pension. He was getting on in years, and he wanted to get on a ship at Liverpool as a stoker, so that he could get away from this dismal country. (Laughter.) He was a first-class musician, and—Alderman Harrison here interposed and said that English people appreciated music.—Defendant, continu-, ing said he had played in the streets and in public- houses, but certainly he had not made :a fortune. (Re- newed laughter.) In England there was beer in profu- sion, and workhouses and gaols were rising up, and all this made him think seriously sometimes. The Mayor said prisoner would be discharged on promising to leave the town at once.—Defendant thanked the magistrates for their leniency, and, amidst much laughter,he left the court, saying he would go away as straight as the crow flew.
FElDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the chair) and
Alderman Sutton:

ALLEGED MALICIOUS Tneners.—Mary Cogan was sum- moned for using malicious threats towards Michael Cogan, her brother, on the 20th inst.—Mr. Longland appeared for the defence. The complainant said he lived next door tog the defendant, and was afraid of his sister owing to her threats. On the day in question she threatened to see his head hanging when he came from the forge. Alderman Harrison, in dismissing the case, said it ought not to have been brought into Court. ARREARS CasEs.—John Armstrong was summoned for not contributing 2s. a week towards the support of his father who was chargeable to the Union. Defendant was ordered to pay 4s. a week until the debt, amounting in all to 21s. is cleared off, or in default, 14 days' imprison- ment—Enoch Jervis for the non-payment of LI. 14s. ed., arrears of a maintenance order, was ordered to pax the same within a fortnight, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment. ASSAULT CAszs.—John Dolan was summoned for un- lawfully assaulting Bryan Noon, on the 22nd inst. Com- plainant said on this date defendant went into his house and knocked him down. Defendant, who denied the charge, was ordered to pay the costs, and to give the complainant, who was an old man, 2s. 6d.—William Ed- leston and Martha Edleston were summoned for assault- ing Jane Dagnall, on Sunday. Complainant said on the day in question, shortly before ten p.m. the male de- fendant went to her house, and she ordered him out, , whereupon he hit her with his fist and knocked her down. The female defendant then interfered, and pulled , her by the hair of her head. Defendants were bound over in the sum of £5 each, to be of good behaviour to- wards complainant for six months.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. James Tinsley. A SERIOUS CRARGE.—An elderly man, named Wm. Shepherd, was charged with a serious offence under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, and was committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial. The prisoner was engaged as a foreman or stoker at the Padgate Industrial Schools, but did not;live in the Institution. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, prosecuted. Prisoner's application for bail was refused. MormAz.—Before Mr. Peter Stubs._

ALLEGED THErr.—A collier named John Yates was charged with stealing two silk handkerchiefs, of the value of 7s. 6d., the property of a fellow workman named Thos. BurchalLat Golborne, on the 17th inst. The case was remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions. WILFULLY FIRING A HAYSTACK.—The young man named Arthur Angus, of Manchester, who, on his own confession, wilfully set fire to a haystack, belonging to Mr. John Cross, butcher, of Corporation-street, at Arpley Meadows, on Thursday week, was charged at the Occa- sional Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Peter Stubs, for the offence. Evidence similar to what was last week published was given, and the prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Assizes. EXTENSIVE THErrs.—At this Court, on Thursday morn- ing, before Mr. J. Hylands, a man named Joseph Henry Lord, was charged with stealing a gold watch and chain and several coins, to the value of £3O, the property of Mrs. Charlotte Petford, residing at the Friendship Inn, Oldham-road, Manchester, and formerly a keeper of the Old Red Lion beerhouse, at Rixton. The prisoner was formerly ostler in prosecutrix's employ. It appeared that on the 25th May of this year, prisoner asked Mrs. Petford for an advance of wages. This she said she could not give him, whereupon prisoner said he would leave her employ next day. John Brooks, labourer, residing at Cadishead, on the 26th May was proceeding past the Red Lion in a trap, when the prisoner asked him for a lift, and Brooks accordingly took him up. Whilst going on the way towards Manchester, prisoner pulled out the stolen watch to see what time it was. When nearing Manchester Brooks also gave Ellen Perrin, of Hollins Green, a ride, and in her presence prisoner again pulled out the watch, and this time he remarked that he would not take 14 guineas for it. Mrs. Perrin thought the watch looked very much like Mrs. Petford's, and,-conse- quent on communications, Sergeant Barnes, of Padgate, on the 24th inst., went to Bacup, and arrested the pri- soner, who, in answer to the charge, said, "I hope I will get off with a light time, and I will never do it again." Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Manchester County Sessions.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Mr. Robert Garnett, and Councillor Voisey. NEGLIGENT PARENTS.—The case of James Healey, who was charged a fortnight ago with neglecting his family and remanded on his promise to pay Mr. Shearer £2, was heard. Mr. Shearer said that defendant had com- plied with the conditions as well as he could, and he was willing to withdraw the case.—The case against Charles Fairbrother for neglecting his three cnildren, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union, was adjourned for a fortnight to see whether defendant fulfilled his promises. Mr. Shearer said that the defendant's misconduct had cost, at various times, the Guardians over £2O. DRUNKENNESS IN THE PARK.—A man who gave the name of William Forster, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank Park the previous afternoon. —P.C. Bruen said he heard that the prisoner had insulted a lady in the park, and he took him into custody. The lady, whose name did not transpire, appeared in Court, and severely lectured the prisoner. She hoped it would be a warning to him, and to shun drink, "as it was the curse of the country."—The nrisoner, who promised to take the pledge if the max,- Istrates would look over the offence, was fined 10's. and costs, or 14 days' hard labour. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor Alderman Francomb (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, and Alderman Harrison. DRIINKENNESS.—EIizabeth Comberforth, in Dial-st., on Saturday afternoon, fined 2s. 6d., including costs ; Thos. Humphreys, at Bridge Foot, on Sunday night, fined is. Charles Collins, in Hind-st., on the 15th inst., fined 55.; and costs. Dunn' AND DISORDERLY.—Bridget Brannon, and E. Flanaghan, on Pinners' Brow, on the 17th inst., each fined 2s. 6d. ; Richard Warburton, in Foundry-st., o n the 15th inst.; fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days with hard labour. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—For this offence David Jones was , fined la. Frvrav llOUSES.—Thornas Bradbury of Kinder's-yard, off Old Road, Latchford, was summoned to show cause vrhy he should not abate a nuisance at his house. Mr. Norman, nuisance inspector, said there was a family of three and the house had only one room upstairs, and one downstairs. The house was in a filthy condition, and the bedding, he should think, had not been washed for a year, it as so black with dirt. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs, and to remove to a fresh house by Saturday. A similar case was heard against Mary Ward, (A 9, Edward-st., Bewsey, and she was ordered to pay the costs, she having removed out of the house com- plained of. THEFT OF CABBAOES.—A. labourer named Thomas Leatherbarrow, was charged with stealing from the field of Joseph Lawrenson,near St. James's Church, on Satur- day afternoon, two red cabbages, value Bd. The prisoner pleaded guilty. P.C. Meacock said he saw the prisoner hawking the cabbages in River-road, and he took him into custody. Sentenced to one month's imprisonment. TUESDAY.—Bef ore Messrs. E. J. Guest (in the chair), R. Garnett, and E. M. Crossfield. DRUNKENNESS.—Mary Jane Wolstencroft, in Hill-st., on Monday evening, fined ss. and costs. Scnoor. CASES.—A number of parents were summoned, for failing to send their children regularly to school, andl were fined in various amounts. The names of the offend- ing parents were :—John McDonough, William Banes,l Thomas Bury, Martin Carey, John Clare, Thomas Fearn-1 by, Michael Flynn, John Henry Gordon, Edward, Murray, Daniel Savage, William Crank, Robert Adams, and Joseph Cryan.—The magistrates decided that Clare's boy should be birthed, and that the lad McDonough should be sent to Father Nugent's Industrial School at Liverpool. The attendance of several of the children was most discreditable to them and to their parents. WEDNESDIY.—Before Alderman Holmes (in the chair), Alderman Platt, and Mr. J. Fairclough. DRIINKENNESS.—AmeIia Outram, in Bridge-st., on Tuesday night. Fined ss. and costs or seven days. DRUNKENNESS AND ASSAULT.—Annie Daley was charged with having been drunk in Mersey-st., on Tuesday night; also with assaulting Patrick Mitchell at the same place. She was found, 55. in each case, or 14 days' roprisonment

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Bef era Messrs. E. G - • . Low,. MINOR CAsv.a.—A cripple named Richard Sullivan, was arged with having been drunk and disorderly at Moore on the 2nd November and was fined ss, and costs. Herbert Percival, for allowing his dog to be at large at Little Leigh, on the 23rd October, was fined ss. includ- ing costs. John Buttery, for a similar offence on the 24th October at Dutton, Edward Paley at Little Leigh on the 23rd October, and William T. Whitlow, 10th November, at Preston Brook, were likewise fined.—A Warrington carter, named John Ward was summoned for being asleep in charge of two horses and a lurry at Walton, on the sth November. A fine of Sc. and costs was imposed.—William Whalley, for a like offence at Appleton on the 20th November, was similarly fined. WARRINGTON BUTCHERS SIIMMONED.—Maria Preston„ butcher, Buttermarket-st , Warrington, and William Gill, butcher, Bridge-st., Warrington, were charged with I contravention of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by causing to be removed a cow, on the 25th October, through a pleuro-pneumonia infected area, and the latter with removing two heifers and one bullock without a 1 license authorizing him so to do. Mr. A. Browne ap- peared for the defendants and pleaded not guilty.—Ser-1 geant Booth said that on the day in question he visited, the farm premises of Messrs. Greenall and Company and examined the stock. He found the cattle mentioned . above with Messrs. Greenall's. The defendants had no license to move the cows out of Lancashire. They had only a license to move them in the borough.—Mr. Browne, for the defence, explained that the cattle had strayed out of a field in the borough into another in the county. He admitted the facts of the case, but con- tended that his clients could not be charged with caus- ing the cattle to be removed. The Bench thought the cattle ought to have been better looked after and pre- vented from straying. Mr. Browne said the point was a technical one, and on his promising to pay the costs the case was dismissed—Thomas Ford, farmer, Latchford, was summoned for contravening the order on the Bth November, by removing 20 cows and a bullock. It was stated that the defendant's premises were partially situ- ated in Lancashire and partially in Cheshire. P.C. Mil- lington proved the case. Superintendent Large said that the county had to pay £3OO to the defendant three months ago for compensation, and the consequence was that it was now prohibited for cattle to be removed from one county to another in that particular district. It was stated that the defendant was liable to a penalty of £lO5, five pounds for each cow. The Chairman said it was a very serious offence and fined the defendant £5 and costs. CHAFFING A TEETOTALLER.—A young man named E. Young was summoned for assaulting Patrick Shaugh- nessy, a Ship Canal navvy, at Appleton, on the 3rd Nov- ember. Mr. Browne appeared for the defence.—The complainant said that on the day in question he and the defendant " had some words" with one another and eventually Young struck him and cut his eye.—Mr. Browne said both parties were equally to blame. His client's hand was hurt more than the complainant's face. A gentleman who had been visiting the canal gave eight of the men 2s. between them, and they ad- journed to a neighbouring public-house for drinks. The complainant asked for some brandy, and knowing he was a teetotaller chaffed the complainant. This led to the quarrel. The case was eventually dismissed.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAT.—Before Major Harlehurst and Mr. James Handley. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For being drunk and dis- orderly Thomas Fowler, Joseph Griffiths, Alfred Griffiths, Dora Hayes were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. Ellen Coffey, an old offender was fined 10s. and costs.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. F..H..Gossage and Mr. H. Gas-

kell, jun. DRIINHENNESS.—For this offence Albert Flollingworth, Albert Hotel, Widnes, and Edward J. Paterson, Mersey- road, were each fined fis. and costs.—Michael Keegan, Water-st., Michael Allen atild Walter Allen, Pleasant-st., were each fined 10s. and eosts. DRUNK is CHARGE.--.George Johnson, farmer,Cuerdley, pleaded guilty to being (bunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, and he was fined 20s. and costs, or a month.

• indeed after so brilliant a run. The oval was Worked away, and just before the call of half-Vme Gresty forced a minor, after which he was hurt in gathering the drop out, half-time being called as Warrington 1-1-0 ; Rangers 0-0-2. Direct on the restart a speedy invasion was made to the Broughton quarters, but Storer and Edge beat a retreat and Parker trying to force an opening found his ' mattivin Lloyd. Barnes dribbled well, and from an ex- act dribble, wholly manipulated by Berry, the ball was capitally worked through the opposing defence, and a grand try was the result, Evans failing to augment the point. The visitors now set to work with a will, and more than held their own. A series of interesting for- ward movements pressed the homesters, and Parker, with a well-judged run, compelled a minor to be con- ceded. Another fine dribble by Berry was the only in- dividual play that could be gleaned, and as the darkness was fast approaching it was impossible to distinguish the players when the game was being contested on the popular side. Suffice it to say, the Rangers had a trifle the best of it, but only added a minor to their score, and an hour's vlaved ended as Warrington, 1-2-0 ; Broughton Rangers, 0-0-4. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscoe, back; H. Webster, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs; John Bate and H. Rowe, half backs; H. Ashton (captains, Fair Turner E. Dillon, J. Lloyd, W. Bandies, W. Povey, J. T. Thomiley, W. Berry, and J. Holmes, forwards. Broughton Rangers: C. Wardley, back ;E. Gresty. H. Chapman, and E. Parker, three-quarter backs ;W. Edge and T. Wall, half backs; J. Jackson, A. R. Wheeler, W. Storer, E. Higginbottom, S. Oman, W. H. Longworth, J. Fitton, and .1. Pickard, forwards. Referee, Mr. S. Williams (Salford.) ,

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RECS. T. STOCKTON 11EATFI.—Thi8 match was played on the Rees% ground and resulted in a win for the home team by one goal, dropped by Roughly. ORFORD RANGERS, v. BLUE COAT RANGERS.—A match between the above named teams was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and, alter a very good game, ended in a victory for the Orford Rangers, by 3 goals' 7 tries, 6 minors Blue Coat Rangers, nil. ORFORDRANGERS 2ND V. BUIE COAT RANGERS.—This macth was played on the ground of the former on Satur- day. After a few minutes fine play by the borne team Lawless landed a splendid try failing at goal. Orford charged down the kick off, Lawless getting a second try and a goal resulting: Ruttittr gct a third try for the home team. Other tries were secured by Looker,Rutter, and Lawless, the game ending—Orford Rangers, 3 goals, 5 tries, and 4 minors; Blue Coat Rangers, nil. Wmtres V. MOSSLEY.—At Widnes, before a good atten- dance, Smith opened the play, which at once settled down in the Mossley quarters. After a severe pressure Peter's scored, and Brennan converted the point. Re- suming, Mossley pinned their opponents, but could not score, and on Stubbs passing to Peters, that player notched his second try, which Brennan failed to im- prove. With a lead of a goal and a try the teams changed ends. For a time the play ruled even, but at length Widnes held their opponents well in hand, but could not add to their score, a hard game resulting— Widnes, 1 goal and 1 try ' • Mosslev, 2 minors. WARRINGTONRANGERS V. RED ROCK (Wroas).—Played at Warrington. Whitfield, on behalf of the home team, kicked off, and no return being made, the visitors were at once defending, but by strong forward play they cleared to neutral ground, neither side scoring up to half time. Upon the restart both teams played with great dash, Ashurst, Clare and Savage being prominent for the Rangers, but eventually the visitors captain obtained possession, and after a strong rush secured a try, which remained unimproved. This being the only major point in the match the strangers retired 'victors by I try 1 minor to 2 minors. Rtmcorm v. LENDS.—This match was played at Run- corn, in wretched weather. The game opeled at a great pace, and after some spirited play in the Tykes' quarters a passing movement by Evans, Abrams, and Crompten, i resulted n the last-named scoring, but the place kick was unsuccessful. After the drop out the play became exciting, and the ball travelled up and down in quick succession. Riley headed a strong rush, but the visitors retaliated, and Davies in his own 25 intercepted a pass,. raced the length of the field, and scored, but again the kick at goal failed. The Runcornians had the best of the second half, and late on a nthvement by Abrams and Hampson was followed by a try by Hancock, Crompton this time piloting the ball over the bar. Leeds failed to add to their score, and were beaten by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 4 minors, to 2 minors.

WARRINGTON STAR v. ST. HELENS RECREATION 2ND.— The above match was played at St. Helens on Satur- day. The visitors started in a drizzling rain and with onlyl3. men, and after some even play the Stars forced a minor. The Recs. then came with a rush and gained a minor, score at half time 1 minor each. The home team kicked off and took the play to the visitors lines, but the Stars again took play to half way. From a line out, the Recs. scored a try and also kicked a goal. Owing to the heavy showers, the visitor's captain called time, leaving the home team winners after an uninteresting game. Score: St. Helens Recs., 1 goal and 1 minor • War- rington Star, 1 minor. Barratt and Newey played a good game for the visitors, and Bolton and Turton for the Recs. side. WARRINGTON A v. 13ROLTONTON RANGERS A.—This annual fixture was decided on the ground of the last- named club on Saturday. A slight mist prevailed when Shaughnessy started the game, causing play to hover about the visitors' 25. After the ball had been trans- ferred to neutral territory, Mather got away and passed to Jolley, who effected a magnificent run through his opponents, ending by punting over the line. A ra, then ensueda bic opponents, 0- vrT"S. ar-Thentht

----seierto a bad kick lost posses- sion, and only a minor was allowed—a piece of very hard lines. Following this, a spell of pretty passing between Williams and Mather to Jolley was spoiled by a bad pass, the Rangers racing away to midfield. At this time War- rington werehaving decidedly thebest of matters,a grand dribble by Jolley, Turner, Teare, and Davies forcing the leather to the line, where a rare chance was missed. A strong attack was kept up, Williams, Knowles, Moly- neux, and Creaghan being notable; but eventually Hcward completely altered matters by a grand run, caus- ing play to fluctuate on the centre line. Some smart work by Massey caused the oval to be momentarily located in the home quarters, Kennedy ultimately reliev- ing. and enabling his side to be attackers. Notwith- standing drawbacks the play now became animated, and a grand piece of passing by Knowles, Isherwood, and Jolley transferred matters to more desirable quarters. In close following, Teare, Mather, Barnes, and Davies drib- bled finely to the goal, but only a minor was registered. Again the Rangers were pressed, chiefly owing to the instrumentality of Turner, Phillips, Creaghan, and Moly- neux, and directly afterwards Barnes was almost in. Nowell and Shaughnessy then headed a rush to halfway, but Massey, intercepting a pass, ran and kicked to the home quarters, half-time arriving with Warrington two minors to nil. The players were in a pitiable plight on restarting, but Barnes, Davies, Isherwood, and Phillips rushed the ball over the line, Roberts subsequently smartly getting the oval to midfield. The ball then rapidly travelled about, Turner, Teare, Primrose, and Dalton being prominent for their respective sides. Samp- son was next called upon to defend his charge, which he did splendidly. The position was further improved by a grand pick up and kick by Daniels, and a try obtained, but disallowed. Immediately afterwards Williams secured an unimproved try. From the drop out the Rangers rushed to neutral quarters, where Williams saved a dangerous rush. The old position was soon re- gained, however, by some clever play by Daniels, and Mather took the oval further into the Rangers' lines. The ball then hovered about midfield, until Massey got away with a run and kick. The Rangers, by some good foot work, nullified, but Sampson, who was again playing a safe game, was not to be passed. A grand rush by Knowles was further enhanced by Turner, Davies, Molyneux. and Isherwood. Nowell relieved by a strong run, but Massey stopped his career. The remainder ot the play was played in semi darkness, and it was impos- sible to follow the game. Warrington 0-1-3 to nil. Warrington: Sampson, back ; Daniels, Jolley, and Mason three-ouarters ; Mather and Williams half backs: Moly- neux, Creaghan, Isherwood, Knowles, Turner, Teare, Barnes, Phillips, and Davies forwards. Rangers: M'Cresh, back; Adams, Kennedy, and Lane three- quarters: Rainford and Roberts half backs ; Shaughnessy, Nowell, Howard, Primrose, Dalton, Quinnay, Dickinson, Shore, and Green, forwards.

WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS. Fresh from their victory over Swinton, the Rangers encountered Warrington at Wilderspool, on Saturday, before three thousand spectators. The weather was of a dull description, but despite the heavy rain of the pre- vious days, the ground was in capital order. The Rangers played their strongest fifteen, a remark which certainly could not be applied to the Warring- tonians. It was 3.30 before Fair Turner kicked off towards the pavilion goal, and Ashton foiling Parker's attempt to reply, hostilities were at the onset opened at Broughton quarters. A short bout of passing, followed by Parker putting in a kick, was neutralized by Povey, who dribbled with neatness, and the advantage lost by the Warringtonians was speedily regained. The Rangers' forwards, ever noted for their smart play, at once showed that they had in no way deterioratedoand,taking advan tage of some scrambling play by their opponents, worked the oval by degrees to the Warrington line. Boscoe and Evans each had an anxious time of it, but both gallantly stood their ground, and eventually Barnes cleared, Parker luckily saving as Wairington were bent on scor- ing. It was left to the visiting forwards once more to work the oval out of danger, which they did with credit, and after Boscoe had saved on the line when the other home backs had failed, Ashton, Bate and Bandies each with equal efforts changed the scene to the quarter flag. Barnes now ran and passed to Webster, and play was again located at the visitors' quarter flag, but Jackson, ever prominent amongst the Rangers' front van, with an exact dribble, took the game once more within easy each of the railway goal. The combination of the home backs at this point was invaluable, for after a spell of passing by the home backs, Evans was sure to have scored but for slipping in taking their opponent's pass. Fair Turner punted into touch at the Broughton 25, and then a wide pass travelled to Gresty, who fell into Webster's long reach, and, of course, did not travel 'far. Wardley and Webster exchanged kicks, and then the home forwards, realizing their position, responded to .a call from their supporters, and the game was fixed at the corner flag. From a line out, Turner passed to Bate, who: handed over to Bandies, and a clever try was the result, Barnes placing a neat goal. A minor resulted from the restart to the visitors. Broughton aggressed in deter- mined style, and charging a kick of Turner's under the post they all but scored. Rowe, Bandies, Berry, and Dillon worked the oval out of danger, and a fine rum by Evans resulted in a final pass not being taken, and a score lost. It, however, led to a brilliant piece of work by Bate, who, after tricking Edge, puzzled Gresty, and finally passing to Webster the latter easily shook off Wardley and a try was the result, Evans failing with the difficult place. No sooner had the drop-out been effected than a short passing movement saw Barnes transferring to Webster who ran through the thick of his opponents, and alter a long chase, a Ranger, who had been tempor- arily disabled came to the assistance of his side, and Webster was pulled up on the line. This was hard lines

FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

- The fixture between Lancashire and Westmorland at Kendal, on Saturday, was fought out under the most dismal conditions, in regard to weather, and in the pres- ence of a very ordinary gate. All things considered, the visitors acquitted themselves astonishingly well, the large score being remarkable for such an afternoon. A victory by four goals and four tries is strong testimony to the brilliant play of the Lancastrians, who,as may be imagined, had never much anxiety as to the result. After the first few minutes, indeed, the game became very one-sided.

So far the men of Lancashire have swept the board. In all their three matches they have come through with credit, and with Marsh as centre three-quarter there is every reaSon for hope as to the big contest of to-day. All the back division have done extremely well in every engagement, and with the Swintonian in the place of Gwynn,the backs will be stronger than for some seasons. They have had the advantage of playing together on three successive Saturdays, and this should assist them very materially against Yorkshire. Although Berry was not in the best of health at Kendal, he again showed his great worth, whilst Coop's display at full back admitted of no grumbling. The forwards pulled well together, and this department is now a vast advance on the lot that did duty against Cheshire. There is no shirking of work.

Although Yorkshire had not much difficulty in shaking off Northumberland, they had not such a balance in their favour as had the Lancastrians a week ago. Moreover, the Yorkshiremen were playing at home and not away, as was the case with the victors in the other game refer- red to. If comparisons are worth anything, therefore, the battle of Roses should this year be anything but a gift for the county of many acres. The Yorkshire for- wards did not satisfy the critics on Saturday, and they wore not a whit better than the scrimmagers on the other side. Behind the pack, however, there was a difference. Mawson (Otley) wts a smart full back, and Lockwood as clever as usual at three-quarter. Dyson and Stadden are expected to be in the team that come to Whalley Range at the end of the week.

-- The Lancashire County Committee met on Tuesday evening, and selectod the following team tor at the Palatine against Yorkshire, at Whalley itange, to-day (Saturday) :—T. Coop (Leigh), full back; J. Valentine (Swinton), J. Marsh (Swinton), and E. H. Flower (Broughton), three-quarter backs; J. Berry (Tyldesley), and W. Bumby (Swinton), half backs; R. P. Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), T. Kent (Salford), J. Strang (Liverpool), T. Craven (Salford), T. Brayshaw (Wigan), T. Bothwell (Swinton), W. Atkinson (Wigan), T. Whittaker (Manchester), and J. Pike (St. Helens Recreation), forwards. Reserves: W. B. Steel (Man- chester), back; M`Cutcheon, Gwynn, and Sudlow, three- quarter backs; Nolan, half back; Rome, Bullough, and Paul, forwards.
vuumy

Football accidents of a fatal nature are happily rather rare, but Leeds has lately had a couple to account for. Two young fellows, named Armitage and Scholey, have died at the infirmary of that town from injuries received whilst playing the Rugby game. Both were pure acci- dents, and it was stated that there was no rough play in any way.

"The suspension of a Warrington player for abusing a referee, should, a Manchester paper remarks, have a salutary effect. Gentlemen who officiate in matches cannot have too much protection. As a rule, players abuse referees with great liberality, but this lesson is not likely to be thrown away." The Warrington player is F. Nevins, and the unparliamentary language he used was on the occasion of the Wigan match, when the re- feree in the opinion of others besides himself, was not altogether impartial.

In the three matches they have played this season Lancashire have scored nine goals and eleven tries to one try. Valentine and Flower have each obtained five tries, and Berry and Gwynn two each, so that the three threequarters have had most of the fun to themselves. Singularly enough, Valentine did not score once last Saturday.
Bradf(ard are the only team that have beaten Runcorn yet this season, and none have touched them yet on their own ground since the Maories' match.
ASSOCIATION.

The position of the topmost clubs in the League under- went another change on Saturday. By their failure at Deepdale, Everton again give way to Wolverhampton, who gained another point at Nottingham. The North End came out of their shell for once in a way, and beat the Liverpool club by two goals to nothing. They had quite this much of the game, their forwards showing splendid combination, whilst the back play was sound- ness itself. The Evertan forwards have fallen away very perceptibly, having lost their goal taking power almost completely. Geary, their flying centre, is now rarely conspicuous. The match between Notts and the Wolverhampton Wanderers was fiercely contested, but of scientific play there was very little. Notts came very near being beaten at home for the second Saturday in succession.

Up to the interval,Burnley had the pull in their return with the Rovers at Blackburn, but the change of ends brought a gre.t change in the operations. The cup- holders delighted their large following, and ultimately won by five to two. The Rovers are just now doing grandly. The Bolton Wanderers cut up roughly at Bir- mingham. Not many weeks ago they ran away with Aston Villa by four goals to none, but now the tables were reversed, the Boltonians being beaten by five to none.

It was unfortunate for Sunderland that they should visit Accrington on such a terrible day as Saturday. The ground is never one of the best, but now the rain reduced it to a perfect quagmire. No wonder, therefore, that the Wearsiders could make no show at all. West Bromwich Albion fell before Derby County, a result that was hardly looked for.

div.head: MANCHESTER POISONING CASE.
div.p: MANCHESTER POISONING CASE.

John Corfield, a carter, was charged at Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, with the murder of his two chil- dren and the attempted murder of his wife by putting arsenic in their food. Eventually, however, the charge of murder was withdrawn, and prisoner, being con- victed of manslaughter, was sentenced to penal servi- tude for life.

div.head: DEATH OF THE KING OF HOLLAND.
div.p: DEATH OF THE KING OF HOLLAND.

Count de Bylandt, the Netherlands Minister in Lon- don, received a brief telegram at the Legislation on Sunday morning, announcing that the King of Hol- land died at six o'clock a.m. Sir Horace Rumboldt, the British Minister at the Hague, sent a similar des- patch to the Foreign Office, adding that his Majesty had been unconscious for some time previous to his death. A Reuter'stelegram from the Castle of Loo,dated Sunday, says :—The King of the Netherlands expired peacefully at a quarter to six on Sunday morning. The Queen, with Dr. Vlaanderf and Dr. Roessingh, spent the night at the King's bedside, remaining until the end. The religious service which was to have been held at the Royal Chapel, has been conntermanded. The shutters of the royal palace are closed, and the flag on the build- ing is flying half mast. A Reuter's telegram from Berlin of Sunday's date states that the Emperor has sent a telegram to Queen Emma of Holland expressing condolence on account of the King's death. His Majesty has deputed Prince Albrecht the Regent of Brunswick, to represent him at the funeral obsequies. William 111. (Alexander Paul Frederick Louis), King of the Netherlands, Prince of Orange-Nassau, Grand ,Duke 9f Limburg, born February 19th, 1817, the eldest -son of the late King William H., by the Princess Anne Pauline, sister of the late Nicholas 1., Czar of Russia, succeeded March 17, 1849, and devoted himself to the development of the Liberal institutions tlaen recently granted to this counntry.

div.head: CONNEMARA DIVORCE.
div.p: THE CONNEMARA DIVORCE.

In the Divorce Division on Thursday, before Sir J. Hannen, the case of Connemara (Tweedale and Brigs in- tervening) came on. Lady Connemara sued for the dis- solution of her marriage on the ground of her husband's alleged cruelty and adultery. Answers had been filed denying the charge. The respondent did not appear. Lady Connemara, Sir Robert Peel, and Sir James Fergus- son were present. Mr. Lockwood opened the case for the petitioner, who went to India with Lord Connemara in 1886. They resided at Government House until the petitioner felt compelled to return to England in 1889. Evidence would be given of the alleged adultery with a servant, taken on commission. As regarded the charges of cruelty, it was only recently that certain facts came to Lady Connemara's knowlAge which enabled her to ap- preciate the conduct of the respondent towards her. After filing the petition she received medical advice, which revealed the nature of the treatment her husband' had previously recommended to her. There was no foundation for the counter charge's against the petitioner. Lady Connemara was examined. She denied the charges against her. Dr. Sutton, Dover, spoke to prescribing for LadyConnemara in 1875. Dr. Baker said he prescribed for an affection of the tongue. He had suspicions about the nature of the malady. The evidence of Hannah More wasreadof respondent's connection with her. Sir James Hannen, remarking that the evidence fully established the charge against the respondent, granted a decree nisi.

div.head: BOLTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE BOLTON TRAGEDY.

RESUMED INQUEST. Mr. S. F. Butcher, coroner for the district, resumed his inquiry on Saturday into the death of Miss Holt, the young schoolmistress who was murdered in Longworth Wood, near Bolton. A startling piece of evidence was given by the aunt of the prisoner. Hitherto Macdonald's connection with the crime has been assumed from purely ' circumstantial evidence. Every known fact pointed to him as the murderer, but the testimony was by no means complete. Honor Bann, the aunt of the prisoner, makes the case strong against him. Macdonald himself has, she says, confessed to her that he murdered the poor girl. Miss Bann's position is peculiarly pathetic. She is an old woman, an unmarried sister of the prisoner's mother, aud has spent a long life in the mill. Macdonald has been the burden and care of her life. From infancy

she has maintained him—except during one long spell of his imprisonment—on her hard-won pittance. He has been her one source of unhappiness and anxiety. Through this last crime of her nephew she is out of work arid, one might also add, out of home, and for the present is treated as a social Pariah. • Since Macdonald's arrest her fellow workers at Eger- ton Mills have declined to have her amongst them. , They blame her for having harboured the son of her dead sister, knowing his worthless and danger- ous character. Everyone who saw the weeping, kindly looking old woman on Saturday felt pity for the unfor- tunate creature. In the early part of her evidence she broke down, cried bitterly, and looking at the prisoner, cried "Oh, Tom! oh, Tom !" Macdonald was the one callous man in Court. With something of contempt he looked at her, asked" What's the matter ?" and told her to go outside and calm herself. A few seconds later he more than taken aback, while the Court was thrilled,

by the first direct piece of evidence yet given. She com- posed herself, wiped her eyes, and then, in Lancashire phrase, unburde,ed herself of a terrible secret. "It's no uselapping it up," said she, and thereupon she told through her sobs the prisoner's confession to her of guilt. On the day of the murder he came to her at the mill and asked her to come out because someone had come from America. She went out, and then he made confession that he had murdered Lizzie Holt. He spoke of giving himself up; she in bitterness advised him to go and I drown himself. Then followed the five days of quietness, during which the mother thought Lizzie was at school and the school master imagined her at home, her body being all the time under the three oak trees in the wood. Honor Bann says she asked no questions of Macdonald during those days. She seems to have half hoped that his confession was untrue, but was yet afraid that her fears might be confirmed, as they sadly were. While the old ,woman told her story the prisoner listened with .a -flushed face, and subsequeritty-ne erassx...t.ad-herja a quick, nervous way. He suggested to her that ne had told her a different tale, to the effect that he heard screams in the wood and that someone else had committed a murder; but Miss Bann was firm in what she had before said. The other evidence given during the day showed that Macdonald closely followed Miss Holt on the morning Qf the murder. Most of the afternoon was occupied with the statement of Dr. Robinson, the import of which has already been published. The Court sat from ten in the morning till six at night, and the inquiry was then adjourned. FULL AND FORMAL CONFESSION.

- Thomas Macdonald was on Tuesday committed, on the coroner's warrant, to take his trial at the ensuing Liverpool assizes en the charge of having wilfully mug- dered Miss Holt, in Longworth Wood, on the 10th in- stant, Towards the close of the inquest the accused made a full confession of his crime. Benjamin Shackle- I ten, sergeant at the County Police Office, Haugh, Bolton, was examined by the Coroner :—During the adjourn- ment of the Court at 6.45, did the prisoner send for you ? He did, sir. And you said, "Before you say anything else I will see my superintendent ?" Yes. You went for Mr. Eataugh ? Yes, and returned with him to the pri- soner. What did you say then? I said, "Whatever statement you make must be unconditional, without reservation." He said, "All right, but I would rather it was not read to-night." Then did he make a statement to you ? I got a piece of paper and wrote on the top of it "C. P. 0., Bolton, 25th November, 1890. Statement of Thomas Macdonald, in the cells at the county police station. Bolton, 645

div.head: MACDONALD'S STATEMENT.
div.p: MACDONALD'S STATEMENT.

Sergeant Shackleton then read the prisoner'sstatement as follows : —On the 10th November,lB9o, at eight o'clock in the morning I started from home to go to near Belmont to see the manager. On my way, at the spot that has been rnentiened, I overtook the deceased. As soon as I overtook her I got hold of her shoulder. I asked her what she had been telling lies about me for. I told her that she had set it out that I followed her some weeks ago for the purpose of doing her some harm. She told me to let go of her shoulder. I told her I would not do so till she retracted what she had said. She jerked her shoulder away out of my hand, shut her umbrella, took hold of the small end of it, and struck me with the handle across the brow. I became enraged, threw her down, and caused those wounds in her head, through being in a violent passion. I then cut her throat—(sen- sation)—dragged her across the footpath down the ravine in which she was found. I made the marks in her neck after making the wounds in her throat to destroy all evidence against me. When I took her in the hollow I got the fern fronds and oak leaves, but before that I tore and cut open her clothes to see if her heart heat. I found it did not beat. I then covered her with fern fronds and oak leaves. The reason the clothes were so disarranged— pulled from the lower parts—were not caused, as people think, trying to violate the girl, as I could easily have done it without if I had so wished, but I did not wish to do so. I did not search for her purse or any other article she may have had. After covering her I did not go the same way back I came, but went over the rails a few yards from the body, went through the dough, and returned home along the wall side until I got into Long- worth-road. A great many people think this girl was simply got hold of for the purpose of ravishing her, but I can swear on my dying oath such is not the case. The witnesses have told a great many lies, especially the milkmen meeting me in certain places. If I had been seen at Longworth Hall at half-past eight I should cer- tainly have been found out the same morning, as Jones came by at a quarter to nine, and that would have been ' the time at which the murder have been committed, had I been seen at Longworth Hall at half-past eight. As regards the spot where the murder was committed it was about three yards from the edge of the trail, close to the footpath, where it happened. At a quarter-past eight in the moring would be the very latest at which this horrible crime was committed. Sergeant Shackleton : That is all, sir, except the pri- soner's signature. The Coroner: Was anyone present when the state- ment was made? Police Constable Bruce and Police Constable Berry. After taking it did you read it over to them in their presence ? I did, sir. • And did he sign it in their presence? He did, sir. Will you produce the statement. The statement was handed in.

div.head: CONFESSION CRITICISED.
div.p: THE CONFESSION CRITICISED.

Sinco his confession of the crime the prisoner Mac- donald has exhibited signs of considerable depression, and has cast off to a great extent the bold recklessness and callousness he had previously displayed. Dr. Robin- son. who made the port-mortem examination of the girl's body, said, that viewed in the light of his investigation, Macdonald's confession was like all his other statements full of cunning and lies. Prisoner knew he was out of sympathy with the public on the question of the alleged motives for the crime, which were violation on the one hand and robbery on the other, and tried to clear him- self ; but, the doctor declares, there is abundant circum- stantial evidence to prove that, whatever prisoner may now say to the contrary, his statement in these respects is false. The doctorconcludes by saying that prisoner's object seems to be to modify public opinion by saying he committed the murder in a passion, thinking probably that the public might be induced to signa petition in his favour.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

At Bolton, on Thursday, the hearing of the charge against Macdonald for the murder of Miss Holt was re- sumed, the magistrates expressing the opinion that, after the prisoners confession, the case might be shortened. Prisoner refrained from cross-examining, and maintained the most stolid composure. On the conclusion of the evidence, prisoner was tormally committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes.

OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The sixth session of the twelfth Parliament of the Queen' and the twenty-fourth of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, was opened on Tuesday by Royal Commission: At the opening ceremony in the House of Lords, which took place at two o'clock in the afternoon, there were only about twenty peers present, and these included the Duke ot Sunderland,. the Duke of

Bedford, Lord Keane, Lord Bramwell, Lord Ashbourne, the Earl of Limerick, Earl Waldegrave, Lord Roden, Lord Ardilaun, Lord Norton, Lord Morris, and the Bishops of Ripon and Southwell. The four back benches on the Op- position side of the house were, as is usual on these oc- cesions, approprated to ladies, and were well filled. The Lord Chancellor, the Earl of Coventry, the Earl of Lathom' Lord Knutsford, and Earl Brovvnlow appeared in their full robes of scarlet and ermine, and having, as Royal Commissioners, taken their seats on the bench placed in front of the throne, the Lord `Chancellor directed Admiral Sir James Drummond (the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod) to summon the Commons. The Deputy-Speaker (Mr. Courtney), accompanied by the Sergeant-at-Arms and the Usher of the Black Rod, and followed by a considerable number of members of the Lower House, shortly afterwards appeared at the
bar. The Lord Cfrancellor then announced that her Majesty,

ho-t.sin-g-11—C.On--th-Zoccasion to be present in person, had caused the commission to be issued under the Great Seal, empowering certain persons therein named to do all things necessary for the opening of the present ses- sion of Parliament.

div.head: QUEEN'S 4PEECH.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S 4PEECH.

The reading clerk having read the commission, The Lord Chancellor proceded to read the Queen's Speech as follows : MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— No change has taken place in the foreign relations of this country during the short period which has elapsed since the close of the preceeding Session. he securities for European peace appear to me to be unOiminiStled I have commenced negotiation . King of Italy for the determination of the frontier which separ- ates the territory under British influence in North-East Africa from that which belongs to the protected empire
W-

of Abyssinia. A treaty was signed on the 20th August, having for its object the ascertainment of the boundaries between British territoiy in Central Africa and the Portuguese provinces of Angola Gaza, and Mozambique. It has, however, not received the ratification of the King , of Portugal, and, pending further negotiations, a tempor- ary arrangement in regard to the most urgent questions has been concluded between the two countries, which will be laid before you. Negotiations have also been commenced in respect to the Newfoundland fishery questions, and I trust that a settlement may be arrived at which will be satisfactory to all parties. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOTISE OF I.,OMMONS, The estimates for the charge of the ensuing year will be submitted to you at the ordinary time. Strict economy will be observed in the preparation of them. MT LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— The general condition of Ireland has sensibly improved under the operation ef the salutary legislation wnich you have applied to it ; but I have learned with deep regret that a serious deficiency in the potato crop in certain parts of Ireland threatens the recurrence of one of those periods of severe distress to which the population of the western counties are peculiarly exposed by the indus- trial and economic conditions under which they live. I trust that the measures of my Government may mitigate the immediate evil, and diminish the probability of its return. It appears to me also desirable, for the increase of con- tentment and the diminution of political disturbance throughout Ireland, to take measures for augmentitig the number of owners engaged in the actual cultivation of the land. A measure having this object in view will be laid before you. Proposals will again be made to you for remedying the difficulties which have arisen from the indirect inci- dence of tithe rent charge upon the land in England and Wales. A measure will be submitted to you far facilitating the transaction in Scotland and Ireland of the more im- portant stages of private legislation affecting those countries. Your attention will be invited to the expediency of alleviatir'ar the burden which the law of compulsory education has. in recent years, imposed upon the poorer portion of my people. There are several other matters upon which legislation is desirable, but recent experience has rendered it doubt- ful whether the time at your disposal will, in your judg- ment,be sufficient for the consideration of many subjects of an important character beyond those to which I have referred. In case time for further legislation should be found, I have directed the preparation of bills for the enactment of a reformed system of county government in Ireland analogous to that which has recently been put in opera- tion for Great Britain, for the establishment of District Councils, for the extension of faculties for purchasing small parcels of land in Great Britain, for amending the law with respect to the compensation payable by em- ployers in case of injury to persons in their employ- ment, for consolidating and amending the laws' relating to public health, for the appointment of a public trustee, and for increasing the security of friendly societies and savings banks. . In the discharge of the arduous duties which are as- signed to you, I commend you heartily to the guidance of Almighty God. After the interchange •of salutations the Commons withdrew from the bar, the Lord's Commissioners retired, and the sitting was suspended, the opening ceremony having occupied a quarter of a hour. On the re-assembling of the House of Lords, Lord WINDSOR moved and Lord ARDILAXIN seconded the Address in reply, Lord GRANVILLE referred to the lateness of the period at which Parliament assembled last session as contributing to the legislative collapse which took place, and complained of three weeks being now deemed suffi- cient to make up for that which more than six months had been utterly Inadequate to deal with. After referring with satisfaction to the prospects of peace, Lord GRANVILLE expressed his concurrence with the statement that no action could be taken with regard to the hostile M'Kinley Tariff unless by the means of an old, fatal, and useless tariff war. Our trade with America had increased notwith- standing all the 'commercial difficulties in the States Lord Granville also asked if it was the fact that the Government, without giving a guarantee, stood behind the Bank of England in the recent crisis to the amount of £2,000,000 ; and whether Ministers intended to take action regarding the rear column scandals. He asked for information regarding the list of measures mentioned in what he termed the " bogus" part of the Queen's Speech, and touched upon the Government policy re- garding the Tipperary prosecutions. Lord Salisbury, in reply, declined to discuss the financial crisis, and said it was not the duty of the Government under the circum- stances to take cognisance of the events in Africa which had been alluded to. Referring to Tipperary, Lord Salisbury said there was always some difficulty with re- gard to the Irish leaders, their strong point just now being escapes, some preferring them by water and some by fire escapes. The Tipperary prosecutions he defended on the ground that the combination was the most dis- honest and tyrannical conspiracy the annals of Irish disorder had produced. The House adjourned till Tuesday next. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. In the Commons, the chair was taken by Mr. L Courtney, there being a large attendance of members The Deputy-Speaker intimated the arrest of Messrs. Dillon, O'Brien, and others for being concerned in a criminal conspiracy, and the result of the trial. Upon Mr. Balfour entering the House he was most cor- dially received. The right hon. gentleman intimated that on Thursday measures would be introduced dealing the Irish land pur- chase and the improvement of the congested districts in that country.
