WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTO- GRAPHIC SOCIETY. This Society, which has been established over three, years, and which has a membership of about 60, has been greatly instrumental in developing the art /of photography amcng the amateurs of the • district. Since its establishment, three free exhibi- • tions have been given, at each of which between 400 and 500 persons were present. On Tuesday evening, another limelight entertainment was given in the Museum Lecture Room. Museum-st., and there was a very large atteladance. The first portion of the pro- gramme consisted of a display of slides, the produc- tions of several members of the Society. For the most part, the scenes presented were familiar, the picturesque spots of Winwick and Lymm evoking much applause. The slides were such that the respective producers need feel justly proud of. They were exceedingly distinct, and at such a cold season as this, it was specially fascinating to look upon those scenes of country grandeur, when nature was seen in all her loveliness. Views from Dublin, through County Wicklow, to the Lakes of Killarney were thrown upon the sheet to illustrate a descriptive reading by Mr. T. .1. Garnett. All the principal places of Dublin were shown including views of historical structures, once celebrated for their architectural beauty, and the seats of Irish noblmen, and various ruins of great antiquity. A marked contrast was observed between the views of Dublin and those of various spots in Wicklow. Whilst the former is characteristic for its noble ecclesiastical edifices, and magnificent palatial buildings, the result of modern contrivances and man's ingenuity, the latter county, almost from end to end, is nature in its wildest state, and this is seen to great advantage. A great number of the pictures of this county showed that cultivation was impossible, yet, in the stead of a bucolic condition, there were scenes of great natural beauty. Perhaps the most captivating views of the evening were those of the Lakes of Kil- !limey. Looking upon these unsurpassed scenes one is struck with the words of Richard Cobden which had reference to the mountains and lakes, to the effect that these constiteted two sublimities of nature—rest and motion. The sublimity of rest was the towering mountains, and that of motion the gently flowing lakes. In one place was Seen the groups of mountains, the sum- mits of which appeared beyond the scan of human beings. Some there were with passes; but others were most rugged and clothed with a blackness which made the spectacle wild, though in the extreme beautiful. Again, in the distance could be seen the meeting of waters; and, splashing down an almost perpendicular crag a celebrated waterfall, all of which tended to make the scene one which will not soon be forgotten by the appreciative auoience. One or two scenes illustrating a ride from Edinbergh to London in the old coach days 'were also given and these were the slides of professionals. During the evening Mr. R. H. Pearson gave a violin solo, and Mr. A. .1. Garfield rendered the song," The village blacksmith." Mrs. Varley presided at the piano, and Mr. W. H. Harrison manipulated the lantern. Al- together the entertainment was very much enjoyed. WARRINGTON AND, DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION ' . A meeting of the Warrington and District -Teachers' Association was held on Saturday after- noon, in Heath-side (Girls') School, under the presi- dency of Mr. William Wallace (Christ Church Schools, Latchford.) There was a full attendance. `The meeting was called mainly for the, purpose of -hearing an address from Mr. Heller, secretary of the National Union of Teachers. The CHAIRMAN explained that the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), who had been announced to preside, was prevented by a prior engagement from attending. Mr. Hezzen,who was received with applause, remarked that it was ten years since he last met the teachers of Warrington. The Warring ton Association had had a somewhat chequered career, and his object in coming that afternoon was to find out why the teachers of War- rington had not rendered the professional movement more help than they had in the past. He was told that within a radius of three or four miles there must be at least 160 or 170 teachers at work—teachers engaged in the same great work, whose individual interests, although they might not be practically the same, were to a very large degree identical. He wanted to find out how it was that they had not ueen actuated by that spirit of profes- sional unity which was necessary to success and very beneficial to every member. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that they were starting upon a new era with reference to the Association, and his duty that afternoon would be to indicate the points to which their attention should be directed in order to make the Association for Warrington serve the cause of education in the• town, and preserve and conserve the interests of those who carried on the work. (Hear, hear.) The National Union numbered now close upon 16,000 members, a very fair proportion of the whole body of teachers working in the schools, but kr no means a satisfactory proportion. After 25 years of educational blundering the Department had, at last, altered their plans, not entirely, but they had taken the first step towards sweeping away that irrational, unreasonable, and disastrous system which attempted tO govern the schools according to the results which could be tested on a particular day of the year at a- simple examination. It was only by the persistent work of the Union during the last 20 years that that change had been brought about. (Applause.) Ten years ago when they spoke of affecting that change they weae laughed at. He remembered that one of the Warrington newspapers took exception to the course, but since that time a complete revolution had taken place in education. The first stage of that change was exemplified in the vide issued this year. He did not wish to talk about the code. He wanted rather to point out that if there were to be any improvements in educational arrangements, the teachers opinion ought not to be left out of consideration. Thereat blunders which had been made were due So the fact that the voice of the teachers had not been heard, and it was the fault of the teachers themselves, because they did not,as a body, express their opinion. He should have thought that the value and power of combination would have been appreciated by teachers almost as soon as by anyone in these days. (Hear, hear.) It was in support of that principle and to urge the strengthening of the combination in this district that he had come among them. The Union had from the Srst adopted the principles of Local Associations. It was, he thought, the wiser way, because if the Union attempted to control or regulate a body of some 20,000 or 30,000 teachers in different parts of the country with- out any means of comparing notes, it would be extremely difficult and would not give satisfaction to the members at large. The Local Association was the basis of their organization; the Union was a Union of Associations. The teachers in any given town or district had special difficulties and special interests, which marked them off from the general body of teachers throughout the coun- try. For instance, the teachers in the "half-time," districts had special conditions and difficulties under which they laboured, and which the teachers in another part of the country could not appreciate, because \ they knew nothing about them. Repre- sentatiOns made by the Associations to the Union received very careful, candid, and fair considera- tion from the executive, who, to the best of their ability, endeavoured to make those representations to the Department or Parliament reflect, in as complete and direct a manner as possible, the various opinions which had been collected from different parts of the country. An Association ought to bind together the teachers of a town or district in a company of friends and fellow-helpers. If that spirit of professional friend- ship and brotherhood did not exist in a town it was difficult, almost impossible, to make a successful aSsocia- tion. (Hear, hear.) The miserable, wretched, and illusive system of percentages was the cause of much of the unpleasantness ,• it had tended to set one teacher against another. Unless they got rid of that unreason- able straining after impossible and useless results, they would never have success in their work. (Hear. hear.) When teachers knew how those results were obtained, and how far they depended upon an accident of the occasion, they knew what value to put upon them. He was very glad that under the present code they had not got percentages in the way they used to have; and he was hoping that the teachers of the country would not strive to say "I have passed such and such percentages,' thus misleading School boards or other bodies; but that they would try honestly and faithfully to carry out the education of the school in such a way that they would do their very best for each individual scholar. (Hear, hear.) So long as the standard" system existed—they would get rid of it before long—(hear, hear)—they could not help having a percentage—the Royal Commission put it at,2o per cent—of children who ought to be in a higher standard • and a similar percentage who should be in a lower. A Local association should be the means of placing teachers before the other public bodies of a town or dis- trict. In Warrington they were not fortunute enough to have a School Board, but the Association should be of great assistance to the School Attendance Committee, and should exercise some influence upon public opinion. For example, who were so ready and able to advise and , help the local bodies in the disposition of the County council grant for technical educationias the teachers of ' the town? (Hear, hear.) By the action of the Union the Teachers' Pension Fund had been reinstated, and a • sum of £lOO,OOO had already been distributed among the older teachers. The executive were now busy upon a scheme by which the body f the teachers generally might secure for themselves a fair prospect of a retiring pension. He asked increased support for the Union, 'whose work spoke for itself, and confidence in the execu- tive, who were doing the best they possibly could for the • profession at large. (Applause.) Mr. WALLACE proposed that a hearty vote of thanks be given to Mr. Heller for his very able address.—Mr. CORNEY seconded and Mr. DEWHURST supported the reso- lution which was carried enthusiastically.—Mr. Heller having replied, Mr. JORDAN proposed. and Mr. FINNEY seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Wallace for presiding. Mr. SixotErox,proposed and Mr. Twiss seconded,a hearty vote of thanks to the managers of St. Paul's Schools for granting them the use of the room. Both propositions were carried unanimously. The members of the Association afterwards had tea together, the carterer, being Mr. T. W. Chantry of 20, Horsemarket-st.

THE LATCHFORD WARD VACANCY. Sir,—As a voter in the Latchford Ward, lam surprised to hear that we are to have another candidate interested in the drink traffic. I refer to Mr. Peter Chrimes as be- ing the one likely to be selected to fight the battle. I should have thought that we had quite enough of this kind of representatives in Messrs. Taylor and Ashton. What do the respectable inhabitants think about it? Are they satisfied? I think not. I for one protest against such men being selected. What is the use of having men sent to the Council who cannot address it intelligently? What claim has Mr. Chrimes to our suf- frages? I know of none. I am prepared to vote for Radical or Conservative, Whig or Tory. There is not a Ward in the Borough that has such poor representatives as we have. Tories as well as Liberals are quite tired of it, and intend to put an end to it.—l remain yours truly, A VOTER. Warrington, Nov. 28th, 1890.

THE CASE OF EX-SERGEANT SHAW. Sir,—Now that" A member of the Watch Committee" (who, not withstanding his none de plume is discernable by his phrases ") has condescended to give us some facts in connection with this case, I would suggest that, in order to have the matter in question properly threshed out, a resolution be proposed in the Town Council, ask- ing for a committee to inquire into the whole matter, and especially to inquire, receive evidence, and report, upon the administration and discipline of the Police Force generally. At the present time, amongst the rate- payers and the police force a great amount of dissatis- faction exists, not only as to the treatment of ex-Ser- geant Shaw but other matters. To show there is a screw loose somewhere, there are men now in the force who ought to be having the maximum salary as first •elass constables, and have been entitled to it some years, but for some reason or other, known only to the higher powers, they are deprived of it ; also there are men in the force at the present time who had been recommended for the position of sergeant several times before the vacancy caused through Shaw's dismissal, but who nevertheless had to "stand down" whilst Jones was promoted over their heads. Let" A member of the Watch Committee "if he can, disprove this, and at the same time let him deny the charge I now make viz : That there were more serious reports against Jones than against these men and yet the appointment is given to Jones. If Councillor Roberts will only persevere in the Council, and get some light thrown upon these matters he will have rendered a service to the ratepayers, and to that which is the pride of all men, especially Englishmen —fair play. RATEPAYER. Warrington, Nov. 25th 1890. XX-POLICE SERGEANT SHAW AGAIN DEFENDS HIMSELF.

Sir,—ln answer to the letter of 80.1ilInt:y" last from " A meibber of the Watch Committee," I must say thAt if that member was present when the report of the Chief Constable was read over to me, I think he will remember me telling the Watch Committee that it was untrue. I think I proved clear enough, through the witness named inhis letter, that I was quite calm, and that I used no strong or insubordinate language whatever. I also proved that it was not me but Of? Man who preferred the charge who lost his temper. I think I had every rigiit, to defend and not stand there to be stormed at, and not answer back, Now to the question of pay and club money. From the Way that he puts it in his letter, the public will think that I have been receiving all my wages whilst off duty, sick ; but I must explain that all members of the force, when sick, have one shilling per day stoppc l off, and, according to the rules of the force, each member is sup- posed to be in a sick society. Now the writer says that I have paid £8 or £9 into the Police Mutual. I beg to differ from him, and also those who gave him the in- formation. I think that if they can look over the amount from the commencement of my police duty, they will find that they are a good few pounds wrong in their cal- culation, as I consider that I have paid fully that amount since I have been sergeant. Now, as "A member of the Watch Committee" I should think that the Chief Constable will explain to him how many hours extra duty the other sergeants and in- spectors had to do whilst I was off duty. lam afraid that if some member of the committee was to examine their visiting books, he would find that they do quite as mach when all are on duty as they do when anyoneis off sick. lam able to prove this by the books kept by the superior officers, and, if anyone can get access to them to see whether lam right or wrong, "A member of the Watch

Committee can. Now, as to the 14th August. I handed in my protest at 9 a.m. to Inspector Spinks, and he took it up to the Chief Constable, and brought word down that I could attend the committee if I liked. I did so, and when I was called in I was asked if I intended them to take that as a resignation, to which I replied—" that" (meaning the paper) "is what I intend to put in, and, if I have to go, I wish you would let me go at once." The Mayor asked the thief Constable it he had any objections, to which he replied, "None whatever." Of course, I knew he would have none, only too glad to be rid of a man like me. I wonder if "A member of the Watch Com- mittee " and sympathising friend, kturiv9 Low much a —.sr is naid from th rates for policemen doing County lourt bailiffs/ work How many, hours do the polite spend in a year going and knocking people up to get them to open tlaeir doors, and as soon as they are open, • a bailiff steps in ? Is that part of a policeman's duty', In England, and do the rateyayers pay them for that "sort of work, instead of working their beats No more about sickness, as I still teltrUtid that it was not through sickness that I was got ekt of. but that I was in the-way of some one else.—l tannin, yours truly, E'-P.S. ROBERT SHAW. 195, Manchester-road, November 26th, 1890.
A DEFENCE OF SERGEANT SHAW.

Sir,—Your correspondent, who is so prone to drop into the style of eloquence which usually characterizes a monthly nurse of the " Sairey Gamp," style, commences his letter with one or two somewhat glaring inaccuracies. His generous use of such terms as " Bombastos Furioso," kc., Azc., rather suggests that when he penned his famous epistle he must have been somewhat "intoxicated," probably with the "exuberance of his own verbosity." I have never yet said that I won my election "by making the conduct of the Watch Committee on this Shaw business alone the test question by which I defeated my Opponent in the Whitecress Ward." What I did say was that I had made it" a leading question, and that the result was that I obtained the biggest majority we should have in Warrington for a long time." To that statement and opinion I still adhere. But what a miserable coward your correspondent must be? Why did he not face up this question like a man in the Council Chamber on the two occasions upon which it has already been discussed there? Why should he now seek

to cover his identity with an anonymous signature? The only reason which I can suggest for this futile- at- tempt at concealment—because the style of writing re- veals the author as plainly as if we were listening to his musical, high-toned voice—is that he is a man whose opinions change so frequently and so rapidly that he might soon wish to" jump Jim Crow " on this question as he has done on many a previous occasion. Now, what is the nature of the reply to my charges ? The case for the other side is, first, that Shaw has been absent from I duty so long a time as to seriously interfere with the proper management of the police force; and, secondly, it is insinuated by your correspondent that a good deal of Shaves illness was " shammed," because, he says, " the longar he remain 1 on the sick list the greater was the pecuniary advantage to him." My answer to the first allegation is that Shaw's illness has all been contracted in the performance of his duties as a police officer. When he joined the force, and for a long time after, he enjoyed good sound health, and probably would have continued to do Ea if he had not had on so many occasions to keep on his wst uniform for hours after his beat was finished, in order that he might keep up with the office work, which he, for some reason or other, seems to have had an excessive share of. As to the insinuation con- veyed by your correspondent to the effect that a good deal of Shaw's sickness was "shammed." and that the inducement to him to carry on this hypocrisy was the pecuniary advantages he would enjoy by lie reason of his sick pay from the club of which he is a member, and also the allowance from the force, this will not bear a moment's investigation. Before Shaw could be entitled to sick leave and sick pay, ho must have a certificate as to the bona fides ,of his illnels from the police doctor and also from his club doctor. I don't know who the gentleman is who is the medical adviser to the club in question, but your re:: ders, will, I am sure, agree with me in saying that I don't think there is a medical man in practice in Warrington, who is such a fool as to be repeatedly deceived as to Shaw's true condi- tion of health, or such a knave as to act in collusion with Shaw for the purpose of enabling him to draw sick pay from his club. When your readers are further aware that the gentleman who holds the appointment of medi- cal officer of the police force is Dr. Starkey Smith. and that he is responsible for the prevention ,of any such imposition as yona correspondent suggests, they will, I am sure,' meet with the contempt it deservesan insinua- tion which is as discreditable as it is untrue. I regret sincerely that Shaw sent in is resigna- tion. By so doing he put himself very largely "out of court." wish he had declined to .do So, as it would have been much latter to have ' had the whole case fought out in the Council Chamber, [ and then probably better resuPs would have followed. [ Shaw is now in good health. Why? Partly because he 'is free from thatconstant worrying, and nagging, which when persisted in by those who are" dressed in a little brief authority," goes so far towards destroying both mental and physical strength. Having myself on more than one occasion received somewhat peculiar treatment at the hands of the Chief Constable, who seems to forget that he is a public servant, for carrying out what I con- ceive to be my duty as a representative of the ratepayers, I can readily understand the manner in which he would deal with a subordinate who might have the misfortune to get " across " with him. What we want is a thorough reform in the constitution of the Watch Com- mittee, which would be speedily followed by an improve- ment in the administration of the police force.—' am yours, &c.,

div.head: HENRY ROBERTS. Rose Cottage, Latchford, Nov. 27th, 1890. LOCAL HISTORY—PAST AND PRESENT: A REVIEW.
div.p: HENRY ROBERTS. Rose Cottage, Latchford, Nov. 27th, 1890. LOCAL HISTORY—PAST AND PRESENT: A REVIEW.

Sir,—The instalment of the late Mr, Peter Rylands' biography, which you printed on Saturday last, must have been most interesting to all who take an interest in the welfare of the town. In reading it, I was impressed with the fact that the three subjects dealt with in the article, even now, after some thirty years have elapsed, press themselves upon public attention. Firstly, with regard to the public footpaths at the bottom of Bold-st. From the article, and from present observation, it is glaringly apparent that the Railway Company can do just what they like with the town. Not only can the Company take down a bridge, without a voice being raised, but they can now impede pedestrians over the paths they have made, by couple of gates at each end of Arpley bridge w the least protest on the part of the Corporation. These gates are as intolerable a nuisance as the level croEsing ; and, so far as I have observed, they se: :a no other purpose than to delay the progr of passers-by and to provoke their profanity. Should pedestrians emerge from the gates with unruffled feelings, they are likely to b .ve them disturb iby the disgraceful condition of the road leadine• round the Slate Co.'s warehouse to Arpley Station. Eleven months out of twelve, this road is nothing but a quagmire, and calls for immediate and effective repair. There is another peculiar feature about the road, and it is this : Should you, by any chance, on a dark night, escape a drenching in the pools of water around this spot, the probability is, that you will injure yourself by comin,,, in contact with a cart or other obstruction drawn right across the road. It passes my comprehension how Councillor Hutchinson can use this road as frequently as he does, and yet never open his lips as to its condition. Again, the footpath leading to Arpley Station, on the Slate Co.'s side is in a discreditable state, and ought to be tiled at once. Secondly, as to police matters. I read the epistle of a "Member of the Watch Committee " with lively interest, and his view of the case Seemed to be very convincing. But there is an old Latin maxim that bids one hear the other side, and, fortunately, the "other side" was given immediately below that of the " powers that be." Now, having the opportunity, given so opportunely, of hearing the two sidev, one could not rise from a perusal of the two letters without the conviction that ex-P.S. Shaw, has been very hardly used. Neither the Watch Committee nor the Chief Constable should make "fish of one and fish of another," I have personal knowledge of the fact that of the three officers Shaw mentions, two of them—Clynes and Flitchmough, were on the sick list a very long time —Clynes especially—and yet both these officers were granted allowances. But a similar grant is denied to Shaw simply, as it seems to me, because he refused o degrade his manhood by accepting an inferior • ,sitoo when there was no sufficient reason for so doin„. As Shaw himself put it—if he was fit to be constable lie was, most certainly fit to be sergeant; and, being sergeant, there was nO °earthly reason to reduce him. I cannot help feeling that there has been too much of this" Irishman's rise " about the police office lately. We have recently seen the anything but gratifying spectacle of ex-Inspector Singleton and ex-Sergeant Jones serving in the ranks at the same time, and only by standing on his dignity has Shaw escaped a similar fate. But the peculiarityof the cases is that while Jones again climbs into office poor Singleton is left to linger in the ranks to atone for some mysterious offence which I could never fathom. Why is this? Surely Singleton deserved promotion for setting a pre- cedent the Chief Constable finds so highly convenient. But if Singleton was passed, why was not Jones, when there are men in the ranks well qualified for the position of sergeant? It was hard on the force to suggest, as the Chief Constable recently did, that there was not a man of sufficient education to fulfil the duties of ser- geant • and if I had had the engagement of such men, I should' have been ashamed to admit that I had taken them on. The worst thing a man in the Warrington Police Force can do is to show that he has the spirit of an Eng- lishman. The Goliath of the Watch Committee turned with the usual contempt upon the little David of the Council Chamber who dares to champion the cause of justice; and, in his usual flowery style, attempts to pul- verise the little champion for daring to give battle to so lofty a body. It may yet, however, come to pass that the oratorical pebbles which the tiny troubler flings may strike a vulnerable part in the armour of the autocrats of the Watch Committee, and thus bring to the ground those who refuse t) render justice when it is due. Thirdly, as to 'politics in the Council Chamber. We have heard a great deal through the Tory organ lately that it was thevasty Radicals who first introduced politics into the Council, but if the writers of that paper will read Mr. Ryland's biography, or the history of the Town Council, they will discover that not the Radiala but the Tories first introduced ))olitics into our Lota.l Parliament. This fact being so well attested, it is to be hoped the Tories will 113-77,e less to say on this subject in future.— Yours A TRADESMAN.

WHY I LEFT CONGREGATIONALISM. Sir,—l was glad to read in last week's " Examiner " that you had found time to criticise—although very mildly—Mr. Reaney's late production. I saw it on a bookstall, and, in a momentary weakness, purchased it, but why, I know not, for a fourpenny Testament is worth a large number of them. However, I bought it, and thought I would see what he had to say for himself. Why he should feel it needful to try and enlighten the reading public as to his reasons for leaving Congrega- tionalism, he does not make very clear : but is it not somewhat presumptive on his part to suppose the British public were suffering anxiety to know the cause of his defection? Anyone who knew Mr. Reaney, as his War- rington friends knew hi:n, could hardly wonder at any step he took; but, if he had been at all serious in giving his reasons for leaving the church that has 'fostered and fed him for a quarter of a century, he might surely have put it all in the form of a tract or leaflet, and got it pub- lished by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, who, under the special circumstances, would have done It cheaply, and given a large concession to purchasers wholesale. But what I quarrel with MOTO than anything is the want of honesty contained in the subject written. It purports to be "Why I left Congregationalism," and I find two-thirds of the book taken up and not giving any reasons whatever, the remaining third only giving partly his reasons and partly a, strong eulogium on the Church that has now adopted him. I think we shall all agree that the Church of England, whatevertfaults

div.head: EY kviTNER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29.1890
div.p: THE EY kviTNER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29.1890

she has, has much charity to accept one who for a long time not only seemed to think she ought to be Dises- tablished but used many opportunities for advocating his opinions. Let us feel thankful there is a "refuge for the destitute" inthe Mother Church. I hope no one Will think that I personally feel ,any ob- jection to his leaving Congregationalism, or, if bethought it needful, to givelis reasons for such a radical change of front but what Ido object to is this—that three- fourths of his book should he occupied bya wretched on- slaught upon the Church he has professed to serve for so many years. Why should he indulge in such a series of accusations with ass evident endeavour to deprecate aS much as possible a Church that has done noble work fcrt. centuries? There is an economy of that" charity that thinketh no evil " which, with all his fault., I could not, give him credit for. Why should he have wasted so much, ink in trying to undermine, or overthrow,or tear to pieces a church of all churches? Surely the spirit that inspired his writing is not the spirit of the New Testament. regret exceedingly, fcr his own sake, that he has done so much to lower himself in the estimation of all whose good opinion is worth having. I have my impressions about his leaving which, pos- sibly, he will not agree with ; bet I think he was unequal to sustain this position except for a limited time. This he seems to have felt and acknowledged both in Warring- ton, Reading, and Stepney ; but,why in the name of .com-' mon honesty, should ;hese heart quaking,s about Dade- pendency take hold of him years ago, increasing in force and intensity during his pastorate at Stepney, and while dividing his admiration between the Church of England and the Church of Rome,—l say, while his ' mind was in a state of unhealthy unrest, why should he open up or listen to negotiations with Cavendish Chapel ; and then,in so short a tirrc,after so much forbearance, on their parr, leave them with the impression that he should a ccept no clerical work in future ? Does his acceptance of a call from Cavendish„,under circumstances so uncer- tain, indicate the sort of principle one should expect to find in a Christian minister? I trust this may be cap- able of explanation, but fecz, looking at the readiness , with which he came to Warrington, a few weeks ago, to I I hold forth in a pulpit a Etone43 throw from Wycliffe, that ally explanation would not much mend matters. Surely. Mr. Reaney, cannot thinktiais was done with very good taste in the eyes of his friends. It reminds one of children who, having got on some new article of dress, lose no time in putting it on, and strutting past some of their companions by way of showing it and themselves off. In any case, a decent time might have elapsed before any public ministration in Warrington. I have not heard whether he has been to Stepney or Reading yet. Sir, lam sorry there is, or seems to be, any need for remarks like this; but a pastor who .acts so unwisely lays himself open to remark, and, what is worse, these things lead the "enemies of the Cross to triumph."—Yours Sze., OBSERVER.

DISESTABLISHMENT Y5i5E CHURCH OF SCOTLAND.—Dr. CAMERON gave notice that at an early day after the re- cess he should move that the Church of Scogand be dis- established and disendowed. THE SUPPLY OF OPIUM.—Mr. SAMUEL SMITH asked the Under Secretary of State for India whether he was aware that the Indian Government were arranging for an additional supply of opium to be prepared for con- sumption in India in consequence of the falling off of the demand for China. SMITH moved for precedence of all Government business until Christmas. Mr. LABOUCHERE objected in the interest of private members.—Mr. GLADSTONE demanded an explanation of the intentions of the Government after Christmas.—Mr. Smith, however, declined to give any pledge, and, after a discussion, the house divided: for motion 223; against, 173; Government majority, 50. PERPETUAL PENSIONS.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. BRADLAUGH moved that the House disapproved so much of the Treasury minutes re- lating to perpetual pensions, hereditary payments and allowances as proposed to commute some of such pensions by payments and allowances at the rate of practically twenty-seven years' purchase. He pro- tested against the action of the Treasury, and besought the House to fol )tv the recommendation of the Select Com- mittee.—Mr. JENNINGS seconded the resolution which, he said, was intended to give effect to the recommendations which had been put aside, by the Treasury.—CirAxesuba of the EXCHEQUER assured the House that the Govern- ment had given attention to the report of the Committee which had inquired into the subject and were carrying out the recommendations as far as possible. He thought that the rate of commutation proposed in some cases, namely 27 years, was too high, but if holders 0 the pen- sions refused to accept lower terms the only way to force those would be to introduce a bill setting aside the pledge of the nation. He did not see any difference between grants of land and grants of money, but it was not sug- gested that, though the money might be refused, the land might be resumed—Sir W. HARCOURT objected to the Chancellor of the Exchequer making 27 years' pur- chase the standard which the Treasury was bound to ' give holders of pensions, provided they refused to take less.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL defended the action of • the Government, and said he should have declined to • have assented to the report if he had thought it was to be used for breaking the faith of the House.—Mr. MOE- DELLA expressed his concurrence with the views of Sir W. Harcourt.—Dr. CLARK, although opposed altogether ; to perpetual pensions, did not think they ought to haggle L whether the commutation should be 27 or 25 years.—Mr. Bradlaugh's motion was rejected by a majority of 33.

div.p: "THE DEADLY CIGARETTE."

Sir,—Under the above heading the ." British Medical Journal "of the 15th inst. contains an article relating to the deaths of three lads which were directly or indirectly associated with the habit of smoking. The Editor de- serves the thanks of every well wisher of youth, for cal- ling attention to the terrible risks which many lads run ; who are addicted to the use of tobacco. But disastrous as were the results in the cases referred to, they by no means furnish an adequate idea of the variety,and ex- tent of the evils which juvenile smoking givez rise to. Through sheer ignorance and fatuity, boys adopt.a prac- tice which cannot benefit them in the slightest degree. On the contrary, not one of them can escape injury in one way or another. The physical injuries inflicted on a boy will depend chiefly on three things: Ist. The soundness or unsound- ness of the constitution ; 2nd. On the extent to which smoking is indulged in ; 3rd. On the method of smoking adopted. ;Smoking must inevitably do some harm, how- ever strong may be the constitution, but the less the vigour possessed, the greater will be the harm done., The very first condition of perfect health is pure air, but smoking renders the air highly impure. The respiratory processes are specially important in early life. Youths breathe more quickly than adults, because tissue changes are more rapid during the developmental stage than they are subsequently. div.head: EARLY NONCONFORMITY.
div.p: EARLY NONCONFORMITY.
SECOND SECTION.

On Thursday evening the Rev. John Yonge delivered a lecture on the history of Nonconforniity during the reigns of James 1 and Charles I. This was the second lecture of the series, and there 'WM a very large attendance. The rev, gentleman said tt might be remembered that in the former lecture they endeavoured to describe the beginning of Nonconformity in this country. They sketched its history through the long reign of Queen Elizabeth ; and, in doing so,it was pointed out that the founda- ations of our civil and religious freedom were lai6l at great cost and sacrifice on the part of the men who were their ecclesiastical ancestors. They would proceed that evening to review a further period in the deeply-interesting portion of their natural history_ They were Still to Trithcss the great fistrugmle of religious freedom, although, perhaps, more upon the side of civil efforts for its attainments, than upon that of mere persecutions and suffering. Still, however the struggle be considered, they would see that present privileges had laFien dearly gained and should be strongly held. At the outset, let them pass in review some of the men against whose power and tryanny Nonconformity had had to contend. Among these, the foremost place must be assigned to the two kings,whose reigns were under their present survey. King James ascended the English throne in 1603, and there was a general expectation,that, with the advent of his monachy,a better day would dawn for the reformation of religion. The King, however, had prejudices against the Church, and any hopes the Puri- tan party had cherished of a better day under his reign, had but very slender foundation, and soon after the King's arrival in England a large body of the Puritan clergy presented him with a respectful petition, more than 800 signatures being appended to it. Ile received It with outward courtesy, and promised to fix a day on which the matter would be discussed. The petition covered a good deal of debatable grmnd, finally urging that " subscriptions in future, should be restricte4 t.o the doctrines of religion, and to the article of his 3146 is ty's supremacy; that it should not have respect to the offices of the Church, and that certain matters pertaining to the ecclesiastical courts should be reformed." Six months passed and the date of the conference still remained un- fixed. James then issued a proclamation forbidding all writing and petitioning on the subject of religious reform on pain of his displeasure. Having done that to clear the road for the future, he convened the long looked for conference. It consisted of four Puritan ministers, nominated by the King himself, who were opposed by twenty ecclesiastical dignitaries, and the meeting was held in the Royal Palace at Hampton Court. The date of the conference was January 14th, 1603. The members of the Royal Council were present, and also a crowd of courtiers, and King James was the president. It must be noted that to this Puritan petition and this Hampton Court conference England owed the valuable boon of the authorised version of the Scriptures. But so far as ecclesiastical questions disputed between Puritans and Anglicans were concerned, harm came from the Con- ference rather than good. Indeed the result was a fore- gone conclusion. His Majesty soon showed on which side he had placed himself, and did nothing but browbeat the Puritans. James also held that the divine right of Bishops was as sacred and as absolute as the divine right of Kings. The two systems, as Mr. Green, the historian pointed out, confirmed each other "No Bishop, noking," ran the formula, which embodied James's theory. Here, then, were furnished all the elements for a great national struggle, and they could readily perceive Ow reason of the Puritan revolt. The rev, gentleman went on to show how the King soon found himself embodied in conflict with Catholics as well as Puritans, and in the very midst of the conflict he had provoked by his foolish assertion of audacious authority, lames died. He was at once suc- ceeded his by son Charles I , who was a very different man from his father. By the mere awe of his presence, he drove from his court the vices which his father had fostered, and in which his son afterwards revelled, and he (Charles), had a reverent appreciation of divine and eter- nal things. These, then, were the two Sovereigns with whom their Nonconformist ancestors had to fight the battle of religious liberty at that period. After referring to Buckingham, Cromwell, Lord Stafford, Archbishop Laud, Milton, the lecturer illustrated, by limelight, the three Puritans Prymne, Breton, and Bastwich in the pillory,and the execution of King Charles,and concluded by saying they were not concerned to uphold everything that was done in the matter. They would not ',send either princes or peasants to the blocks in these days. Indeed, they were becoming wisely jealous of all forms of capital punish- ment. But in the main the success of the Puritans and Nonconformists in this national struggle made our Eng- land of to-day possible. Tyranny cf the mostdangerous kind would hate been established, possibly for genera- tions, if the rttritans had been defeated. Their victory made civil iiind religious liberty the birthright of eve?", Briton', Bd made the Empire over which Queen Vic- toria presided to-day, take it all round, the freest and htipplest Empire in the world. Once more they said that 'principles of religious faith, which inspired so noble a contest, and achieved so splendid a triumph, must never be despised or forgotten. (Applause.)

div.p: CONINGSBY DISRAELI AT LYMIT

Speaking at the annual social gathering of the Lymm Constitutional and Conservative Association an Wednesday evening, Mr. Coningsby Disraeli characterized a recent statement by Mr. Leadam on Irish affairs as scandalous and false. Mr. Balfour's tour had exposed a secret which the Irish mem- bers had done their best to hide, viz., that in the remotedistricts of Ireland, where the organization of the National League did not extend, the peasants had accorded to a man who was supposed to be the worst- hated man in that country as favourable a reoeAlon as they would have given to Mr. Parnell. The Bnionist opposed Home Buie both from considerationa of political theory and practice, because they felt it was certain to cause disaster to the realm, and beeause the claim on which it was based was unsound and impracticable. He did not consider—although his view was against that of a great many Unionists and 'Unionists journals—that however bad a man's conduct mir.,dtt be, it could never affect the party or cause which he was fighting for. They might argue, and argue very justiv, that the cause of Home Rule had been scotched and scarred by breaches of the sixth and eighth commandments, that it could not be very moch more materially blackened by a breach of the seventh.

div.p: . young guish and sonaeti lof atmospheric ir

cfn—impurities which only slightly ;affect persons whose constitutions are matured. Sanatarians are making most praiseworthy efforts to improve the health of town dwellers by doing what they can to pre- vent the pollution of the atmosphere by the smoke nuisance caused by the pouring forth of noxious vapours from fact )rx and other chimmes. It is too well-known that children brought up in manufacturing towns lack the vitality, the physical strength, the mental vigour, the relish for plain wholesome food, as well as the digestive power which country bred children possess. Now the vapours polluting the town atmosphere as a rule are far less noxious than are those which are produced in tobacco smoking. For not only do the fumes issuing from the pipe or cigarette which contain such poisonous gases as carbonic oxide, cart )nic acid, sulphuretted hydrogen, prussic acid, &c., but there are emitted in addition a number of volatile alkaloids of a highly poisonous character, nicotine, pysidin, collidin, Sm. Thus it is apparent that healthy country boys acquiring the habit of smoking, place themselves thereby in the lamentable insanitary condition in which town bred children exist, if not in even a worse state. What then must be the condition of boys in towns who by smoking greatly aggravate a state of things which was already highly prejudicial to health, strength, and growth. Smoking has a tendency to injure the throat, the air passages, the lungs, the heart, the stomach, &c., &c. The consequence is that where boys smoke, if there is already a weakened condition of a particular organ, or a predisposition to disease, smoking sows seed in a fertile soil which will bring crops of disease; in one case we ' see successive quinsies, In another etiron4; sPre throat, in a third recurring bronchial troubles, in a- fourth cardiac disease. In a few instances a defective organ fails to bear the strain put upon it and the result is fatal. One of the cases referred to by the "British Medical Journal" was that of a boy of 13 residing at Oldham. The lad had time after time made himself very ill by smoking cigarettes. On a Saturday morning, having nothing to do, he was seen to be again trying to smoke; he soon became very ill, and an hour afterwards was found in an insensible condition. Ile was taken into the house, laid on a sofa ; his mother expecting that he would sleep off the attack, as she had seen him do on former occasions. But instead of improving he became worse ; convulsions set in; the mother became alarmed, Dr. Brownhead was sent for, but in spite of all that could be done for him the lad died in a short space of time. A postmortem examination showed that the heart was diseased, and that apparently the straining caused by vomiting had led to the rupture of some of the vessels in the brain, the lateral cavities being filled with clotted blood. But for the lad's attempt at cigarette smoking, it is quite possible that he might have lived in a fairly healthy state for many years. The practice of smoking has spread like a pestilence amongst boys during the last two years. Unless the terrible evil can be effectually checked, or better still, suppressed, it is impossible to estimate the extent of the injury which will be inflicted on the nation. A great and aggressive evil must be met by preventive as well as by sternly repressive measures. lam glad to find that the Anti-Narcotic League of Manchester are taking'action in the matter, and that they suggest special teaching in schools on the subject, so that boys may no longer be left to fall headlong into the error of believing that there is something manly in smoking; and, further, that a law should be passed prohibiting boys under the age of six- teen years from smoking, and inflicting a penalty on any one who shall in any way supply young persons with tobacco. It is since.rely hoped that hearty support will be given to this most timely policy of the League.—l am, yours &c., M.D.

THE ALLOTS QUESTION, Sir.—ln your issue of the Bth inst I noticed a discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority with respect to the provision of allotments by the Authority for the farm labourers within its district. The question came up upon a letter from the County Council asking what had been done in that matter and how many applications for allotments had been received, and how they had been dealt with. But it was stated by the clerk and the Inspector that not a single applica- tion had been made to put that Act in force, and doubts were expressed as to whether the people knew who was the Authority to administer this production of a Tory Government. Loudly do the Tories crow about their love for the working-man and they point to the Allotment Act as a striking instances of their real and deep interest in the welfare of the working-man generally and of the farmlabourer in particular. The statement is invariably received with bursts of applause, and the story is retailed as to how the Tories gave the working-man an allotment while the Radicals—l beg pardon—the separatists only talked about it. It's surprising what an amount of ignorance there is even amongst Radicals as to the working of this Act, and as to its advantages, or disadvantages. But anyone who knows anything of the subject will readily admit that the Allotment Act is a splendid example of the love the Tories have for the working-man and the pains they take to give him practical benefits. Yes! the Act is a capital type of Tory legislation, that is, it verifies that political axiom that a Tory Act of Parliament gives with one hand and withholds with the other. An Act to enable the labourer to get a piece of land, forsooth. It has been rightly termed " An Act for preventing the labourer getting allotments." The very first time the Act was put into, operation brought into light its uselessness, its intentional uselessness, caused by the insincerity of its promoters. Instead of giving tha labourer an allotment, it practically made it impossible for him to get one by its difficulties and its gross iniquity. To come to facts, I may say that it was first put in

NOTICE is Hereby Given, that the CHESHIRE 1.1 COUNTY COUNCIL are preparedto consider applica- tions from the Managers of all &hodla or Institutions in the Administrative County of Chester at ;present in existence, or beesafter to bedormed, desirous of obtaining grants in aid of the-supply of Technical or Manual Instruction In accordance with the Technical Instruction Act, 1389, !FORMS OF APPLICATION can be •obtained from the rsigned.to whom they must he =returned, 'together with siculars required, on or beforethe2orli DAY'OF DECEM- MR NEXT.. lagrilINALD TOTTS, Clerk of tisecOlseshireCounty'Council. Chester, Mth November, 1890. MUNICIPAL ELECTION. , rino _ TILE BURGESSES OF ST. 'JOHN'S WARD. LaDIES tiND GENTLEMEN,—A wacancy having occurred in your Ward through the elevation of your late represent attys., , Mr. John Platt, to the Alciermanic Bench, I'have been solic- ited by a number of the electors to allow myself to be put in nomination for the vacant seat, and, having consented, I. now offer myself for your sit:lmages. For se,7enteen years I have been engaged in 'business in the old North-E..st Ward of which -St. John's Ward is a section, and the•refore am no stranger amongst you. For several years past I havelaken an active interest in the many local questions that have agitated the public mind. The question of the Intercepting Deptts .is one which I know closely concerns the welbbeing and comfort of a great number of the electors, and, timing ascertained the opinions orthose who live in their immediate vicinity,and who should, therefore, be the best judges as to whether they constitute a grievance or not, I should ,be prepared to support the 'adoption of any remedy, however drastic, fortheir improve- ment, and, failing that, I ehorllB not hesitate-to vote for their gsliofftion. Attention as early as possibleefhould be given by the Conn- airto the unsatisfactory state Of 'many of the streets in the Waed, which in rainy weather, mein a deplorable condition. • I am desirous of seeing, earlyin the coming year, the lend- ing department of our Library free, as is the case in some of our neighbouring towns not nearso;ponulous as our own. Another question is that of 'the Public Baths, and I shall .heartily support any scheme f ortheir improvement, so that the greatest facilities and encouragement may be given to alto:asses to use them, and particalarly the young that they ,may under favourable conditions acquire the artof swimming. These, and many other questions affecting:the economical and•efficient government of the town, should you do me the • honour to elect me as your representative, shall receive my most earnest attention.—l cm, Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, FELIX LOUGHLIN. Buttermarket-st., Warrington, Nov. 14, 1890.

• WHY DOES A woman's health so often breaks down at an early age? THE HOME RULE CRISIS. The "Central News" learns that Mr. Parnell has expressed the opinion that there is nothing in the situa- tion which has arisen to call for his withdrawal from public life. WHAT THE IRISH VENDER SAYS.. The "Daily Telegraph" of yesterday morning mays Mr. Pp.rnell is nonvineedthat the movement to drive him from public life has been started by the Radical section of the Liberal party for the purpose of destroying the independence .of the Irish party., and snaking them a mere appanage of Ilse Liberal varty, and that it is especially in revenge for the attitude he took 'upon the question of the Royal grazes last summer. He will resist this move- ment to the last, and on Monday he will make a most important statement to the party. DECLARATION OF MR. DILLON. New Tome, FRIDLY, 8 J.M.--Mr.. Dillon, before leaving Elmira, made a statement to a Press reporter, to Whom he is represented to have intimated that no matter how much love and abiding faith were still reposed in Mr. t erne!, Mr. Glaelistezm held the key to the Situation, and his wishes must, therefore, be respected. The conference at Cincinnati would probably result in a request to Mr. Parnell to resign. THE SPLIT IN THE IRISH PARTY. Up to yesterday afternoon no reply has been received at the Irish Parliamentary Offices at Westminster, from the American delegates, but a message was hourly ex- pected. Much activity prevails at the headquarters of the party, and telegraphic despatches are constantly being received. Since Thursday the strained relations between the two sections of Mr. Parnell's followers have become more marked. A special correspondent tele- graphs :—I am enabled to state on the best authority that the Irish party are almost unanimous in the demand that Mr. Parnell should immediately and finally retire. The opinion is confirmed most positively that what Mr. Parnell is now relying upon is his control over the funds of the National League and those of the Irish Parliamentary party, but it is understood that on this delicate point there is a sufficient majority of the unpaid amongst his late followers to disregard his mandate, and to be able to take an independent course. MR. PARNELL TO ISSUE A MANIFESTO. The London correspondent of the "Freeman's Journal." telegraphing yesterday morning, says : "Mr. Parnell requests me to state that he proposes to issue a manifesto to the Irish people to-night, and that he asks them to suspend their judgment on the situation until they have read it." SUPPORTING MR. GLADSTONE. The Liberal Council, representing the seven divisions of Glasgow and the Liberal Association of Glasgow, have adopted resolutions entirely supporting Mr. Gladstone in the political crisis. MESSAGE FROM Mr. O'BRIEN. A New York correspondent, telegraphing on Wednes- day night, says :—Mr. W. O'Brien has just sent a cablegram to the members of the Irish party in London. He says in this message that, in view of the Nationa- lists' obligation to Mr. Gladstone, of the interests of the cause, and of their responsibilities to the Irish tenantry on the faith of the next general election being fought in cord:al alliance with the Liberals, he earnestly recom- mends his party to open immediately friendly communi- cation with Mr. Gladstone. MR. DAVIT'. SPEAKS OUT. Mr. Michael Devitt, in an article in this week's "Labour We.td," says that the speeches delivered in Dublin, and the action of the Irish party in unanim- ously re-electing Mr. Parnell, have lost the Irish cause thousands of friends, who, it is to be feared, will not return. Mr. Parnell declined to yield to the prayers or requests, and we see the workings of hidden influences, which, if permitted free reign, will ruin for a genera- tion the chances of Home Rule for Ireland.
